digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-28
digests.theme:
Today's useful pattern is the coordinate system is part of the claim. A Top-k SAE is not interpretable merely because it has k active units; the unused activation tail and effective support still matter. A physical world model is not grounded merely because it predicts video; the state space should carry geometry and motion directly. An uncertainty score is not deployment-relevant merely because it is proper or calibrated; it needs to align with the decision utility it is supposed to serve.

I kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan deliberately covered interpretability, uncertainty evaluation, 3D/scientific world modeling, medical VLMs, neuro/cognitive modeling, generative media, continual learning, and robotics/VLA. Robotics/VLA had many fresh titles in the June 26 arXiv batch, including world-action and VLA safety work, but none beat the best non-robotics mechanisms today after the topic-balance guardrail.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv pages were reachable for the three preserved arXiv IDs, and I used them as a reachability supplement. Discovery therefore relied on arXiv recent category listings, arXiv abstract pages, downloaded arXiv PDFs, and one direct project page check for PhysiFormer. Discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

At 08:00 Pacific on Sunday, June 28, arXiv's visible recent AI/ML/CV/CL/RO/eess/q-bio lists were still anchored on the Friday, June 26 batch. I treated today's run as a second-pass scout over candidates not already preserved in the June 26 and June 27 digests. I inspected full PDFs, with targeted reads through methods, experiments, results, ablations, and limitations, for Beyond the Hard Budget, PhysiFormer, Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification, and TAVR-VLM. I also scanned title listings across the relevant lanes, including medical imaging, neuro/cognitive systems, 3D/video generation, robotics/VLA, uncertainty evaluation, interpretability, and scientific ML. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification is the most relevant paper today. It gives a decision-theoretic way to ask whether an uncertainty metric actually ranks models by downstream usefulness, then shows why many standard scores are misaligned or secretly encode strange priors.

PhysiFormer is the strongest world-model mechanism. It predicts full 3D mesh trajectories directly in world coordinates instead of doing view-bound video prediction or autoregressive coordinate rollout.

Beyond the Hard Budget is the strongest interpretability training detail. It shows Top-k SAEs still benefit from soft regularization when the pressure is applied to pre-selection activations and masked to batch-active units.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today all make the hidden coordinate system visible. Decision-Aligned UQ says an uncertainty metric is secretly a decision prior, so write that prior down or stop pretending the metric is deployment-neutral. PhysiFormer says physical prediction should happen in world-space geometry, not in pixels when mesh state is available. Beyond the Hard Budget says Top-k sparsity is only a hard cardinality rule; feature cleanliness still depends on how the unused activation tail is shaped. Same rule across levels: do not trust structure just because the paper named it; check whether the coordinates make the claimed behavior possible.
rankedTitles: Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification
PhysiFormer: Learning to Simulate Mechanics in World Space
Beyond the Hard Budget: Sparsity Regularizers for More Interpretable Top-k Sparse Autoencoders

Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers is the strongest scientific-ML mechanism. It argues that minimizing a PDE residual can be the wrong objective in ill-conditioned systems, then uses the residual field as input so the model can learn a correction policy.

Same rule across domains: preserve the structure of the error signal long enough for the model to use it.

digests.theme:

A factuality metric that collapses all retrieved evidence into one corpus misses the case where some sources support a claim and others contradict it. A model-diffing tool that reports reconstruction fidelity can miss the single feature that actually gates tool use.

I kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. Life After Benchmark Saturation is the most relevant paper today. It argues that benchmark usefulness does not end when accuracy saturates; the remaining signal lives in validity threats, efficiency, reliability, scaffold effects, out-of-distribution behavior, and real human-agent uplift.

ConflictScore is the strongest evidence-evaluation paper. It fixes a real blind spot in factuality metrics: a claim can be supported by some retrieved documents and contradicted by others, and a metric that collapses the corpus hides that conflict.

Localizing RL-Induced Tool Use to a Single Crosscoder Feature is the sharpest internal-mechanism paper. It finds that an RL-induced tool-use behavior in a Qwen2.5-3B pair can be strongly steered through a tiny A-exclusive crosscoder feature set, with one feature producing a large tool-correctness jump.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today all reject the easy aggregate. Life After Benchmark Saturation says saturated accuracy is not saturated evaluation. ConflictScore says a supported answer can still be misleading if it ignores contradictory retrieved evidence. Localizing RL-Induced Tool Use says reconstruction quality is not enough; the behavior may be controlled by a sparse feature hidden inside the representation. Same rule across levels: measure the thing that can fail, not the headline number that stays smooth while the failure moves underneath.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-24
digests.theme:
Today's useful pattern is the proxy only counts if it preserves the interface that later does work. ImageNet FID is not a sufficient proxy for text-to-image DiT progress. A volumetric Gaussian render is not the same thing as usable surface geometry. A file path is not the same thing as a diagnostic handoff to a code-repair agent.

I deliberately kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan covered generative-model evaluation, 3D scene generation, code-repair agents, medical robustness, agent training data, video evidence grounding, agent memory systems, continual learning, scientific/medical AI, and robotics/VLA candidates. The best robotics/VLA candidates were InSight, World Value Models, and RoBoSR, but none beat the strongest non-robotics papers on transferable mechanism today.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv pages were reachable for the serious arXiv IDs I checked, but I used them only as supplemental metadata reachability checks. Discovery therefore relied mainly on the arXiv API and direct arXiv PDFs; discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

At 08:00 Pacific on June 24, the arXiv API returned June 23 uploads as the newest batch in the checked AI, ML, CV, CL, IR, robotics, HCI, statistics, medical, signal-processing, and neuro/scientific lanes. Full PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text with targeted reads through method, experiments, ablations, results, and limitations for DiffusionBench, FLAT, SHERLOC, BenchX, OpenThoughts-Agent, GeoT2V-Bench, SER, DeepBD, Can Scale Save Us From Plasticity Loss in Large Language Models?, World Models in Pieces, Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System?, InSight, World Value Models, RoBoSR, and several adjacent candidates. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

DiffusionBench is the most relevant paper today. It makes a clean evaluation argument: if a DiT method claims broad generative progress, it should not get to hide behind class-conditional ImageNet FID after that proxy stops predicting text-to-image behavior.

FLAT is the strongest 3D/generative-media paper today. It decodes video-diffusion latents into explicit triangle splats, and its ablations show that geometry-friendly representation requires real parameterization work rather than a surface-shaped label.

SHERLOC is the strongest agent-engineering paper today. It treats code localization as a structured diagnostic object that has to improve a downstream repair agent, not just as a file-retrieval score.

Several runner-ups were useful but stayed below the note line. BenchX is a strong medical robustness benchmark: 85,355 CT scans, 12 tumor-detection models, and subgroup/protocol analysis that exposes failures hidden by average F1. I kept it as a runner-up because its main contribution is evaluation coverage rather than a reusable modeling primitive, but it is good deployment-pressure material. OpenThoughts-Agent is a serious open data-recipe report with more than 100 ablations and a 100K-example agentic SFT set; it is useful, but more training-data operations than mechanism. GeoT2V-Bench is a sharp reconstruction-based audit for camera-prompted text-to-video models, but DiffusionBench and FLAT covered the day's evaluation and 3D representation lanes more directly. SER has a good idea, semantic evidence rewards for video reasoning, but the gains are modest and the VLM-referee reward is a place to watch for reward hacking. DeepBD is an interesting grounded medical-agent workflow, but its strongest evidence is from an in-house cohort and needs external/prospective validation. Can Scale Save Us From Plasticity Loss in Large Language Models? is a useful continual-learning warning, but the model scale remains far below frontier LLMs and the probe design is narrow.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today all punish a bad substitute. DiffusionBench says ImageNet FID is not the same thing as text-to-image progress. FLAT says a Gaussian render is not the same thing as explicit scene geometry. SHERLOC says a file path is not the same thing as a repair-ready diagnosis. Different domains, same standard: do not flatten the thing that the next system actually needs.

digests.theme:
Today's useful pattern is state management should be keyed to structure, not surface thresholds. The strongest papers all reject a cheap proxy: token count is not a good trigger for agent memory compaction, a single evaluation-awareness score is not a safety claim, and a single document vector is too blunt for long-context retrieval.

I deliberately kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan covered agent memory, evaluation validity, long-context retrieval, enterprise-agent benchmarking, causal-discovery tooling, knowledge editing, medical representation learning, latent-group robustness, 3D / 4D generation, and VLA safety. Full PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text, especially methods, experiments, results, and limitations, for Self-Compacting Language Model Agents, Evaluation Awareness Is Not One Capability, Improving Long-Context Retrieval with Multi-Prefix Embedding, EnterpriseClawBench, Causal Discovery in the Era of Agents, Exposing the Illusion of Erasure in Knowledge Editing, Patient-Aware Contrastive Learning, Discovering Latent Groups for Robust Classification, Semantic Browsing, Lift4D, and LIBERO-Safety. Self-Compacting Language Model Agents is the most relevant paper today. It treats compaction timing as a trajectory-state decision rather than a token-budget reflex, using a rubric-gated summary tool that fires after closed reasoning units and suppresses compaction mid-derivation or while stuck.

Evaluation Awareness Is Not One Capability is the strongest evaluation and interpretability paper in the scan. Its useful move is to split evaluation awareness into behavioral detection, safety-framing sensitivity, latent representation, and causal controllability instead of pretending one awareness score carries deployment validity.

Improving Long-Context Retrieval with Multi-Prefix Embedding is the strongest retrieval/infrastructure paper today. It extracts multiple EOS prefix embeddings from one causal forward pass, giving long documents chunk-level matching and evidence localization without token-level late interaction or chunk-level labels.

Several runner-ups were useful but stayed below the note line. EnterpriseClawBench has good deployment-evaluation taste: it reports harness-model pairs, artifact quality, cost, runtime, and skill-transfer behavior, and its unreleased proprietary data makes the reusable contribution mostly protocol. Causal Discovery in the Era of Agents is aligned with the house standard that agents assist while formal algorithms discover, but it is closer to a design manifesto plus platform description than a preserved mechanism paper. Patient-Aware Contrastive Learning is a clean medical representation note candidate, especially for the same-patient/same-class positive construction, but it is single-dataset and narrower than the retrieval paper. Discovering Latent Groups for Robust Classification is good structural robustness work, but its worst-group gains are competitive rather than dominant and its assumptions around difficulty routing need care.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today all make the same demand in different systems: keep the unit of state visible. Self-Compacting Language Model Agents says the unit is a closed reasoning subtask, not a token count. Evaluation Awareness Is Not One Capability says the unit is a measured eval/deploy axis, not a single safety score. Improving Long-Context Retrieval with Multi-Prefix Embedding says the unit is a local evidence-bearing prefix, not the whole document squeezed into one vector. If the claim depends on state, do not flatten the state before evaluating it.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-22
digests.theme:
Today's useful pattern is do not average away the variable that carries the risk. The strongest papers I found all attack a different kind of hidden aggregation failure: an agent monitor that collapses uncertain predicates into local thresholds, a calibration theorem that previously needed prediction-time randomness, and a federated medical calibration protocol where pooled guarantees hide vulnerable hospitals.

I deliberately kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan covered agent verification, calibration theory, medical uncertainty, MLLM bias, continual adaptation, EEG foundation-model evaluation, Bayesian in-context learning, and navigation uncertainty. GroundControl was the best robotics/navigation candidate, but it did not beat the strongest non-robotics papers on mechanism or transfer value today.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv pages were reachable for the serious candidates and useful as metadata checks, but I did not find useful discussion or related-paper trails there. I used AlphaXiv only as a supplement, then relied on the arXiv API and direct arXiv PDFs for primary-source inspection. Discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

At 08:00 Pacific on June 22, the arXiv API still returned June 18 uploads as the newest entries in the checked AI, ML, CV, CL, statistics, medical, and robotics lanes; I did not find a fresh June 22 batch yet. I therefore treated today as a remaining-strong-paper scan rather than pretending there was a new Monday drop. Full PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text, especially method, results, and limitations, for Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents, Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction, When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital, StylisticBias, GroundControl, FlowEdit, Multi-Task Bayesian In-Context Learning, and Evaluation of EEG Foundation Models for Event-Based Burst-Suppression Detection in ICU. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents is the most relevant paper today. It treats agent monitoring as probabilistic inference over an execution trace instead of local thresholding of noisy predicates. The useful move is the distributionally robust bound: the monitor does not get to assume independence just because independence would make the action look safe.

Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction is the strongest theory paper in the scan. It resolves whether prediction-time randomization is statistically necessary for sample-optimal multicalibration and extends the same derandomization idea to outcome indistinguishability and omniprediction.

When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital is the strongest medical/healthcare paper today. It shows pooled federated conformal risk control can satisfy an average guarantee while failing 40 percent of hospitals in a real brain-tumor segmentation setting, then proposes a shrinkage risk-curve protocol that trades coverage and efficiency more sanely than local calibration.

Several runner-ups were useful but stayed below the note line. StylisticBias is a good MLLM bias benchmark: holding synthetic identity fixed while changing one visual cue reveals that roughly 15 appearance attributes account for nearly 80 percent of aggregate bias. I kept it as a runner-up because the setup is synthetic and the mechanism is more audit design than modeling primitive. GroundControl is a clean robotics/navigation uncertainty paper: distance-to-goal dynamics plus risk-coverage evaluation beats entropy-style uncertainty on EB-Navigation, but it stayed out of the top three under the topic-balance guardrail. FlowEdit has an attractive external-memory pronunciation adaptation mechanism for frozen TTS, but the paper is short and narrower than the preserved agent-verification and medical-calibration papers.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today all refuse an easy average. Efficient and Sound Probabilistic Verification for AI Agents keeps uncertain predicates alive until the whole agent trace can be bounded. Optimal Deterministic Multicalibration and Omniprediction removes prediction-time coins from calibration guarantees without losing the optimal sample rate. When Calibration Fails the Vulnerable Hospital keeps hospital identity visible instead of hiding failures inside a pooled guarantee. Different domains, same standard: if the risk lives in a dependency, a group, or a randomization channel, do not summarize it away before testing the claim.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-21
digests.theme:
Today's useful pattern is make the bottleneck carry evidence. The strongest papers I found are not just making latent or structured systems sound legible. They put pressure on the exact object that is supposed to carry the claim: a diffusion language model's inter-step bottleneck, a soft-routed MoE's aggregate confidence, or a 3D editor's source-to-target box specification.

I deliberately kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan covered interpretability, calibration under distribution shift, 3D/generative media, healthcare deployment, long-video temporal reasoning, Bayesian in-context learning, geometric representation learning, and skill/context compression. No robotics/VLA paper beat the best non-robotics alternatives today.

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable for individual paper pages and useful for metadata checks, but the pages I inspected exposed mostly abstracts, metrics, and empty comments/resources rather than useful discussion trails. I used AlphaXiv as a supplement, then relied on the arXiv API and direct arXiv PDFs for primary-source inspection. Discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

The arXiv API returned no new submissions in the checked cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CV, and stat.ML categories for June 19-21, so the strongest available set came from the June 18 uploads. I did not reuse yesterday's already-preserved top papers. Full PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the paper text, especially method, results, and limitations, for How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?, Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift, Thinking in Boxes, GEN-Guard, TimeProVe, SoftSkill, Multi-Task Bayesian In-Context Learning, and The Token Is a Group Element. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

How Transparent is DiffusionGemma? is the most relevant paper today. It turns the vague worry that text diffusion models may reason opaquely in latent space into a set of auditable measurements: opaque serial depth, bottleneck token ablations, monitorability, and case studies of non-autoregressive reasoning.

Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift is the strongest calibration paper in the scan. Its useful move is the distinction between hard-routing robustness and soft-routing fragility: calibrated experts do not guarantee calibrated aggregate probabilities once routing configurations get reweighted.

Thinking in Boxes is the best 3D/generative media paper today. It uses 3D boxes as an actual edit specification, not a decorative condition. The source and target boxes plus a depth-aligned floor give the generator a compact geometric contract for translation, rotation, scale, disocclusion, and camera change.

Several runner-ups were useful but stayed below the note line. GEN-Guard is a strong healthcare/deployment paper: client-blocked evaluation exposes model-selection failures in federated surgical AI, and disagreement-aware distillation gives a practical post-hoc correction. I kept it as a runner-up because the correction is more deployment hygiene than a broadly reusable modeling primitive. TimeProVe is a sensible propose-then-verify system for long ADL video QA, but it depends heavily on action detectors and heuristic evidence ranking. The Token Is a Group Element has a sharp geometric premise, but the empirical evidence is still toy sequence completion. SoftSkill is directly interesting for skill systems, but its strongest results are single-round QA; the paper itself admits long-horizon agentic compression is not robust yet.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today all refuse to let the hidden part stay hand-wavy. How Transparent is DiffusionGemma? asks whether a latent diffusion language model's inter-step state is readable enough to monitor. Toward Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Under Distribution Shift asks whether the routed aggregate remains calibrated when soft-routing configurations shift. Thinking in Boxes asks whether a 3D editor can be controlled by an explicit geometric specification instead of prompt vibes. Different domains, same standard: find the bottleneck, state what it must preserve, and test the claim at that bottleneck instead of admiring the system around it.

AlphaXiv was reachable for individual paper pages and useful for metadata/title checks, but the pages I inspected mostly exposed abstracts, metadata, and empty comments/resources rather than useful related-paper trails. I used AlphaXiv as a supplement, then relied on the arXiv API and direct arXiv PDFs for primary-source inspection. Discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

There was no fresh Saturday arXiv batch, so the strongest available set came from the June 18 uploads. I avoided simply reusing yesterday's already-preserved top papers. Full-text PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text, especially method, results, and limitations, for Sensorimotor World Models, DeepSWIP, Judging to Improve, Sparsity, Superposition, and Forgetting, Scalable Training of Spatially Grounded 2D VLMs for Radiology, Through the PRISM, UNIEGO, Marginal Advantage Accumulation, SurgVista, and Holo-World. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

Sensorimotor World Models: Perception for Action via Inverse Dynamics is the most relevant paper today. It adds a single inverse-dynamics head to a JEPA-style latent world model and lets action recoverability prevent collapse. The useful part is not just "inverse dynamics helps"; it is that the latent state is pushed toward controllable degrees of freedom and away from uncontrollable distractors.

DeepSWIP is the strongest neurosymbolic paper in the scan. It materializes fixed-context neural predicates into ordinary ProbLog choices, applies a single-world intervention program, and computes counterfactuals as a quotient of weighted model counts. The paper is unusually clear about the boundary: exact symbolic counterfactual inference is still only exact relative to the learned, calibrated neural probabilities.

Judging to Improve is the most useful evaluation/protocol paper today. Its headline result is negative: lightweight public-data adaptation of TRELLIS reaches parity with a strong base, not a win. The part worth preserving is the hardened VLM-as-3D-judge protocol: separate training and evaluation judge families, swap-consistency position-bias filtering, normal-map mesh montages, and clear-gap sanity checks.

Several runner-ups were useful but stayed below the note line. Sparsity, Superposition, and Forgetting gives a controlled toy-world diagnostic for continual learning; I liked the low-representation/high-overlap vulnerability story, but the paper is deliberately synthetic and should be treated as hypothesis generation. RadGrounder is a solid healthcare grounding paper with a 1.2M CT/MRI slice corpus and tokenized bounding-box grounding, but the labels are anatomical rather than pathology-level and come from one hospital. Through the PRISM is a good video-diffusion reward-modeling paper, using frozen diffusion-backbone intermediate states as noisy-latent preference features, but its claims are closer to reward-model engineering than a new general mechanism.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today all make a hidden layer accountable. Sensorimotor World Models asks latent state to recover the action that caused a transition. DeepSWIP turns neural predicate uncertainty into explicit probabilistic choices before doing counterfactual surgery. Judging to Improve refuses to optimize against a judge until the judge survives presentation, rendering, and clear-gap controls. Different domains, same standard: if a latent, symbol, or evaluator is carrying the claim, expose the exact job it must perform and test that job directly.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-19
digests.theme:
Today's useful pattern is state has to survive the moment it is not convenient. The best papers do not ask whether a model can emit plausible surface behavior. They ask whether the hidden state, task state, or evaluation state remains explicit enough to be checked when the easy observation disappears.

I kept robotics/VLA work as a lane rather than the center. The scan deliberately covered video world-model evaluation, tool-using agents, generative-model evaluation, diffusion-LM transparency, surgical/medical deployment, neurosymbolic counterfactuals, long-video temporal reasoning, spatial tool-use agents, skill mining, and physical-AI serving. No robotics/VLA paper landed in the top three today.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable for individual paper pages, but the fetched content was mostly title/navigation stubs rather than useful related-paper text. I used the arXiv API, arXiv new listings, individual AlphaXiv title checks, and direct arXiv PDFs for full-text inspection. Discovery may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

Full-text PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text, especially method, results, and limitations, for Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core, LedgerAgent: Structured State for Policy-Adherent Tool-Calling Agents, The FID Lottery, How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?, TimeProVe, GEN-Guard, DeepSWIP, MemoryWAM, S-Agent, SoftSkill, Automating SKILL.md Generation, and Execution-State Capsules. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core is the most relevant paper today. It turns "world model" into an intervention test: move the camera away, return, and ask whether the object state kept evolving while unobserved. Across 9,600 videos from 23 models, the answer is mostly no; visible quality and re-observation access do not imply re-observed state correctness.

LedgerAgent is the cleanest agent-systems mechanism. It stores successful read-tool returns in a typed ledger, renders that observed state back into the prompt, and checks environment-changing calls against executable policy predicates before they touch the external system. It is not glamorous, but it is exactly the kind of explicit state boundary tool agents usually fake.

The FID Lottery is the strongest evaluation paper today. It treats FID as a random variable over both training seeds and sampling seeds, then shows that retraining the same recipe moves FID much more than redrawing samples from one fixed model. The useful lesson is not just "report error bars"; it is that many single-seed generative-model gains sit below the evaluation noise floor.

Several other papers were worth reading but stayed below the preservation line. How Transparent is DiffusionGemma? is a strong foundation-model behavior audit: the token bottleneck between denoising steps appears much more interpretable than the worst-case latent-reasoning story, but algorithmic transparency remains hard because the model can revise the whole canvas non-chronologically. GEN-Guard is a useful surgical-AI deployment paper because it names "performance leakage" in federated model selection and tests a client-blocked detection/correction stack; I kept it below the top three because the mechanism is more specialized. TimeProVe is a good long-video evidence search system, reducing VLM calls and cost through propose-then-verify temporal grounding, but it is less conceptually sharp than LedgerAgent today. MemoryWAM was the best robotics/VLA candidate, with hybrid recent-frame, anchor-frame, and gist-token memory for long-horizon manipulation, but it did not beat the non-robotics top three on transfer value.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today all punish fake state. Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core asks whether a video model keeps an event endpoint alive when the camera is not watching. LedgerAgent asks whether a tool agent has a real observed-state object before it changes the world. The FID Lottery asks whether a generative-model claim survives the hidden state of training randomness. Different domains, same standard: if the state matters, isolate it, perturb observability, and make it carry the claim.
digests.mostRelevantPaper: Most relevant today: Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-18
digests.theme:
Today's useful pattern is mechanism claims should be executable, resampled, or intervened on. The strongest papers do not merely describe attention, consistency, or uncertainty. They turn those claims into something that can be substituted into a model, iteratively sampled as a structured state, or stress-tested by calibration rather than a flattering aggregate metric.

I deliberately kept robotics/VLA work as one lane rather than the center. The scan covered interpretability, structured inference, medical uncertainty and clinical decision support, 3D scene understanding, active multimodal perception, scientific ML for climate emulation, deepfake-detector evaluation, VLA knowledge retention, and user simulation.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable, and individual AlphaXiv pages opened, but fetchable content was mostly title/navigation stubs rather than useful related-paper text. I used arXiv new listings, the arXiv API, individual AlphaXiv title checks, and direct arXiv PDFs for full-text inspection. Discovery may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

Full-text PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text, especially method, results, and limitations, for Explaining Attention with Program Synthesis, Structured Inference with Large Language Gibbs, Confidence is Not Reliability: Rethinking MC Dropout in Brain Tumour Segmentation, Native Active Perception as Reasoning for Omni-Modal Understanding, OneCanvas, Language Models as Interfaces, Not Oracles, Does VLA Even Know the Basics?, Optimal scenario design for climate emulation, and When AUC Misleads. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

Explaining Attention with Program Synthesis is the most relevant paper today. It asks whether an attention-head explanation can be a runnable Python program, not a loose natural-language label. The important part is the causal check: high-fit programs can replace a meaningful fraction of real attention heads while preserving perplexity and downstream QA behavior.

Structured Inference with Large Language Gibbs is the cleanest mechanism paper. It treats an LLM's local conditionals as transition operators over a structured state, then uses Gibbs-style resampling to reduce fixed-order autoregressive bias. The result is a useful bridge between language-model priors and probabilistic state inference.

Confidence is Not Reliability is the strongest medical/evaluation paper today. It shows that high voxel-level uncertainty-error AUROC can coexist with clinically useless sub-region calibration. The paper's useful lesson is simple: a ranking metric can look excellent while the actual confidence signal is unsafe for a treatment-critical class.

Several other papers were worth reading but stayed below the preservation line. OneCanvas is a strong adjacent 3D representation paper: lift multi-view patch features into a shared equirectangular canvas with metric 3D position embeddings, then let a VLM read the result as one image. OmniAgent is a good active-perception systems paper, but it is more benchmark-and-training-stack heavy than today's top three. Language Models as Interfaces, Not Oracles has the right clinical deployment pattern: LLM for feature extraction and communication, XGBoost for risk prediction, plus deterministic plausibility checks; the caveat is that its note-like clinical narratives were synthesized from structured EHR variables, so real-note extraction robustness remains unproven. Act2Answer is the best robotics/VLA candidate, because it isolates whether VLA models can express retained commonsense knowledge through action, but it did not beat the non-robotics top three on transferable mechanism today.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today are about forcing representations to earn their names. Explaining Attention with Program Synthesis asks whether an explanation can run in the model. Large Language Gibbs asks whether structured LLM outputs should be resampled as a state rather than emitted once in a biased order. Confidence is Not Reliability asks whether an uncertainty metric remains meaningful in the clinically relevant slice, not merely on average. Same lesson, three domains: when a paper claims a mechanism, make the mechanism carry weight under intervention.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-17
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is aggregate success is not evidence of the right mechanism. The strongest papers ask whether a memory system used reachable evidence, whether a medical VLM used the image, and whether deception leaves a different internal state than ordinary wrongness. I deliberately kept robotics/VLA work as one lane rather than the center. The scan covered agent memory, clinical AI, interpretability, source/provenance verification, prompt-injection sanitization, agent-search scaling, VLM reliability, clinical speech, environment-model RL, code-reasoning diagnostics, 3D/CAD data, and a list-level robotics/VLA pass.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv's lightweight search route returned a 404 page again. Individual AlphaXiv paper pages were reachable for some candidates, but the fetchable text exposed only title/navigation stubs, so it was not useful for discovery or related-paper branching. I used arXiv new listings, the arXiv API, and direct arXiv PDFs for the serious candidates.

Full-text PDFs were available for the papers I considered preserving. I inspected the full text, especially method, results, and limitation sections, for MemTrace: Probing What Final Accuracy Misses in Long-Term Memory, Vision-language models for chest radiography do not always need the image, Rift: A Conflict Signature for Deception in Language Models, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents, PARSE, Beyond Parallel Sampling, Dissecting model behavior through agent trajectories, Visuals Lie, Consistency Speaks, SpeechDx, EnvRL, and From Brewing to Resolution. The robotics/VLA scan found several plausible candidates, including technical reports and VLA memory/control papers, but none beat the best non-robotics papers today on mechanism, evidence quality, and future usefulness.

MemTrace is the most relevant paper today. It changes the unit of long-term memory evaluation from independent QA rows to knowledge points: a single user fact probed across age, question type, and evidence condition. The important result is not merely that memory systems forget. It is that most hard failures are evidence-use failures after relevant evidence is already reachable.

Vision-language models for chest radiography do not always need the image is the strongest healthcare/evaluation paper in the scan. The paper builds an interventional audit using label-matched image swaps, radiologist-box target masks, and irrelevant masks to test whether a correct answer causally depends on the radiograph. The uncomfortable result is that a text-only model lands close to the best multimodal system, and several medical VLMs either ignore the image or use it only selectively.

Rift is the most provocative interpretability paper today, but I am keeping it below the two preserved notes because it needs replication and has a narrow experimental regime. The mechanism is interesting: residual rank rises during deceptive forward passes relative to both honest answers and naive wrong answers. The paper controls for wrongness and tests roleplay, strategic bluffing, concealment prompts, length, and cross-domain probes. That is worth attention. It is not yet a deployment-ready lie detector.

Several other papers were useful but stayed below the preservation line. ProvenanceGuard is highly aligned with MCP-style agents because it verifies not just whether a claim is supported somewhere, but whether it is attributed to the right tool/source. PARSE is a practical warning that prompt-injection defenses proven on synthetic tasks may collapse on real enterprise documents. DivInit is a clean agent-search trick: diversify first-turn queries before parallel rollouts instead of letting threads collapse onto the same retrieval path. Dissecting model behavior through agent trajectories is valuable as an agent-harness paper, but the paper is partly a systems report around one harness. SpeechDx is a strong benchmark contribution for clinical speech AI, but today's two preserved notes have sharper mechanism transfer.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today are all refusing a lazy metric. MemTrace says memory is not row-level accuracy; it is fact-level behavior across time, question type, and evidence condition. Chest radiography VLMs do not always need the image says medical VQA accuracy is not evidence of image use; grounding needs causal intervention. Rift says wrongness is not the same as deception; compare a model lying while knowing against a model that is merely wrong. The shared lesson is simple and useful: before trusting a success number, identify the mechanism that was supposed to produce it and test that mechanism directly.

Vision-language models for chest radiography do not always need the image

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-16
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is diagnostic interfaces beat aggregate success. The strongest papers do not merely report higher task scores. They expose where a model thinks it is on track, whether an answer is grounded in the supplied context, and where a scientific evidence pipeline loses eligible studies. I deliberately kept robotics/VLA work as one lane rather than the center. The scan looked first at interpretability, agent grounding, healthcare/evidence synthesis, search-agent security, KV-cache context management, generative world models, representation learning, and medical imaging, then used the robotics papers as comparison cases.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level, but the lightweight /search route returned a 404 page, so it was not useful for discovery today. I used the arXiv API plus direct arXiv PDFs. Full-text PDFs were available for the leading candidates. I inspected the method, result, and limitation sections for The Value Axis: Language Models Encode Whether They're on the Right Track, Context-Aware RL for Agentic and Multimodal LLMs, Benchmarking LLM Agents on Meta-Analysis Articles from Nature Portfolio, How Much Can We Trust LLM Search Agents?, and KVEraser. I did lighter full-text skims for DreamX-World 1.0, Selection Without Signal, Recovery Through Expression, T-Rex, and adjacent technical candidates including posterior-score inverse problems, urban inverse rendering, phase in neural representations, and non-contrast abdominal CT diagnosis.

The Value Axis is the most relevant paper today. It constructs a linear activation direction in Qwen3-8B from synthetic in-context RL conversations, then shows that the direction tracks and causally modulates confidence-like behavior across math, code, DPO word preferences, SFT domains, and evaluation-awareness settings. This should not be treated as a general truth detector: it is one model, one axis-construction recipe, and a set of selected validation domains. But it is exactly the right kind of interpretability object for cabbageland: an internal state variable that can be measured, steered, and audited against external behavior.

Context-Aware RL is the strongest training-method paper in the scan. The method adds a context-selection loss to GRPO: given a query, an answer, and two similar contexts, the policy is rewarded for identifying which context actually supports the answer. The important part is not the contrastive data by itself. The paper shows that supervised augmentation can collapse an agentic policy and outcome-only RL mostly fails to use the signal; the bounded auxiliary loss is what preserves the policy while improving grounding.

MetaSyn is the strongest healthcare/scientific-evidence evaluation paper today. It builds a benchmark from 442 Nature Portfolio meta-analyses, a PubMed-anchored corpus of 140,585 articles, 8,674 corpus-matched positives, hard negatives, and PI/ECO-structured inclusion criteria. The headline is sharp: retrieval can reach 90.9% Recall@200, but no end-to-end pipeline recovers more than 52.7% of included studies. The bottleneck is not "can it retrieve relevant papers?" but "can it screen topically similar distractors against protocol criteria?"

SearchGEO is a strong security/evaluation warning. It tests whether manipulated web evidence becomes user-facing endorsement in LLM search agents. The useful result is the source-diversity effect: distinct corroborating attacker pages move endorsement far more than repetition of one source. I did not preserve a detailed note because today's top two papers are more reusable as model-training and model-debugging mechanisms, but SearchGEO is worth revisiting for agent-search hardening.

KVEraser is a very relevant systems paper, but just below the preservation line today. It learns local KV-cache steering states to erase a harmful, stale, or retracted span without recomputing the entire suffix. The mechanism is attractive for long-running agents because "forget this tool observation" should be an actual cache edit, not a polite instruction appended after contamination. I did not write a note today because the two preserved papers were more central and the pipeline is already audio-heavy, but this one should stay in the follow-up queue.

The robotics lane had one genuinely strong candidate: T-Rex: Tactile-Reactive Dexterous Manipulation. It combines human egocentric pretraining, a 100-hour tactile-rich teleoperation dataset, a variable-rate Mixture-of-Transformers, and a temporal tactile VQ-VAE for high-frequency residual tactile refinement. On a robotics-only day it would likely deserve a note. Today it stays out of the top three because the non-robotics candidates are stronger for general mechanism transfer.
digests.takeaway: The best papers today are about making hidden interfaces visible. The Value Axis finds a candidate internal gauge for whether a model thinks its current trajectory will succeed. Context-Aware RL trains models to bind answers to the context that actually supports them. MetaSyn shows that scientific-agent pipelines fail at protocol screening even when retrieval is strong. The shared lesson is that end scores are too blunt: the useful object is the stage, span, head, cache state, or activation direction where the failure can actually be localized.
digests.mostRelevantPaper: Most relevant today: The Value Axis.
rankedTitles: The Value Axis: Language Models Encode Whether They're on the Right Track
Context-Aware RL for Agentic and Multimodal LLMs
Benchmarking LLM Agents on Meta-Analysis Articles from Nature Portfolio

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-15
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is failure localization needs explicit interfaces, not aggregate comfort metrics. There was no fresh Monday arXiv wave visible at the 08:00 Pacific scan time; the recent API/category surface was still dominated by the June 12 batch. I deliberately kept robotics out of the center today and inspected non-robotics lanes first: production agent reliability, VLM interpretability, medical hallucination diagnosis, self-improvement evaluation, diffusion language-model behavior, agent scaffolds, visual part representations, and generative-model memorization. When Errors Become Narratives is the strongest paper because it turns long-running LLM-agent failure into a mechanism taxonomy with real postmortems. Gaze Heads is the strongest mechanistic ML paper because it finds a small causal attention-head control surface for what a VLM describes. ClinHallu is the best healthcare/evaluation note because it asks where a medical MLLM hallucination enters the reasoning chain, not only whether the final answer is wrong.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level, but the lightweight fetched /search URL returned 404, so it was not useful for discovery. I used the arXiv API plus direct arXiv PDFs. Full arXiv PDFs were inspected for When Errors Become Narratives: A Longitudinal Taxonomy of Silent Failures in a Production LLM Agent Runtime, Gaze Heads: How VLMs Look at What They Describe, ClinHallu: A Benchmark for Diagnosing Stage-Wise Hallucinations in Medical MLLM Reasoning, When Good Verifiers Go Bad: Self-Improving VLMs Can Regress on New Tasks, Neither Parallel Nor Sequential: How DiffusionGemma Actually Commits Tokens, AgentSpec: Understanding Embodied Agent Scaffolds Through Controlled Composition, RATS! Patches Talk Through Registers, Local Coverage Governs Memorization in Diffusion Models, Memento: Reconstruct to Remember for Consistent Long Video Generation, A Low-Rank Subspace Analysis of LLM Interventions, and Compressed Computation is (probably) not Computation in Superposition. I preserved detailed notes for When Errors Become Narratives and Gaze Heads.

When Errors Become Narratives is the most relevant paper today. It is a single-system case study, so the frequencies should not be generalized casually, but the mechanism taxonomy is exactly the right object: environment quirks, design-assumption mismatches, swallowed/diluted errors, fail-plausible fabrication, and operational/forensic blind spots. The strongest idea is the trigger/amplifier/concealer decomposition. Fixing the trigger is usually cosmetic; the durable work is removing the amplifier and making the concealer impossible. The paper is unusually close to cabbageland's own agent-runtime concerns, but that is not why it wins. It wins because the observed failures are concrete, longitudinal, and architecturally reusable.

Gaze Heads is the cleanest mechanistic model paper in the scan. In Qwen3-VL-8B, fewer than 9% of attention heads track the image region currently being described, and forcing those heads to attend to a chosen region steers the VLM's answer toward that region at 83.1% accuracy on six-panel comics. The intervention also works dynamically mid-generation and transfers imperfectly to natural COCO images and several VLM families. The caveat is that the testbed is heavily shaped by comics and the mechanism is not universal: some frozen-encoder architectures show no comparable head set. Still, this is real causal interpretability, not merely heatmap poetry.

ClinHallu is the strongest medical/evaluation paper today. It builds 7,031 validated medical VQA instances with structured traces split into Visual Recognition, Knowledge Recall, and Reasoning Integration, then uses stage-replacement interventions to diagnose where hallucinations enter. That decomposition is more useful than a final-answer hallucination score because it says whether the model is seeing wrong, remembering wrong, or combining evidence badly. The limitation is that the benchmark leans on generated traces, LLM-as-judge filtering/evaluation, and VQA-style tasks, so it is a diagnostic testbed rather than clinical deployment evidence.

When Good Verifiers Go Bad is the best deployment warning. It shows verifier-driven self-DPO can silently regress VLM students on MMMU even while DPO loss decreases, and argues that task-rubric verifier accuracy should be measured before running the loop. The single-family Qwen ladder and small verifier scale limit the claim, but the warning is practical: a verifier is not a moral authority. If it is confidently wrong on the target task, preference optimization can amplify the wrong direction.

Neither Parallel Nor Sequential is a useful foundation-model behavior audit. By hooking DiffusionGemma's own commit mechanism, it finds partial, granularity-dependent left-to-right token commitment rather than clean parallel or block-autoregressive decoding. The paper's most portable contribution is methodological: commit-order studies need to handle EOS padding artifacts, same-call ties, non-monotonic commits, pooling traps, and block-size sensitivity.

AgentSpec is aligned but broader and less decisive. It treats embodied LLM agents as typed compositions of perception, memory, reasoning, reflection, action, and learning modules, then compares scaffold combinations across interactive benchmarks. The useful lesson is that scaffold compatibility matters: memory helps only when matched to the reasoner and task, and policy optimization should train against the scaffold expected at deployment. I did not preserve it today because it is more framework-plus-sweep than sharp mechanism.

RATS and Local Coverage Governs Memorization are strong adjacent representation papers. RATS turns register tokens into a bottleneck that surfaces unsupervised part-level visual structure under a DINO objective. Local Coverage reframes diffusion memorization as a local data-coverage phenomenon rather than a global model property. Both are useful, but today's preserved notes are more directly actionable for agent reliability and multimodal control.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is When Errors Become Narratives because it treats production agent failures as mechanism classes, not embarrassing one-offs. Gaze Heads is the mechanistic ML note to keep because it finds a small causal control surface for VLM grounding. ClinHallu is the healthcare/evaluation reminder that hallucination diagnosis needs stage-local interventions, not just final-answer scoring. The common thread is diagnostic resolution: systems get better when they expose where the failure entered, how it propagated, and which interface can actually be repaired.
digests.mostRelevantPaper: Most relevant today: When Errors Become Narratives.
rankedTitles: When Errors Become Narratives: A Longitudinal Taxonomy of Silent Failures in a Production LLM Agent Runtime
Gaze Heads: How VLMs Look at What They Describe
ClinHallu: A Benchmark for Diagnosing Stage-Wise Hallucinations in Medical MLLM Reasoning

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-14
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is small interfaces beat decorative generality when they are tested honestly. There is no fresh Sunday arXiv batch in the scoped categories, so today's scan revisited the current June 10-11 arXiv robotics/CV/AI/CL batch and avoided papers already preserved in the June 12-13 digests. muVLA is the strongest paper because it isolates recurrence itself inside a pretrained VLA and shows exactly where minimal latent memory helps and where it fails. Sparse2Act is the strongest representation note because it uses task-space robot actions as supervision for sparse 3D features, rather than hoping reconstruction or downstream behavior cloning will discover control relevance. DIRECT is the best adjacent systems note: test-time compute should be routed by task demand, not paid uniformly as a tax.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level, but the lightweight fetched /search URL returned 404 again, so it was not useful for discovery. The arXiv API submittedDate:[202606120000 TO 202606142359] query over relevant categories returned zero entries even though the arXiv recent category pages listed the Friday June 12 batch, so today's discovery used arXiv recent category pages plus direct arXiv pages and PDFs. I inspected full arXiv PDFs for muVLA: On Recurrent Memory for Partially Observable Manipulation in VLA Models, Improving Robotic Generalist Policies via Flow Reversal Steering, Sparse2Act: Learning Action-Aligned Sparse 3D Representations for Cross-Domain Robot Manipulation, Mana: Dexterous Manipulation of Articulated Tools, DIRECT: When and Where Should You Allocate Test-Time Compute in Embodied Planners?, SERF: Spatiotemporal Environment and Robot Feature Map for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation, and MCR-Bionic Hand: Anatomical Structural Priors for Dexterous Manipulation. muVLA and Sparse2Act are preserved today.

muVLA is the strongest direct hit. It adds a small bank of recurrent memory tokens to OpenVLA-OFT and deliberately avoids retrieval modules, compression heads, hierarchical memory, and auxiliary objectives. The payoff is a cleaner measurement: minimal recurrence lifts partially observable MIKASA-Robo training tasks sharply, transfers modestly to held-out tasks with matching memory semantics, and mostly fails when the memory semantics change. That limit is the value. The paper gives future VLA memory work a baseline and a warning: if a fancier memory system cannot beat tiny recurrent tokens under the same cadence and latency budget, it is probably ornament.

Sparse2Act is the best representation paper today. It pretrains sparse point-cloud encoders by masking 3D tokens and predicting one-step task-space end-effector actions, then transfers only the encoder initialization into downstream policies. The ablations are the useful part: action-only and reconstruction-only help, but masked action alignment helps far more, and the gain persists with simplified downstream decoders. The design lesson is portable: use robot action to organize geometry around control, then let the downstream policy choose its own action parameterization.

DIRECT is adjacent but practically important. It treats the high-level embodied planner as a routed variable across reasoning depth, model size, and memory history. The paper's best claim is not "bigger reasoning helps"; it is the opposite: compute axes help on different task types and can hurt or waste latency elsewhere. A lightweight multimodal router recovers much of the expensive planner's success at lower cost in simulation and Franka DROID experiments. This is more systems and deployment than core representation, so I did not preserve a separate note today, but the framing is worth stealing.

Flow Reversal Steering is good policy-improvement material. It reverses a flow-matching VLA from coarse reference actions into latent noise, then denoises back into in-distribution actions that follow the rough semantic direction. It is especially useful for turning human or VLM guidance into noise-space BC or RL warm starts. I am not preserving it today because it is a steering wrapper over a behavioral prior rather than a stronger state, memory, or representation interface.

SERF is a strong explicit-memory mobile-manipulation paper, but with simulation caveats. It builds a spatiotemporal feature map of environment and robot neural points, updates environment points by object-level SE(3) tracking and robot points by forward kinematics, then conditions a VLA on map tokens. The idea is aligned with cabbageland: persistent spatial memory should be an input, not hidden in image history. The limitation is also clear: prior map features, privileged simulator instance labels, rigid-object updates, and no real-world mobile-manipulation validation yet.

Mana and MCR-Bionic Hand are useful physical-structure papers. Mana turns articulated tool manipulation into an animation-like data pipeline: human marks functional affordances, the system samples grasp keyframes, plans geometric phases, and uses RL only for short contact-rich transitions before training a point-cloud diffusion policy for zero-shot sim-to-real. MCR-Bionic is more hardware/anatomy than learning: it argues that wrist-finger tenodesis, extensor hoods, and intrinsic pathways are physical computation, not mere biomimetic decoration. Both are adjacent inspiration for "structure does work," but neither displaces today's two preserved representation/memory papers.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is muVLA because it gives VLA memory a controlled lower bound: tiny recurrent tokens can be powerful, but they do not magically generalize to new memory semantics. Sparse2Act is the representation note to keep because it uses robot action to shape sparse 3D geometry around control before downstream policy training. DIRECT is the adjacent systems lesson: expensive reasoning, bigger planners, and longer memory should be routed by task demand. The common thread is that useful long-horizon systems need small explicit interfaces with honest budgets, not bigger hidden mush.
rankedTitles: muVLA: On Recurrent Memory for Partially Observable Manipulation in VLA Models
Sparse2Act: Learning Action-Aligned Sparse 3D Representations for Cross-Domain Robot Manipulation
DIRECT: When and Where Should You Allocate Test-Time Compute in Embodied Planners?

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-13
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is trust and memory need explicit budgets. There does not appear to be a fresh Saturday arXiv batch in the scoped robotics/CV/AI categories, so today's scan widened across the current week and avoided papers already preserved in the June 10-12 digests. Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon is the strongest paper because it turns world-model trust into a predictable-horizon certificate rather than an average rollout score. Action-Effect Memory Pretraining is the best practical robotics note because it learns a compact action-conditioned history state before policy training. Learning What to Remember is adjacent but useful: it makes the forgetting decision blind to future queries and learns a multi-factor value for retention rather than leaning on recency or query similarity.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level. The arXiv API query for submittedDate:[202606120000 TO 202606132359] over the relevant AI/CV/robotics categories returned no entries, so discovery quality today is a current-week fallback rather than a true new-Saturday batch. I used arXiv API search plus direct arXiv PDFs, and inspected extracted full PDFs for Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon: Certified Predictability for Equivariant World Models, Learning What to Remember: A Cognitively Grounded Multi-Factor Value Model for Agentic Memory, Bounding Boxes as Goals: Language-Conditioned Grasping via Neuro-Symbolic Planning, Action-Effect Memory Pretraining for Robot Manipulation, ProPlay: Procedural World Models for Self-Evolving LLM Agents, TetherCache: Stabilizing Autoregressive Long-Form Video Generation with Gated Recall and Trusted Alignment, and MoVerse: Real-Time Video World Modeling with Panoramic Gaussian Scaffold. Scale Buys and AEM are preserved today.

Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon is the strongest direct hit. The paper argues that an equivariant latent world model can certify how far a rollout remains trustworthy: exact equivariance makes rollout error constant over symmetry orbits, while approximate equivariance yields a finite per-channel horizon controlled by the latent predictor's Lyapunov spectrum. The best idea is the distinction between a universal audit and an a-priori guarantee. Any smooth latent loop can be spectrally audited, but exact structure is what makes the number trustworthy without a held-out divergence check. I did not independently verify the proofs, so the note preserves the framing and caveats rather than treating the theorem stack as settled law.

Action-Effect Memory Pretraining for Robot Manipulation is the best robot-memory note. AEM interleaves visual and action tokens, masks aligned action-effect timesteps, and trains a Mamba encoder to compress history into the encoded final vision token. That one vector is then concatenated with current perception inside Diffusion Policy or ManiFlow. The results are useful because the paper compares against no-history policies, direct DINOv2 feature stacking, randomized scenes, and memory-dependent tasks. The caveat is that the real-world result prose has inconsistent averages, so I trust the direction more than every exact margin.

Learning What to Remember is adjacent inspiration for long-running agents. Its useful point is methodological: if a retention policy scores memory relevance against the held-out future question, it is measuring retrieval with an oracle, not forgetting. In the blind consolidation regime, a learned multi-factor value over reliability, emotion, self/user relevance, and goal/session relevance beats recency and single-factor policies on LongMemEval gold-evidence retention. I am not preserving a separate note today because the evaluation is still retention-only, three of the seven factors are inert in the API-free setup, and final QA/task return is left for follow-up. Still, the oracle-vs-blind distinction is worth remembering.

MoVerse is the strongest 3D adjacent paper. It turns a single narrow-FOV image into a gravity-aligned panorama, lifts it into a persistent panoramic 3D Gaussian scaffold, and uses a distilled causal video renderer for interactive roaming. The representation lesson is excellent: keep long-range spatial memory in explicit geometry and let the video model repair local rendering quality. I am not preserving it today only because the paper is mostly a large staged system with qualitative-heavy evidence, while today's two kept papers are sharper for trust and robot-memory interfaces.

TetherCache is useful citation material for long-form video/world-model memory. Its sink/memory/recent cache split, attention-diversity recall, and trusted statistic alignment are sensible for drift-resistant autoregressive video. It is less central to cabbageland today because the mechanism is cache management for generation rather than embodied state or planning.

ProPlay is useful agent-memory/planning material. It builds a procedure graph with reliability records, preplays likely procedural trajectories, and updates the graph after environment feedback. The idea is aligned with procedural world models for LLM agents, but the abstraction remains natural-language procedural guidance over public text/game benchmarks, not a stronger direct hit than today's preserved papers.

Bounding Boxes as Goals is mostly citation material. It compiles language into bounding-box goal states and uses GroundingDINO plus closed-loop proportional control. The explicit goal-state interface is nice, but the evaluated robot task is still mostly grasp-and-lift; full end-to-end sorting and goal-similarity verification are left to future work.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon because it gives world-model trust a shape: a per-situation horizon that structure can certify and generic latents must cross-check. Action-Effect Memory Pretraining is the robot-memory note to keep because it compresses vision-action history into a small pretrained state that downstream policies can actually use. Learning What to Remember is the agent-memory warning label: do not evaluate forgetting with future-query information. The common lesson is that long-horizon systems need explicit budget interfaces, whether the budget is rollout trust, history length, or memory survival.
digests.mostRelevantPaper: Most relevant today: Scale Buys Interpolation, Structure Buys a Horizon.

Action-Effect Memory Pretraining for Robot Manipulation
