digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-12
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is world models are being judged by the interfaces they expose to control, not by rollout aesthetics alone. WEAVER is the strongest paper because it treats a robotic world model as a learned simulator that must support policy evaluation, synthetic policy improvement, and test-time planning under latency constraints. MaskWAM is the cleanest object-centric WAM paper: masks are both a future prediction target and an optional first-frame spatial prompt, so the model predicts what matters, not only what happens. EA-WM is the predicate-level companion: it adds event prediction and verification on top of feature-space rollouts so a planner can score imagined futures by task progress rather than feature distance alone.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level, but the lightweight fetched /search URL returned 404, so it was not useful for discovery today. Discovery and inspection for this run used the arXiv API over the June 11, 2026 batch plus direct arXiv PDFs. I inspected full arXiv PDFs for WEAVER, Better, Faster, Longer: An Effective World Model for Robotic Manipulation, RepWAM: World Action Modeling with Representation Visual-Action Tokenizers, MaskWAM: Unifying Mask Prompting and Prediction for World-Action Models, EA-WM: Event-Aware World Models with Task-Specification Grounding for Long-Horizon Manipulation, NavWAM: A Navigation World Action Model for Goal-Conditioned Visual Navigation, World Tracing: Generative Pixel-Aligned Geometry Beyond the Visible, SpatialClaw: Rethinking Action Interface for Agentic Spatial Reasoning, SPARC: Reliable Spatial Annotations from Robot Demonstrations at Scale, VISA: VLM-Guided Instance Semantic Auditing for 3D Occupancy World Models, Real-Time Execution with Autoregressive Policies, See Selectively, Act Adaptively, and LabVLA / RoboGenesis. WEAVER, MaskWAM, and EA-WM are preserved today.

WEAVER is the best direct hit. Its central claim is practical and useful: a manipulation world model should jointly satisfy fidelity, temporal consistency, and inference speed because the downstream uses are policy evaluation, policy improvement, and online planning. The architecture combines multi-view visual latents, proprioception prediction, sparse long-term memory, short-term history, flow-matched latent dynamics, diffusion-forcing style noise, accelerated denoising, and latent reward/critic heads. The paper is strongest where it connects the world model to decisions: predicted rollouts correlate with real success after finetuning, synthetic segments improve a pi0.5 policy without extra real interaction, and latent best-of-4 steering improves test-time task success.

MaskWAM is the strongest object-centric WAM interface paper. It treats masks as first-class latent streams, jointly predicting future RGB, future masks, and action chunks. That makes target regions explicit during training and enables a deployment-time mask prompt for language-ambiguous manipulation. The best result is not the tiny LIBERO gain over other strong baselines; it is the ablation showing that a mask prompt without future-mask prediction collapses in ambiguous tasks, while joint mask prediction plus prompting stays robust across distractors, novel instances, and lighting shifts.

EA-WM is worth preserving with caveats. The mechanism is exactly aligned with explicit-state taste: roll out candidate actions in frozen visual-feature space, decode task-grounded event predicates, and score futures with task, semantic, physical, and uncertainty terms before CEM or hybrid selection. The red flag is that event supervision is simulator-derived, LIBERO online evaluation is short-window rather than full autonomous episodes, and Goal10 gains are modest. Still, the design pattern is useful: visual-feature closeness is not the same as event progress.

RepWAM is directly relevant but not preserved as a separate note today. It trains a representation visual-action tokenizer aligned to a visual foundation model, then learns latent actions as transitions inside that semantic visual space. The ablations are useful, especially the two-stage latent-action training result, but the paper overlaps with the last few days of WAM interface/alignment papers and is less sharply explicit than MaskWAM or EA-WM.

NavWAM is strong adjacent direct work for navigation. It represents current state, goal image, future observations, action chunk, future state, and goal-progress value as a shared latent canvas inside a Cosmos Predict2-style video model. It beats CEM-style navigation world-model baselines and reports 19/24 real-world image-goal navigation successes. I am not preserving it today because the strongest cabbageland thread is manipulation/world-action interfaces, but NavWAM is good citation material for "future prediction is useful when trained with action and value targets."

World Tracing is the best 3D/geometry paper in the batch. It predicts layered pixel-aligned 3D point stacks, where layer 0 is the visible surface and deeper layers complete occluded intersections along each input ray. This is a serious representation paper, especially for input-faithful hidden geometry, but it is adjacent to today's robotics-control thread rather than the main preserved story.

SpatialClaw, SPARC, and VISA are useful citation material. SpatialClaw argues that code in a persistent kernel is a better spatial-reasoning action interface than single-pass code or fixed tool calls. SPARC scores robot-demo annotations by phase-aware object motion, 3D gripper proximity, and robot-overlap filtering. VISA converts offline VLM object audits into voxel-grounded semantic supervision for 3D occupancy world models. All three are useful, but none displace today's WAM/control-interface papers.

Real-Time Execution with Autoregressive Policies, See Selectively, Act Adaptively, and LabVLA / RoboGenesis are mostly baseline/framing material for deployment, bimanual routing, and synthetic lab robotics data. The ideas are useful, but they are less central than today's top three.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is WEAVER because it asks whether a world model can do real policy work: evaluate trajectories, generate useful synthetic improvement data, and steer actions online quickly enough to matter. MaskWAM is the clean object-centric complement, showing that predicting and prompting masks gives the action head a target-specific interface instead of a generic RGB future. EA-WM is the event-level complement, using predicted predicates and verifier scores to judge whether imagined futures make task progress. The common lesson is blunt: world models become useful when their hidden state is exposed as the right control object, whether that object is a value-scored latent rollout, a future target mask, or a task-event scorecard.
rankedTitles: WEAVER, Better, Faster, Longer: An Effective World Model for Robotic Manipulation
MaskWAM: Unifying Mask Prompting and Prediction for World-Action Models
EA-WM: Event-Aware World Models with Task-Specification Grounding for Long-Horizon Manipulation

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-11
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is the world-action interface is becoming the actual research object. Making Foresight Actionable is the strongest paper because it does not accept "the world model made a plausible video" as evidence that the action head can use the representation. It probes where action attention and causal sensitivity land, then regularizes WAM hidden states toward spatially coherent DINOv2 features so the action decoder reads task-relevant interaction regions. World Pilot is the complementary integration recipe: route a WAM's scene-evolution latent into VLA hidden states and its anticipated trajectory into the action generator as a soft prior. DAM-VLA is the sensor-time version of the same idea: stop forcing vision, language, force, proprioception, and action onto one synchronous clock, and let each modality keep its own buffer and update rhythm.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the site level. Discovery and inspection for this run used arXiv API search over the June 8-10, 2026 batch plus direct arXiv PDFs. I inspected full arXiv PDFs for Making Foresight Actionable: Repurposing Representation Alignment in World Action Models, World Pilot: Steering Vision-Language-Action Models with World-Action Priors, DAM-VLA: Decoupled Asynchronous Multimodal Vision Language Action model, PLUME: Probabilistic Latent Unified World Modeling and Parameter Estimation for Multi-Finger Manipulation, DIRECT: When and Where Should You Allocate Test-Time Compute in Embodied Planners?, Slots, Transitions, Loops: Learning Composable World Models for ARC, World Model Self-Distillation: Training World Models to Solve General Tasks, VICX: Generalizable Robot Manipulation via Video Generation and In-Context Operator Network, VLGA: Vision-Language-Geometry-Action Models for Autonomous Driving, ATM: Action-Consistency Transfer Matrix for Diagnosing and Improving Latent World Models, Plan-and-Verify Video Reward Reasoning with Spatio-Temporal Scene Graph Grounding, ISAP-3D: Identity-Slot Aligned Part-Aware 3D Generation, and CP4D: Compositional Physics-aware 4D Scene Generation. AGRA, World Pilot, and DAM-VLA are preserved today.

Making Foresight Actionable is the strongest direct hit. The paper diagnoses a concrete failure mode in world-action models: a WAM can generate a plausible future while the action decoder attends to background, static hands, or other task-irrelevant regions. AGRA adds an auxiliary alignment loss between selected video-diffusion hidden states and DINOv2 patch features, which makes the feature field more spatially coherent and action-readable. The paper's best contribution is not the headline success number; it is the attention plus causal-intervention audit that turns "world model features" into something testable.

World Pilot is the best companion integration paper. It keeps the WAM frozen and injects two priors into a VLA: Latent Steering routes the scene-evolution latent through residual cross-attention into VLM hidden states, while Action Steering compresses the WAM's anticipated trajectory into a single prefix token for the flow-matching action generator. The ablations are useful: latent injection beats decoded future images, a single trajectory token beats per-step or raw trajectory conditioning, and even a scene-prediction-only Cosmos model helps before action post-training.

DAM-VLA is the strongest asynchronous multimodal VLA paper. Its argument is clean: a synchronous VLA oversamples slow vision and language, undersamples fast contact signals, and gates action generation on a complete observation bundle. DAM-VLA keeps per-modality latent buffers, refreshes them at their sensor rates, and lets the action head read them continuously through gated cross-attention. The real-robot evidence is small but sharp: seven contact-rich tasks, 15 trials each, and a large gap between the full model and synchronous or concatenation baselines.

PLUME is strong adjacent inspiration and may deserve a later dedicated note. It learns a latent belief over physical parameters and rewards, updates that belief online with a flow-matching world model, and plans with likelihood-penalized rollouts. The hardware screwdriver result is especially relevant for explicit physical state. I am not preserving it today because the top three form a tighter VLA/WAM interface story, not because PLUME is weak.

DIRECT is strong systems framing for embodied planner deployment. The key point is that test-time compute has different capability profiles depending on whether it is reasoning depth, model size, or memory history. The router is useful, but it is more about compute allocation for high-level planners than about state/action representation.

Loop-OWM is useful compositional-reasoning inspiration. It frames ARC as object-centric transition learning over structured visual-symbolic states. I am not promoting it above today's robotics papers because the internal recurrent steps are not yet semantically stable, and the result is more a controlled reasoning lens than an embodied mechanism.

World Model Self-Distillation, VICX, VLGA, ATM, SG-PVR, ISAP-3D, and CP4D are all citation material for narrower purposes: data-free video-world-model task transfer, video-plan-to-trajectory grounding, dense driving geometry supervision, latent-world-model diagnostics, structured video reward reasoning, identity-slot 3D parts, and physics-aware 4D composition. None displaced the three preserved notes today.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is Making Foresight Actionable because it makes the world-action interface inspectable: a useful future representation should focus the action head on interaction regions and be causally robust to irrelevant background changes. World Pilot is the matching integration recipe, routing WAM latents and trajectory priors into different parts of a VLA. DAM-VLA generalizes the same taste to multimodal timing, with per-modality buffers and gated updates instead of synchronous token mush. The common lesson is blunt: a "world model" only matters when its hidden state reaches the control computation in the right form, at the right layer, and at the right time.
digests.mostRelevantPaper: Most relevant today: Making Foresight Actionable.

World Pilot: Steering Vision-Language-Action Models with World-Action Priors
DAM-VLA: Decoupled Asynchronous Multimodal Vision Language Action model

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-10
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is predictive structure is being pushed closer to the hidden state that actually matters for action. Next Forcing is the strongest paper because it changes the training target for autoregressive video world models: instead of denoising only the current chunk, it asks lightweight auxiliary heads to predict multiple future chunks and backpropagate longer-range temporal pressure into the main model. TacForeSight is the strongest contact-world-model paper because it uses force/torque as a leading signal to forecast tactile latent dynamics before local contact changes fully appear. LIBERO-Occ is the best VLA robustness paper because it turns occlusion into a controlled partial-observability benchmark, then tests whether generated complementary views can recover task-relevant evidence.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider brave / missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv was reachable at the site level, but discovery and inspection for this run used arXiv API search over the June 9, 2026 batch plus direct arXiv PDFs. I inspected full arXiv PDFs for Next Forcing: Causal World Modeling with Multi-Chunk Prediction, TacForeSight: Force-Guided Tactile World Model for Contact-Rich Manipulation, LIBERO-Occ: Evaluating and Improving Vision-Language-Action Models under Scene-Induced Occlusion via Viewpoint Imagination, MV-Actor: Aligning Multi-View Semantics and Spatial Awareness for Bimanual Manipulation, IMPACT: Learning Internal-Model Predictive Control for Forceful Robotic Manipulation, WorldOlympiad: Can Your World Model Survive a Triathlon?, P3D-Bench: Benchmarking MLLMs for Parametric 3D Generation and Structural Reasoning, and Bridging Semantics and Physical Execution: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Multi-Pair Robotic Assembly. Next Forcing, TacForeSight, and LIBERO-Occ are preserved today.

Next Forcing is the strongest direct hit. Its claim is simple and useful: teacher-forced next-chunk denoising lets high-frame-rate video world models lean on appearance copying, so the model needs a denser target that makes dynamics unavoidable. The method adds multi-chunk prediction modules for next1, next2, and next3 chunks, chains them causally, fuses intermediate main-model layers, and optionally keeps the depth-1 module at inference to generate the next video chunk in parallel. The results are strong on RoboTwin, PhyWorld, and a general video pretraining setting, though the training scale and proprietary data mean I trust the mechanism more than any single headline number.

TacForeSight is the best contact-rich manipulation note. It treats wrist force/torque as a high-frequency global cue that can precede local tactile deformation, then predicts future tactile latents and feeds them into a flow-based policy through current-future tactile cross-attention and adaptive visuo-tactile gating. The real-robot results are much stronger than the baselines across five contact tasks and three perturbation settings. The caveat is that the system assumes force and tactile hardware, and the evaluation is specialized, but the mechanism is exactly the kind of explicit physical foresight worth remembering.

LIBERO-Occ is the strongest VLA evaluation/framing note. The benchmark physically instantiates occluders in LIBERO scenes, verifies visibility/validity/executability, and separates manipulated-object, receptacle, and dual occlusion. The main empirical point is blunt: models that look strong on standard LIBERO collapse under scene-induced occlusion. VIM then imagines a complementary viewpoint from the occluded primary view and conditions action prediction on both observed and generated evidence. It improves substantially, but the paper is honest that this is a simulation benchmark and generated views remain bounded by learned priors.

IMPACT is strong adjacent inspiration and may deserve a later control note. It decouples high-level diffusion-policy planning from low-level force compensation by learning an online internal model from joint torque residuals, then applying feedforward wrench compensation. It is not a VLA/world-model paper in the narrow sense, but it is a very clean example of putting hidden physical state into a control interface instead of expecting imitation learning to absorb payload dynamics implicitly.

MV-Actor is useful citation material for multi-view bimanual perception. It aligns semantic tokens across physically corresponding camera regions, injects feed-forward reconstruction features for spatial awareness, and repairs noisy depth. I am not preserving it as a top note because it is mostly a perception-front-end improvement, while today's stronger thread is predictive hidden-state completion for action.

WorldOlympiad and P3D-Bench are good benchmark papers, not today's core preserved mechanisms. WorldOlympiad is useful for evaluating whether video world models preserve physics, 3D consistency, and interaction state. P3D-Bench is useful for checking whether code-generating MLLMs recover parametric 3D structure rather than merely producing plausible shapes. Both may be worth citing when framing evaluation, but they do not change the architecture/control story as directly as today's top three.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is Next Forcing because it changes what a causal video world model is forced to learn: multi-horizon dynamics rather than local chunk copying. TacForeSight is the tactile/contact note to remember because it predicts future tactile latents from force/torque, giving the policy physical foresight instead of reactive fusion. LIBERO-Occ is the VLA robustness note because it turns occlusion into a real partial-observability test and uses imagined complementary views as inspectable missing evidence. The common lesson is that hidden state should not be left as a hope inside a giant latent. Make the missing future, contact, or view into an explicit interface.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-09
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is world models are becoming structured memory and action interfaces, not just future-frame generators. MemoryVLA++ is the most relevant paper because it gives a VLA an explicit past-present-future temporal interface: perceptual/cognitive memory for past context, current working tokens, and latent future imagination for action prediction. iMaC is the sharpest action-conditioning paper because it turns robot actions into rendered motion images and two contact-distance image streams instead of asking a video model to infer contact from a compact vector. Latent Spatial Memory / Mirage is the best video-world-model memory paper because it stores a 3D cache directly in diffusion latent space, avoiding the expensive RGB point-cloud render-and-reencode loop.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv pages for the main candidates returned HTTP 403 in this environment. Discovery therefore used arXiv API search over the June 8, 2026 batch plus direct arXiv PDFs. I inspected full PDFs for MemoryVLA++: Temporal Modeling via Memory and Imagination in Vision-Language-Action Models, Latent Spatial Memory for Video World Models, iMaC: Translating Actions into Motion and Contact Images for Embodied World Models, Echo-Memory: A Controlled Study of Memory in Action World Models, AHA-WAM: Asynchronous Horizon-Adaptive World-Action Modeling with Observation-Guided Context Routing, omega-EVA: Envision, Verify, and Act with Latent Interactive World Models, Prisma-World: Camera-Controllable Multi-Agent Video World Model, MotionWAM: Towards Foundation World Action Models for Real-Time Humanoid Loco-Manipulation, FF-JEPA: Long-Horizon Planning in World Models with Latent Planners, and Your Model Already Knows: Attention-Guided Safety Filter for Vision-Language-Action Models. MemoryVLA++, iMaC, and Latent Spatial Memory are preserved today.

MemoryVLA++ is the strongest direct hit. It builds a full temporal VLA interface: current RGB and language become perceptual and cognitive working-memory tokens; a Perceptual-Cognitive Memory Bank stores low-level details and high-level semantics from past interaction; a manipulation-adapted video world model provides compact latent future imagination; and a diffusion action expert consumes the fused temporal tokens. The evidence is broad: Libero, SimplerEnv, Mikasa-Robo, Calvin, Libero-Plus, and several real-robot task categories. The paper is not perfectly controlled across all comparisons, but the ablations support the useful mechanism: both memory retrieval/consolidation and memory-guided imagination matter.

iMaC is the most concrete action-world-model interface paper. It asks a better question than whether generated robot videos look plausible: can a learned world model rank policy checkpoints in the same direction as real hardware? The method renders future robot motion from URDF and forward kinematics, predicts/uses depth, and builds two contact-image streams from scene-to-gripper and robot-to-scene distances. Across eight real-robot tasks, world-model scores are strongly positively correlated with real-world performance on most tasks, while the two weaker tasks expose missing-observation failure modes rather than generic metric noise.

Latent Spatial Memory / Mirage is the strongest memory-system paper for camera-controllable video world models. Instead of accumulating an RGB point cloud and repeatedly rendering it back to pixels before VAE encoding, Mirage stores VAE latent tokens at 3D world coordinates. Readout is a latent-resolution projection into the target camera view, then a ControlNet-style branch injects the memory into the diffusion backbone. The result is both a representation claim and a systems claim: better or competitive consistency on WorldScore and RealEstate10K, with much lower cache read cost and memory.

Echo-Memory is strong citation material and may deserve a later synthesis note. Its most useful result is that replay fidelity is not a proxy for revisit memory: spatial memory can win replay PSNR while failing open-domain return, and block-wise state-space recurrence can win semantic return while losing replay metrics. I am not preserving it as a full note today because it is mainly an evaluation/design-space study, while today's three notes provide more directly reusable architecture surfaces.

AHA-WAM is useful but not preserved. The two-timescale split between a slow video-DiT planner and fast action-DiT executor is a good deployment idea, and the latency story is concrete. I am treating it as adjacent because it is close to yesterday's action/world-model interface thread, and part of the result is systems optimization rather than a cleaner representation mechanism.

omega-EVA is also useful but not preserved. The proposal-conditioned Envision-Verify-Act loop is conceptually aligned with CAPE from June 8: make the policy inspect a latent consequence of its own proposed action before execution. The evidence is mostly simulation and the Stage 3 deltas are real but modest, so it is citation material rather than one of today's top three.

Prisma-World is adjacent for multi-agent video simulation. Its joint denoising, multi-agent RoPE, relative camera geometry, and minimap conditioning address cross-view consistency, but it is less directly tied to robot memory/planning than the preserved papers.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is MemoryVLA++ because it makes temporal modeling in VLAs explicit enough to reason about: past memory, present tokens, and future imagination each have a job. iMaC is the action-conditioning note to remember because it converts actions into robot motion and contact geometry before asking a video model to simulate manipulation. Latent Spatial Memory is the video-world-model note to keep because it treats persistent 3D memory as latent features rather than RGB cache clutter. The common lesson is blunt: world models get more useful when their memory and action interfaces expose the structure that decisions actually depend on.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-08
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is the action interface is becoming the real planning interface. CAPE is the strongest paper because it trains a latent world model around action-conditioned future differences instead of dense visual reconstruction. Coarse-to-Control is the best VLA planning paper because it puts the intermediate plan into the action-token vocabulary rather than text or image space. At 08:00 Pacific on Monday, June 8, 2026, the Monday arXiv announcement had not landed yet, so the live recent window was still dominated by the June 5 batch. I filtered that leftover cluster rather than pretending there was a fresh Monday release.

I inspected arXiv PDFs for CAPE: Contrastive Action-conditioned Parallel Encoding for Embodied Planning, Coarse-to-Control: Action-Token Planning for Vision-Language-Action Models, Spline Policy: A Structured Representation for Robot Policies, Skill-3D: Evolving Scene-Aware Skills for Agentic 3D Spatial Reasoning, LARA: Latent Action Representation Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models, MemDreamer: Decoupling Perception and Reasoning for Long Video Understanding via Hierarchical Graph Memory and Agentic Retrieval Mechanism, Native3D: End-to-End 3D Scene Generation via Unified Mesh-Texture Modeling and Semantic Alignment, AnchorWorld: Embodied Egocentric World Simulation with View-based Evolution Customization, Streaming Video Generation with Streaming Force Control, Dash2Sim: Closed-Loop Driving Simulation from in-the-wild Dashcam Videos, M3Exam: Benchmarking Multimodal Memory for Realistic User-Agent Interactions, The Sim-to-Real Gap of Foundation Model Agents: A Unified MDP Perspective, and Planning-aligned Token Compression for Long-Context Autonomous Driving. CAPE, Coarse-to-Control, and Spline Policy are preserved today. Skill-3D and LARA are useful adjacent notes, but I am not preserving full notes for them in this run because today's stronger common thread is action/world-model interface design.

CAPE is the strongest direct hit. It argues that embodied planning needs predictive representations that distinguish action-induced future outcomes, not models that reconstruct every visually salient future detail. It predicts an entire future latent trajectory in parallel from the current visual context and candidate action sequence, then trains with a goal-convergent contrastive objective. The reported DROID retrieval gains are large, and the planning-time result is the practical point: CAPE stays near-flat from 335 ms at horizon 1 to 356 ms at horizon 5 in the reported CEM setup.

Coarse-to-Control is the cleanest VLA planning interface today. It first predicts coarse long-horizon action tokens, then predicts executable short-horizon action tokens conditioned on that plan. Both live in a shared discrete action vocabulary. The key result is not just the 97.9 LIBERO average or 83.3 SimplerEnv-WidowX average; it is the tokenizer-sharing ablation showing that a shared action vocabulary helps the plan act as control-native guidance rather than an abstract hint.

Spline Policy is worth keeping because it asks a basic but under-discussed question: what should a robot policy emit? Its answer is spline parameters rather than fixed-resolution action chunks. That output can be decoded into a continuous trajectory, queried at different temporal resolutions, edited or constrained in parameter space, and in the quadratic case converted into a local corrective flow field. The benchmark story is modest, which I like: comparable performance with lower output dimensionality and more execution structure, not universal magic.

Skill-3D is good adjacent agent-memory/tool-use work. It constructs a Scene Memory of tool-use trajectories and co-evolves scene-aware skills with failure lessons, improving effective tool usage in 3D spatial reasoning. I am not preserving a full note today because it overlaps yesterday's agent-memory/tool-state thread, and its main value is tool-routing workflow memory rather than action/world-model interface design.

LARA is useful VLA data-alignment context. Jointly aligning a latent action model and a diffusion VLA is a real reciprocal-supervision idea, especially for using unlabeled videos and limited robot data. I am leaving it as citation material today because CAPE and Coarse-to-Control give sharper planning-interface lessons.

MemDreamer and AnchorWorld are also relevant but not preserved. MemDreamer has a hierarchical graph memory and agentic retrieval loop for hours-long video, but it sits close to the LongSpace note from June 7. AnchorWorld's pose-associated anchor views for egocentric world customization are interesting, but the paper is mainly video-simulator controllability rather than a reusable planning or memory mechanism.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is CAPE because it makes latent world modeling answer the action-selection question directly. Coarse-to-Control is the strongest VLA planning note because it makes the plan a coarse action-token object rather than a semantic flourish. Spline Policy is the output-interface note to remember because it turns learned actions into a continuous motion object that downstream control can actually work with. The common lesson is blunt: planning and control improve when the intermediate object is built for the job it must do.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-07
digests.theme: Today's useful pattern is memory and world models are becoming selection-and-state interfaces, not just bigger context. I inspected arXiv PDFs for PatchWorld: Gradient-Free Optimization of Executable World Models, Worth Remembering: Surprise-Gated Robot Episodic Memory, LongSpace: Exploring Long-Horizon Spatial Memory from Perception to Recall in Video, HyperVis: Continuous Latent Visual Relational Graphs on the Lorentz Hyperboloid for Compositional Reasoning, LatentSkill: From In-Context Textual Skills to In-Weight Latent Skills for LLM Agents, and Where Should Knowledge Enter? A Layered Framework for Knowledge Infusion in Multimodal Iterative Generative Models. PatchWorld, Worth Remembering, and LongSpace are preserved today. HyperVis and LatentSkill are useful citation material, but I am not preserving full notes for them in this run. The knowledge-infusion paper is a decent taxonomy, but not close enough to the repo's embodied/world-model center to spend a note slot today.

PatchWorld is the strongest direct hit. It induces Python world models with explicit symbolic belief state, transition rules, correction logic, and readout logic from offline text-agent trajectories. Prediction failures become typed counterexamples for code repair. The most important result is not just better text prediction; it is the observed frontier between observation fidelity and planning utility. The residual-memory variant predicts surface text better, while the simpler symbolic variant gives better live one-step planning utility.

Worth Remembering is the cleanest embodied-memory mechanism. It computes surprise in V-JEPA-2 latent space with a causal sliding-window Gaussian surrogate, stores only thresholded local maxima as visual episodes, and augments a 4D scene-graph memory. On OC-NaVQA, the surprise-gated memory improves question accuracy over DAAAM from 0.711 to 0.796 while storing about 1.7% of frames. The caveat is that the causal predictive model is still a simple Gaussian over embeddings, not a rich action-conditioned video world model.

LongSpace is worth keeping as benchmark and architecture pressure. LongSpace-Bench contains 445 room-tour videos, about 159 hours, and 4,073 QA pairs covering scene perception, spatial relations, and spatial memory. LongSpace combines 3D spatial-token injection with layer-aware hierarchical KV memory. The key result is that long-memory inference reaches 49.2 on LongSpace-Bench versus 36.1 for uniform 32-frame sampling and 37.7 for recent-window inference, with gains growing on longer videos.

HyperVis is a good citation for continuous relational structure. Its strongest point is that textual scene-graph triplets can hurt VLM accuracy, while continuous hyperbolic relation tokens improve compositional scoring. I am not preserving it today because it is static-image VQA/compositional scoring rather than embodied memory, planning, or world modeling.

LatentSkill is useful adjacent agent-systems material. Converting textual skills into LoRA adapters is a real interface move, but the current evidence is mainly ALFWorld and Search-QA efficiency/composition. It belongs in a future agent-skill synthesis more than today's paper daily note set.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is PatchWorld because it makes a world model into an executable belief-state object that can be inspected, tested, repaired, and used for planning. Worth Remembering is the best embodied-memory mechanism because it gives memory writes a causal surprise gate and beats same-budget uniform/random episodic storage. LongSpace is the benchmark/method to remember because it separates long-context video processing from real spatial memory. The common lesson is clean: useful memory is not accumulation, and useful world modeling is not reconstruction theater. The object being stored, updated, retrieved, or repaired has to be explicit enough to do work.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-06
digests.theme: Today's strongest pattern is explicit state interfaces are doing the real work. Astra is the best world-model reasoning paper because it treats a world simulator as an evidence-acquisition tool and shows that both simulator consistency and learned tool-use policy matter. digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider, but it returned missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv search and paper URLs were attempted through web fetch, but the accessible paths returned AlphaXiv 404 pages. Direct arXiv category pages were reachable; expanded arXiv listing URLs with show=150 returned HTTP 400, so discovery used the default recent category listings plus direct arXiv pages and PDFs. I inspected arXiv PDFs for VASO: Formally Verifiable Self-Evolving Skills for Physical AI Agents, Thinking with Imagination: Agentic Visual Spatial Reasoning with World Simulators, What Should Agents Say? Action-state Communication for Efficient Multi-Agent Systems, Beyond Semantic Organization: Memory as Execution State Management for Long-Horizon Agents, Discrete-WAM: Unified Discrete Vision-Action Token Editing for World-Policy Learning, and DexFuture: Hierarchical Future-State Visuomotor Targeting for Bimanual Dexterous Tool Use. I also screened abstracts for TempoVLA and WorldFly. VASO, Astra, and PACT are preserved today. MAGE, DexFuture, and Discrete-WAM are useful context, but I am not preserving full notes for them in this run.

VASO is the strongest direct hit. It represents each LLM-generated robot skill as a semantic contract with a temporal-logic local rule, proposition-aligned labeling function, and planner-facing template. The useful move is that model-checker counterexamples become textual gradients for updating the reusable skill contract. The caveat is important: the verification guarantee depends on the correctness of the proposition-aligned mapping from low-level robot behavior to symbolic propositions.

Astra is strong adjacent-to-direct world-model reasoning work. It couples an RL-trained VLM policy with a Bagel-based world simulator that generates novel views from camera-motion queries. The key point is not merely "generate another view"; off-the-shelf generation is not enough, and forced simulator use can hurt. Astra improves by training the simulator for view consistency and training the policy to decide when, where, and how to imagine.

PACT is the simplest stealable agent architecture idea today. It treats inter-agent communication as a public state-update problem. Agents may reason privately, but only an action, grounded state/evidence, and result enter shared history. The evidence is practical: across controlled multi-agent settings PACT improves the performance-cost frontier, and in OpenHands/SWE-agent ports it reduces cost per solved SWE-bench Verified instance.

MAGE is worth remembering as memory citation material. Its hierarchical execution-state tree, with Grow, Compress, Maintain, and Revise operations, is conceptually good. I am not preserving it as a full note today because PACT carries a cleaner minimal interface lesson, and VASO/Astra are stronger against the repo's embodied/world-model taste.

DexFuture is good adjacent robotics context. It amortizes future target generation for bimanual dexterous tool use instead of running slow online CEM over action-conditioned world-model rollouts. The target-interface idea is useful, but the paper is narrower than today's top three.

Discrete-WAM is relevant world-action modeling for autonomous driving, with a shared discrete token space for visual states, decisions, and actions. It is not weak, but the result stack is more benchmark- and system-heavy than the cleaner mechanism papers preserved today.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is VASO because it turns formal verification from a post-hoc safety check into a reusable skill-optimization signal. Astra is the most interesting world-model reasoning paper because it makes imagined observations answer an evidence question and shows that simulator access alone is not enough. PACT is the most directly reusable agent-systems design because it keeps private reasoning private and turns public communication into compact action-state records. The common lesson is blunt: state interfaces matter. The good papers today do not just add more generation or more agent chatter; they define what must be exposed, verified, imagined, or passed forward.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-05
digests.theme: Today's strongest pattern is world models are being pulled into the evaluation and control loop, not just the video-generation stack. PiL-World is the most relevant paper because it makes generated rollouts answer a closed-loop VLA evaluation question: if the policy sees generated observations and acts again, do imagined success rates track real robot success rates? World-Language-Action is the best architecture paper because it splits next state into textual intention plus compact physical dynamics, then uses that split to tie language progress, future-state supervision, and action generation together. digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider, but it returned missing_brave_api_key. AlphaXiv search was also attempted from the CLI path and returned HTTP 403. The arXiv export API returned Rate exceeded, so discovery used arXiv category listings, ordinary web search, and direct arXiv pages/PDFs. This makes discovery less broad than a working Brave-plus-AlphaXiv pass, but the preserved papers are not abstract-only.

I inspected arXiv PDFs for PiL-World: A Chunk-Wise World Model for VLA Policy-in-the-Loop Evaluation, World-Language-Action Model for Unified World Modeling, Language Reasoning, and Action Synthesis, MPCoT: Reward-Guided Multi-Path Latent Reasoning for Test-Time Scalable Vision-Language-Action, and CLAW: Learning Continuous Latent Action World Models via Adversarial Latent Regularization. I also screened today's arXiv robotics, computer vision, AI, and ML listings for world-model, VLA, memory, planning, action, and 3D-generation candidates. PiL-World and WLA are preserved. MPCoT is treated as useful citation material for latent test-time compute. CLAW is promising but less directly useful today than the closed-loop evaluation and language-world-action papers.

PiL-World is the cleanest hit. It targets the gap between open-loop action-conditioned prediction and real VLA evaluation, where the policy repeatedly observes, acts, and re-plans. The paper alternates a frozen VLA policy with a chunk-wise world model, feeding terminal generated observations back into the policy. It reports the average real-imagined success-rate gap dropping from 63.2% for Ctrl-World to 12.0%, and a 0.94 Pearson correlation across task-checkpoint settings.

World-Language-Action is the broader architecture paper. It argues that the next state for embodied control should include both semantic textual intention and compact physical dynamics. A World Expert supervises the physical-dynamics latent during training, while an Action Expert maps that latent plus proprioception into action chunks. The World Expert can be disabled for fast inference or used for test-time scaling. The most useful evidence is not the leaderboard sweep by itself, but the RMBench result: removing language subtask prediction drops average success from 56.5% to 17.3%, suggesting the textual progress trace is doing real work on memory-dependent tasks.

MPCoT is a reasonable mechanism paper, but I am keeping it as citation material rather than a full note. Its multi-path latent reasoning layer improves CALVIN long-horizon success and preserves the action interface without generating reasoning tokens. The idea is useful, but the paper is narrower and sits closer to an internal compute module than to a new world-model/state contract.

CLAW is good adjacent latent-action work. It jointly learns continuous latent actions and a diffusion world model from action-free videos, using adversarial regularization to discourage future-frame leakage. It is worth remembering for latent action learning from observation, but today's stronger cabbageland signal is about closed-loop evaluation and explicit semantic/physical state interfaces.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is PiL-World because it makes world models serve closed-loop policy evaluation instead of open-loop video prediction. The best architecture paper is World-Language-Action, because it gives next state two operational faces: language-level progress and compact physical dynamics. The day also surfaced useful supporting work on latent test-time compute and action-free latent-action world models, but the main lesson is sharper: world models become valuable when they define what the policy can observe, remember, test, or score next.

digests.theme: Today's strongest pattern is world models are becoming useful as evaluation instruments, but only when the representation makes the evaluation contract sharper. digests.overview:

I inspected arXiv HTML and PDFs for OSCAR: Omni-Embodiment Action-Conditioned World Model for Robotics, Generalization of World Models under Environmental Variability for Vision-based Quadrotor Navigation, A 3D Isovist World Model: Revealing a City's Unseen Geometry and Its Emergent Cross-City Signature, GeoSem-WAM: Geometry- and Semantic-Aware World Action Models, and 3DThinkVLA: Endowing Vision-Language-Action Models with Latent 3D Priors via 3D-Thinking-Guided Co-training. The first three are preserved today. GeoSem-WAM and 3DThinkVLA look useful, but their central moves are closer to incremental training-time structure injection, so I am treating them as citation/background material rather than full notes today.

OSCAR is the most directly relevant paper. It finetunes Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B as an action-conditioned video world model, using 2D kinematic skeleton renderings as a unified conditioning representation across four robot embodiments and human hands. The useful claim is not merely that generated robot videos look better. The useful claim is that a generated-world policy-evaluation protocol on RoboArena correlates with real-world policy ranking, while the skeleton condition gives a better generalization/precision trade-off than latent action or robot-specific mesh renders.

The quadrotor generalization study is less flashy and probably more important for keeping later world-model claims honest. It trains DreamerV3-style world models under different environmental-randomness regimes, evaluates cross-environment reconstruction during self-supervised pretraining and policy performance after RL, then deploys every model on a real quadrotor. The sharp result is that the model that looked best in simulation RL failed in the harder real deployment, while models with better cross-environment SSL reconstruction transferred.

A 3D Isovist World Model is adjacent rather than directly robotic manipulation work, but it has one of the cleaner representation arguments of the week. It predicts the geometry of open navigable volume as a spherical depth map, not RGB appearance or flattened occupancy. It also makes persistent spatial memory explicit through a writable latent BEV map. The empirical claims are still modest, especially the spatial-map ablation, but the representation is conceptually crisp.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is OSCAR because it makes generated robot worlds answer an evaluation question rather than just a visual-fidelity question. The most important cautionary paper is the quadrotor generalization study, which shows that the validation metric deciding model selection can matter more than the simulator leaderboard. The best adjacent representation paper is A 3D Isovist World Model, because it predicts the negative space an agent moves through and gives that geometry a persistent writable memory. The common lesson is simple: world models earn their name when their state or conditioning interface changes what can be tested, transferred, or trusted.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest — 2026-06-01
digests.theme: Today’s strongest pattern is memory or dynamics structure only counts when it changes the control contract. ECHO is the most relevant paper because it makes retrieval structure operational instead of treating memory as an undifferentiated bag of past episodes. SOMA is the clearest embodied systems paper because it gives memory a concrete job, acting on objects that the camera cannot currently see. ELAN4D is weaker conceptually, but still worth keeping because it shows that compact future-geometry supervision can improve robustness without a full architecture rewrite.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was not available as a configured tool surface in this run, and AlphaXiv was likewise unavailable here, so discovery again fell back to recent arXiv listings plus direct arXiv HTML inspection.

I relied on substantial prior full-text inspection already done in this run for ECHO: Continuous Hierarchical Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models and Spatial Memory for Out-of-Vision Manipulation in Vision-Language-Action, and I additionally inspected the arXiv HTML full text for ELAN4D: Embodiment-Centric 4D Supervision for Vision-Language-Action Models via Plug-and-Play Adaptation, including its method framing and visible main-results sections. Confidence is highest for ECHO and SOMA. For ELAN4D, confidence is good on the central mechanism and headline result pattern, but lower on the full empirical texture because I did not exhaustively audit every table and appendix detail.

ECHO is the strongest paper today. Its actual contribution is not “hyperbolic memory” in the shallow branding sense. The meaningful part is that memories are organized hierarchically by abstraction level, retrieved top-down with compatibility constraints, and fused into a frozen VLA only after that filtering. The ablations matter here: short-term buffer helps, flat memory helps less, hierarchy-aware retrieval helps more, and consolidation helps most. That means the representation and retrieval policy are doing real work.

SOMA is the cleanest rebuttal to camera-frustum myopia in current VLAs. It assumes, correctly, that objects keep existing after they leave the current image. The paper builds a persistent spatial-semantic memory from active scanning, refines it during interaction, and retrieves task-relevant regions back into the policy. It is not a minimalist learned world model, but it is one of the better recent examples of explicit persistent state paying rent in a real robotic problem.

ELAN4D is more modest, but still useful. It does not maintain explicit memory or belief state. Instead, it adds training-only predictive supervision using future robot keypoint tracks derived from proprioception and forward kinematics. That makes it less interesting than a true explicit-state system, but more interesting than decorative “4D-aware” marketing, because the reported gains appear strongest under perturbations and longer-horizon settings where reactive image-to-action policies should crack.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is ECHO because it makes memory structure operational through hierarchical retrieval and compatibility filtering rather than vague recurrence rhetoric. SOMA is the best embodied systems paper because it shows that persistent spatial memory really does matter once the relevant object leaves the camera frustum. ELAN4D is the most modest of the three, but still useful because it demonstrates that cheap future-geometry supervision can make VLA control more robust without requiring a full explicit-state redesign. The common lesson is that structure earns respect only when it changes what the controller stores, retrieves, updates, or predicts in a way you can actually point to.
rankedTitles: ECHO: Continuous Hierarchical Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
Spatial Memory for Out-of-Vision Manipulation in Vision-Language-Action

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-31
digests.theme: Today’s strongest pattern is explicit structure only matters when it changes what gets stored, updated, or decomposed, not when it just renames a latent soup. 3D-Belief is the best paper because it really does reframe embodied world modeling as online 3D belief maintenance under partial observability. WEM is interesting because it tries to split persistent scene evolution from robot-centric interaction, but I am more skeptical there because some of the benefit may come from benchmark design plus a heavy video-generation stack. Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting? is not a mechanism breakthrough, but it is the best reality check of the set.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was not available as a configured tool surface in this run, and AlphaXiv was likewise unavailable here, so discovery fell back to recent arXiv papers plus direct arXiv inspection.

I inspected substantial arXiv HTML full text for 3D-Belief: Embodied Belief Inference via Generative 3D World Modeling, World-Ego Modeling for Long-Horizon Evolution in Hybrid Embodied Tasks, and Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting? Confidence is highest for 3D-Belief and the continual-VLA paper. For WEM, I inspected the abstract, introduction, formulation, architecture, and visible experimental framing, but I did not fully recover every result table cleanly enough to claim the same level of confidence on the empirical margins.

3D-Belief is the most relevant paper today. Its core move is to treat world modeling as belief-state inference in explicit 3D space rather than as pixel rollout. The state is a 3D Gaussian-splat scene with semantic embeddings, split into observed structure and imagined unseen structure. New observations update the belief by preserving observed content, replacing stale imagined content, and keeping the result queryable for semantics and planning. That is a much healthier contract than “generate plausible future video and hope the planner can somehow use it.”

The main reason this matters is that the paper is trying to make uncertainty, memory, and semantics live in the same explicit state. Most recent visual world-model papers are still basically rendering systems with nicer branding. This one at least makes a serious attempt to represent what the agent knows, what it has only hypothesized, and how that changes after new evidence arrives.

WEM is a more mixed case. The motivating distinction, world as persistent instruction-agnostic scene structure and ego as robot-centric instruction-conditioned dynamics, is genuinely useful. Hybrid navigation-manipulation tasks probably do want something like that separation. The question is whether the paper’s proposed decomposition is buying real mechanism or mostly wrapping a large video-diffusion system in a better story. My read is that there is some real structure here, especially in assigning different predictive roles, but the implementation is still heavy enough that I would treat it as adjacent inspiration, not as clean evidence that “world-ego disentanglement” is now a solved design principle.

Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting? is the least glamorous but maybe the most useful for keeping later claims honest. It shows that sequential real-world adaptation can collapse badly under naive fine-tuning, and that replay only looks robust when details like action normalization and replay cadence are handled carefully. That is less exciting than a shiny memory module, but it is exactly the kind of paper that should change how later continual-VLA claims are evaluated.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is 3D-Belief because it actually turns embodied world modeling into explicit 3D belief maintenance instead of prettier video prediction. Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting? is the best reality check, showing that continual embodied learning is still fragile enough that protocol details matter as much as algorithm branding. WEM is worth remembering because the world-versus-ego split is a sensible decomposition target for hybrid long-horizon tasks, but the current implementation still feels too generator-heavy to count as decisive evidence. The common lesson is that explicit structure only earns the name when it changes the computational contract, memory update, or evaluation burden in a way you can actually inspect.

Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting?

digests.theme: Today’s useful pattern is making memory or attribution explicit enough that you can inspect the failure mode instead of blaming “context length” or “generalization” in the abstract. digests.overview:
Brave Search was not available as a configured tool surface in this run, and AlphaXiv was likewise unavailable here, so discovery fell back to recent arXiv papers plus direct PDF inspection.

I inspected full paper PDFs for SAM: State-Adaptive Memory for Long-Horizon Reasoning Agent, Embodied Interpretability: Linking Causal Understanding to Generalization in Vision-Language-Action Models, and Towards Responsible Multimodal Medical Reasoning via Context-Aligned Vision-Language Models. Confidence is highest for SAM and Embodied Interpretability because the core mechanism and evaluation are easy to recover from the paper body. The medical paper is readable and directionally sensible, but I am less convinced that the method is strong enough to treat as a major mechanism paper.

SAM is the most relevant paper today. Its core move is simple and real: instead of compressing the past into one rolling summary or blindly retrieving old snippets, it stores trajectory history as raw pages plus lightweight memory cues that stay in context as handles. When the agent later needs something, it chooses cues based on its current intent, then the memory model reconstructs support from the corresponding raw pages. That is a cleaner contract than most “agent memory” work, because the summary is not pretending to be the memory itself.

The second useful part is that SAM is trained as a memory module rather than hand-waved as prompting. The authors supervise both page summarization and recall against stronger frontier models, then add a tree-structured RL objective so individual memory actions get credit instead of only the final task outcome. I do not love the dependence on frontier-model committees for supervision and reward, but the system at least knows what component is being optimized.

Embodied Interpretability is adjacent rather than central, but still worth keeping. It introduces the Interventional Significance Score, which estimates how much masking a visual region changes the action prediction, and then compresses that into a Nuisance Mass Ratio measuring how much causally significant saliency lands on irrelevant regions. The strongest result is not interpretability theater, it is that higher nuisance attribution predicts worse out-of-distribution task success.

I would not oversell the causal language here. The method is still an interventional proxy based on masking and action divergence under teacher forcing, not a full causal identification of what the robot “really reasons about.” But as a diagnostic for spurious visual dependence in VLA policies, it seems more serious than reading off attention maps and calling it understanding.

Context-Aligned Medical Reasoning is the day’s weaker keep-in-view paper. It wraps a frozen Qwen2-VL model with radiomic features, Grad-CAM statistics, vocabulary cues, and a structured safety-conscious output format. That is directionally aligned with explicit evidence checking, but the method looks more like tool-augmented protocol engineering than a deep representational advance. I would cite it as an example of forcing multi-evidence agreement, not as a breakthrough.
digests.takeaway: The strongest paper today is SAM because it treats memory as a real interface with explicit write and read behavior: compress to cues, keep raw pages, reconstruct by current intent. Embodied Interpretability is the best adjacent paper because it turns spurious visual reliance into a measurable diagnostic that actually predicts generalization. Context-Aligned Medical Reasoning is worth remembering as a safety-oriented evidence-checking wrapper, but it feels more like disciplined scaffolding around a frozen VLM than a major new model idea. The common lesson is that explicit structure matters when it changes what gets stored, recalled, or causally attended to, not when it is just a nicer story wrapped around the same latent mush.
rankedTitles: SAM: State-Adaptive Memory for Long-Horizon Reasoning Agent
Embodied Interpretability: Linking Causal Understanding to Generalization in Vision-Language-Action Models
Towards Responsible Multimodal Medical Reasoning via Context-Aligned Vision-Language Models

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-29
digests.theme: Today’s best pattern is moving explicit state or dynamics upstream instead of asking a downstream policy or decoder to hallucinate them back later. The strongest paper is DynaFLIP because it treats robot generalization partly as a representation problem and injects action-relevant motion structure into the visual backbone itself. AdaState is the best adjacent inspiration because it replaces a frozen first-frame anchor in streaming video generation with a hidden recurrent state that actually evolves. Qwen-VLA is useful mostly as scale-and-baseline pressure, not as the main mechanism paper of the day.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was not available as a configured tool surface in this run, and AlphaXiv was likewise unavailable here, so discovery again fell back to recent arXiv results plus direct arXiv abstract, HTML, and PDF inspection.

I inspected substantial primary-source text for DynaFLIP: Rethinking Robotics Perception via Tri-Modal-Dynamics Guided Representation, AdaState: Self-Evolving Anchors for Streaming Video Generation, and Qwen-VLA: Unifying Vision-Language-Action Modeling across Tasks, Environments, and Robot Embodiments. For DynaFLIP and AdaState, confidence is good on the main mechanism because I inspected method text from the paper body, not just the abstract. For Qwen-VLA, confidence is good on the training recipe and framing, but I am treating it mainly as a large-system reference point rather than a source of steal-worthy structure.

DynaFLIP is the most relevant paper today. Its main claim is that robot perception should encode not just appearance but controllable change, so the authors pretrain an image encoder using image transitions, language, and estimated 3D flow as training-time supervision. The notable part is the objective: instead of simple anchor-style pairwise alignment, they minimize the simplex volume spanned by the three modality embeddings, then add a cosine regularizer and contrastive negatives to avoid degenerate geometry and collapse. The encoder used at test time is still image-only, but its representation has been shaped by transition semantics upstream.

I like this paper because the structure is doing real work. It is not merely saying “dynamics matter.” It changes the representation-learning objective so the backbone is explicitly rewarded for encoding motion-relevant scene factors before any policy head sees the features. The main caveat is that some of the appeal depends on estimated 3D flow and generated language over video data, so part of the method’s strength may ride on the quality of those supervision channels.

AdaState is the strongest adjacent paper. It identifies a sharp architectural pathology in autoregressive video diffusion: the first frame’s cache entry becomes a privileged clean anchor, so long rollouts preserve identity partly by freezing scene evolution. AdaState replaces that static anchor with a hidden latent state that is denoised alongside each chunk, never rendered, and then written back into the cache as the next chunk’s anchor. That is a real recurrent state, even if it is implemented with ordinary denoising and KV-cache mechanics rather than a separate memory module.

What I like here is the clarity of the recurrence contract. The state has a location, an update path, and a reason to exist. The main caveat is that this is still a video-generation paper, not a world-model paper in the stronger planning or control sense. But the underlying lesson is useful: if a sequence model already has a privileged reference position, replacing a frozen token with an evolving hidden state can buy real temporal depth.

Qwen-VLA is impressive as a breadth-of-coverage result. It unifies manipulation, navigation, egocentric demonstrations, and trajectory prediction under one Qwen-based vision-language-action stack with embodiment-aware prompts and a DiT action decoder. That matters for baseline framing. But the central move is still large-scale mixture pretraining plus careful staging, not a new explicit-state or memory mechanism. So I would cite it, compare against it, and learn from its data recipe, but not treat it as the most conceptually useful paper of the day.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is DynaFLIP because it treats control-relevant dynamics as something the visual representation itself should encode, using tri-modal alignment rather than only downstream policy pressure. AdaState is the best adjacent paper because it shows a simple but meaningful recurrence trick: replace a frozen cache anchor with a denoised hidden state that evolves chunk by chunk. Qwen-VLA is important mainly as a very strong generalist baseline and framing reference, not as the day’s main mechanism contribution. The common lesson is that explicit structure starts to matter when it changes the representation interface or the recurrent contract, not when it is just another large latent blob with better branding.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-28
digests.theme: Today’s useful pattern is making long-horizon control legible by changing the interface, not by stapling more scale onto the policy. The strongest paper is PrimitiveVLA because it tries to move VLA fine-tuning away from monolithic instruction-to-trajectory imitation and toward reusable motion units with explicit assembly logic. ProgVLA is the best compact-policy paper of the batch because it adds a real progress signal and aggressive token compression instead of just shrinking the model and hoping for the best. MentalMap is not a robotics paper, but it is a sharp diagnostic reminder that text-only “world model” claims still collapse badly once viewpoint transformation and active spatial construction enter the loop.
digests.overview:
Brave Search was attempted first in spirit, but no Brave Search tool is configured in this run, so I could not actually use it here. AlphaXiv was likewise unavailable as a live tool surface in this environment. Discovery therefore fell back to recent arXiv API results, direct arXiv HTML full-text pages when available, and direct arXiv abstract pages otherwise.

I inspected substantial arXiv HTML full text for PrimitiveVLA: Learning Reusable Motion Primitives for Efficient and Generalizable Robotic Manipulation, ProgVLA: Progress-Aware Robot Manipulation Skill Learning, and Do LLMs Build World Models From Text? A Multilingual Diagnostic of Spatial Reasoning. Confidence is reasonably good on the main mechanism and evaluation setup for all three. Confidence is lower on appendix-only hyperparameters and on the exact robustness of some reported gains.

PrimitiveVLA is the most relevant paper today. Its core claim is that standard VLA fine-tuning wastes data by binding high-level instructions directly to task-specific low-level trajectories, which makes reusable motion patterns hard to share across tasks. The paper’s answer is to disassemble demonstrations into an explicit library of 11 primitives, train the VLA on primitive-conditioned masked observations, and then reassemble tasks at inference time with a VLM planner plus switching logic. I like the pressure it puts on the decomposition interface: if compositionality is real, the reusable unit should exist both during training and during execution.

The caveat is that PrimitiveVLA gets a lot of its structure from external scaffolding. Primitive sequences come from VLM reasoning over demonstrations, and boundary logic is generated as code from primitive definitions plus state traces. That is not fake, but it does mean the paper is less “the VLA discovered primitives” and more “the system was carefully forced into a primitive regime.” Honestly that is fine. Forced structure is still structure, and it is much better than vague claims that modularity just emerges.

ProgVLA is less ambitious conceptually, but more disciplined than most compact-VLA work. It uses two-stage Perceiver resampling to aggressively compress multimodal context, then adds progress heads that predict normalized remaining horizon and near-completion success, using those signals to reweight a flow-matching imitation objective. This is not a world model and not a deep memory paper. But it does make long-horizon progress estimation an internal training signal instead of an external evaluator, which is a respectable way to attack the “small policies lose the thread” problem.

MentalMap is the best framing paper of the day. It shows a strong, multilingual L3 cliff in pure-text spatial reasoning: models can recover local facts but break when asked to perform viewpoint transformation or active spatial construction. That matters because people keep talking as if text-only LLMs already have robust internal world models. This benchmark does not prove they do not have any such structure, but it does show that the structure is much weaker and less stable than the branding suggests.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is PrimitiveVLA because it makes compositionality concrete at the actual interface where reuse must happen: demonstrations are disassembled into reusable motion primitives during training and reassembled during execution. ProgVLA is the cleanest compact-policy paper because it couples aggressive multimodal compression with an internal progress signal that directly reweights long-horizon imitation. MentalMap is the best adjacent paper because it punctures mushy text-world-model claims by showing a persistent viewpoint-reasoning cliff across languages. The common lesson is that explicit structure matters when it changes the policy’s real control loop or the benchmark’s real failure diagnosis, not when it is just better branding for a latent blob.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-27
digests.theme: Today’s strongest pattern is structure that actually constrains reuse, not structure as branding. The best direct paper is SMoDP because it tries to make expert routing respect semantically meaningful manipulation phases instead of letting sparse routing fragment similar behaviors arbitrarily. The most useful framing paper is Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting? because it forces a basic but easy-to-ignore point: sequential real-world adaptation can collapse badly, and some reported continual-learning competence depends on implementation details that earlier setups made too easy. digests.overview:
Brave Search was unavailable in this environment because no Brave Search tool is configured for this run. AlphaXiv was also not available as a live tool surface here, so discovery fell back to recent arXiv API results, direct arXiv pages, and arXiv HTML when available.

I inspected full arXiv HTML for Semantically Structured Mixture-of-Experts for Compositional Robotic Manipulation and Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting? Confidence is good on the main mechanism and headline evaluation story for both papers, and weaker on appendix-level hyperparameters and every implementation detail.

SMoDP is the most relevant paper today. Its core claim is that mixture-of-experts routing for manipulation should not be driven only by low-level latent statistics or diffusion noise level, because that tends to split semantically similar behaviors across different experts. The paper uses offline VLM-produced verb-noun skill labels, trains a lightweight skill predictor, and routes action chunks according to predicted skill phase. I like the underlying instinct: if expert modularity is supposed to help compositional reuse, then the routing interface should expose reusable behavioral structure instead of hoping the experts discover it accidentally. The main caveat is that the semantic structure is partly scaffolded by a VLM annotation pipeline, so some of the cleanliness comes from extra supervision rather than from a naturally emerging modular policy.

Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting? is less architecturally exciting, but more important than it looks. The paper builds a four-task real-world sequential manipulation stream and shows that naive sequential fine-tuning of a π0.5-style policy catastrophically forgets earlier tasks. More interestingly, it argues that modest replay can help a lot, but only if practical details like replay frequency and action normalization are handled carefully. This is exactly the kind of paper that should affect how later continual-learning claims are read. If a method says it resists forgetting, the first question should now be whether it was tested in a heterogeneous real-world stream and whether the training protocol avoided future-information leakage.

I also briefly checked Unified 3D Scene Understanding Through Physical World Modeling. The abstract sounds potentially relevant because it frames multiple 3D tasks as inference paths through a shared probabilistic world model. But arXiv HTML was unavailable for that paper in this environment, and I did not do a deeper PDF audit today, so I am treating it as a possible follow-up rather than a preserved note.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is SMoDP because it pushes modularity down to the routing decision instead of merely scaling an MoE policy and hoping experts self-organize into reusable skills. The most practically important paper is Can VLA Models Learn from Real-World Data Continually without Forgetting? because it shows that continual VLA learning in the real world is still fragile, and that small implementation decisions can dominate the conclusion. The shared lesson is that explicit structure matters most when it changes the actual computational bottleneck, either which expert gets activated or whether previously learned skills survive sequential updates at all.

digests.title: Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-26
digests.theme: Today’s strongest pattern is explicit geometry that actually touches the decision interface. The best direct paper is OASIS because it argues, pretty concretely, that robot action prediction gets easier when the intermediate state is aligned with the action space rather than left as image-space mush. TriSplat is the best adjacent paper because it makes 3D reconstruction simulation-ready by choosing triangle primitives that are already usable as a mesh, instead of doing pretty splats first and mesh surgery later. digests.overview:

I inspected substantial full-text arXiv HTML for OASIS: Observation-Action Space Alignment via SE(3) Trajectory Prediction for Robotic Manipulation, TriSplat: Simulation-Ready Feed-Forward 3D Scene Reconstruction, and AgentGrounder: Zero-Shot 3D Visual Pointcloud Grounding using Multimodal Language Models. Confidence is good on the core mechanism, framing, and headline evaluation claims, and weaker on appendix-level details and exact training hyperparameters that I did not audit line by line.

OASIS is the most relevant paper today. Its core move is to make the policy’s intermediate state explicitly predict an SE(3) end-effector trajectory, then condition the action decoder on those pose-supervised hidden states. I like this because the explicit structure is not decorative. The paper is not merely adding another spatial auxiliary head while keeping the actual control pathway unchanged. It tries to align the intermediate representation with the geometry of the action space itself. That is a clean and defensible design claim. The main caveat is that the method still relies on a fairly standard learned decoder to absorb frame conversion, contact residuals, and gripper timing, so this is an alignment bias rather than a full geometric control formulation.

TriSplat is the strongest adjacent inspiration. The paper’s real contribution is not just another splatting variant. It notices that if the downstream use case is simulation, collision, and grasping, then a representation that still needs lossy post-hoc mesh extraction is slightly lying about being simulation-ready. TriSplat fixes that by making oriented triangle primitives the native rendering object, with normals anchored to predicted geometry and refined carefully during training. That is a good example of choosing a representation that matches the artifact you actually need later.

AgentGrounder is less ambitious, but more honest than a lot of “agentic 3D grounding” branding. It builds an object lookup table from point-cloud segmentation, retrieves only query-relevant candidates, applies deterministic geometric reasoning, and renders views only when color or material evidence is needed. The gains over SeeGround are real but not huge, and the system still depends on the quality of the initial segmentation stack. Still, the decomposition is legible and the selective-rendering idea is operationally sensible.

I also briefly considered RePlan-Bot and AnyScene. RePlan-Bot looked competent but more like a strong modular ALFRED stack than a paper I especially need to preserve. AnyScene looks substantial, but today’s cut favored papers with cleaner transfer into cabbageland’s interests around action-space structure, explicit geometry, and simulation-facing representations.
digests.takeaway: The best paper today is OASIS because it makes an unusually clean representational claim for robotic manipulation: if action lives in rigid-body geometry, then the intermediate state should carry pose structure that is closer to that geometry instead of leaving it implicit inside an action decoder. TriSplat is the best adjacent paper because it chooses a triangle-native scene representation that is already the kind of object simulation systems want, rather than pretending post-hoc mesh extraction is a minor detail. AgentGrounder is the best smaller systems paper because it combines selective retrieval, deterministic geometry, and on-demand rendering in a way that stays legible. The shared lesson is simple: explicit structure matters most when it survives all the way to the interface that actually makes decisions or supports downstream use.
