notes.title: Act, Sense, Act: Learning Non-Markovian Active Perception Strategies from Large-Scale Egocentric Human Data
notes.whySelected: It tries to treat active perception as a real control-and-memory problem instead of bolting gaze onto a passive manipulation policy and calling it cognition.
notes.verdictText: This is a serious robotics systems paper with a believable target: long-horizon active perception under occlusion, branching outcomes, and viewpoint-dependent uncertainty. The good part is not the grandiose theory language; it is the practical stack of egocentric action alignment, explicit temporal memory, and a sub-task transition head trained with large-scale human egocentric data plus robot teleoperation. My confidence is good on the framing and core mechanism, but I only had partial paper access through the arXiv HTML extract rather than a full line-by-line audit of every experiment table.
notes.overview: The paper argues that active perception in robotics should be modeled as an "act, sense, act" loop rather than a one-shot perception-to-action mapping. To support that claim, it introduces CoMe-VLA, a cognitive and memory-aware vision-language-action policy that learns exploration and manipulation priors from large-scale human egocentric datasets and then adapts them to a wheel-based humanoid robot. The system combines a visual-language backbone, a flow-matching action decoder, a cognitive auxiliary head for sub-task transitions, and a dual-track memory that stores both visual and proprioceptive temporal context. The paper’s real bet is that long-horizon active perception needs explicit temporal context and branching-aware execution, not just more reactive policy capacity.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it reinforces a useful design principle: if the task is uncertainty-resolving interaction, then the policy should remember, branch, and deliberately seek information. That is a more serious framing than passive reactive VLAs with a slightly larger action space.
notes.finalDecision:
Keep as a useful systems reference. The strongest lesson is that active perception should be treated as a branching memory-dependent control problem, and that egocentric human data may be a practical way to bootstrap those priors. But I would cite this more for architecture and framing than for any claim that it fully solves active perception.

---

notes.title: Simple Recipe Works: Vision-Language-Action Models are Natural Continual Learners with Reinforcement Learning
notes.whySelected: It is a meaningful empirical update suggesting that large pretrained VLAs in an RL post-training regime may avoid the usual continual-learning brittleness better than expected.
notes.verdictText: This is more important as an empirical baseline correction than as a conceptual breakthrough. The main result is that sequential fine-tuning with LoRA and on-policy RL appears surprisingly strong for continual adaptation in large pretrained VLAs, often beating more elaborate continual-RL methods. That is interesting, but it is also narrow: the claim is about a particular regime, not continual learning in general.
notes.overview: The paper studies continual reinforcement learning for large pretrained Vision-Language-Action models across multiple VLA backbones and lifelong RL benchmarks. Contrary to the usual continual-learning story, the authors find that simple sequential fine-tuning with LoRA performs very well: it adapts to new tasks, shows limited forgetting, and preserves zero-shot capabilities better than many more complex continual-learning baselines. Their explanation is that three ingredients work together: large pretrained representations, parameter-efficient LoRA updates, and stable on-policy RL. The paper’s real value is therefore partly negative: it weakens the assumption that sophisticated continual-learning machinery is automatically necessary in this regime.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it affects baseline discipline. If simple sequential adaptation is already strong in some VLA regimes, then papers selling elaborate continual-learning machinery need to beat a stronger and more honest baseline than the field may currently assume.
notes.finalDecision: Worth preserving, mainly as a baseline and framing update. Useful for continual-learning judgment, but not a reason to declare the problem solved.

notes.title: RoboMME: Benchmarking and Understanding Memory for Robotic Generalist Policies
notes.whySelected: It provides a more defensible way to talk about robotic memory by separating distinct memory demands and testing them under a common VLA backbone.
notes.verdictText: This is a benchmark paper, so the contribution is mostly evaluative framing rather than a new mechanism. Still, it is useful because it pushes against the lazy habit of reporting one “memory helps” number without distinguishing temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory demands. I inspected substantial accessible text, but not the full supplement or all benchmark details.
notes.overview: RoboMME introduces a memory-focused robotic manipulation benchmark with 16 tasks grouped into four suites: Counting for temporal memory, Permanence for spatial memory under occlusion and change, Reference for object identity across time, and Imitation for procedural memory. On top of that benchmark, the paper builds 14 memory-augmented VLA variants on a common pi0.5 backbone to compare symbolic, perceptual, and recurrent memory representations across several integration strategies. The main result is not that one memory design wins universally, but that memory representation effectiveness is strongly task-dependent.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it gives a cleaner evaluation frame for future work on memory and embodied systems. It is useful ammunition against papers that use “memory” as branding without showing what kind of memory problem they actually solve.
notes.finalDecision: Worth preserving as framing and citation material. It is not the deepest mechanism paper of the month, but it is genuinely useful for cleaning up how the field talks about memory.

notes.title: MEM: Multi-Scale Embodied Memory for Vision Language Action Models
notes.whySelected: It makes a clean and credible case that robotic memory should be decomposed by timescale and information type instead of shoved into a single generic context mechanism.
notes.verdictText: This is one of the better recent memory papers for VLAs because the decomposition is not decorative. Dense recent video is used for short-horizon perceptual needs like occlusion handling and re-grasping, while long-horizon task progress is compressed into language memory updated by a high-level policy. I inspected substantial accessible text from the paper, but not every appendix and table, so the architectural judgment is firmer than any precise claim about SOTA margins.
notes.overview: MEM equips a VLA with two different memory substrates for two different jobs. A video encoder provides short-horizon dense memory over recent observations so the policy can reason about dynamics, self-occlusion, and fine manipulation details. A separate language-memory mechanism stores compressed semantic summaries of what has already happened over much longer timescales, such as which substeps of a task have been completed. The resulting system factors action generation into a high-level policy that updates subtask instructions and language memory, and a low-level policy that conditions on recent visual history plus those instructions. The paper’s main contribution is not magical new memory capacity; it is a more defensible memory interface.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is a clean example of decomposing memory by actual computational need. It supports the broader cabbageland taste for explicit interfaces over “just add more context” mush.
notes.finalDecision: Worth preserving and likely worth a deeper read. The paper does not solve memory in full, but it advances the interface in a way that is actually legible and likely transferable.

notes.title: Points-to-3D: Structure-Aware 3D Generation with Point Cloud Priors
notes.whySelected: It uses explicit 3D priors in the right place—inside the structure latent—rather than pretending text or image conditioning alone can give reliable geometric control.
notes.verdictText: This is a clean mechanism paper. The idea is modest but solid: do not start the structural latent from pure noise when you already have a partial point cloud. Instead, encode the visible geometry, preserve it with a mask, and treat 3D generation as latent structural inpainting. That is a real interface improvement, not just another branded conditioning trick.
notes.overview: Points-to-3D modifies TRELLIS so partial point clouds become hard geometric anchors for generation. The method voxelizes a visible-region point cloud, encodes it into TRELLIS’s sparse structure latent, keeps observed regions fixed with a mask, fills the rest with noise, and then runs an inpainting model to complete the missing structure before boundary refinement. Because the observed geometry enters the actual structure latent rather than floating around as a side condition, the generator is forced to respect measured 3D evidence while still having freedom to plausibly complete unobserved regions.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is a good example of explicit structure replacing mush. The paper does not claim magic compositionality; it simply inserts measurable geometry where the generator must respect it.
notes.finalDecision: Keep and cite. This is one of the cleaner recent papers on geometry-controlled 3D generation.

notes.title: ManiDreams: An Open-Source Library for Robust Object Manipulation via Uncertainty-aware Task-specific Intuitive Physics
notes.whySelected: It is one of the cleaner recent attempts to make uncertainty an explicit planning object rather than a training-time footnote.
notes.verdictText: This is more framework paper than algorithmic breakthrough, but the framework is pointed at a real bottleneck. Its core contribution is not a new learned world model; it is a reusable sample-predict-constrain interface where uncertainty is represented, propagated, and filtered explicitly. That makes it more relevant than the average manipulation paper that says "robust" and then hides all uncertainty inside policy training.
notes.overview: ManiDreams wraps manipulation planning around a distributional state representation instead of a single predicted future. The system builds a Domain-Randomized Instance Set (DRIS) that holds multiple possible object states and physical contexts, propagates them through a Task-Specific Intuitive Physics (TSIP) backend that can be either a simulator or a learned model, and then selects actions by checking whether the resulting distribution stays inside task-specific caging constraints. In plain terms: sample plausible futures, roll them forward, reject the actions that let uncertainty spill out of the safe task geometry, and keep the interface modular enough to swap backends and solvers.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is a good example of structure doing real work. The paper replaces the vague hope of "robust policy learning" with an explicit interface for uncertainty propagation and action filtering.
notes.finalDecision: Keep the note. Not a must-read paper, but a credible reference for explicit uncertainty handling in manipulation planning.

notes.title: VectorWorld: Efficient Streaming World Model via Diffusion Flow on Vector Graphs
notes.whySelected: It targets the actual deployment bottlenecks of closed-loop driving world models instead of pretending open-loop sample quality is enough.
notes.verdictText: This is a strong systems paper if the implementation details hold up. The pitch I buy is the interface choice: vector graphs, history-aware interaction state, one-step frontier completion, and explicit stabilization against long-horizon drift. I inspected the abstract plus substantial introduction/method text, but not the full experiment section, so I trust the conceptual contribution more than the exact size of the reported gains.
notes.overview: VectorWorld is a streaming driving world model built for closed-loop simulation rather than offline pretty-rollout demos. It represents local scenes as heterogeneous vector graphs of lanes and agents, uses a motion-aware gated VAE to encode a policy-compatible interaction state with short motion history, and performs masked completion / outpainting of frontier graph regions with an edge-gated relational DiT trained for large-step or one-step generation. To keep simulations from slowly turning into nonsense, it also adds a physics-aligned NPC policy, DeltaSim, aimed at preserving kinematic feasibility over kilometer-scale rollouts.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is a good reminder that world-model value often lives in interface design under deployment constraints. The representation and rollout contract matter more than another pretty offline sample.
notes.finalDecision: Worth keeping as a systems reference. Probably not a foundational paper, but it is materially more useful than another generic driving diffusion model.

notes.title: OmniVTA: Visuo-Tactile World Modeling for Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
notes.whySelected: It is one of the cleaner recent cases where a predictive multimodal model is tied directly to a real control interface instead of being bolted on as branding.
notes.verdictText: This is a real mechanism paper, not just a multimodal robotics collage. The strongest part is not the dataset scale by itself, but the way short-horizon tactile prediction is used to modulate policy behavior and drive a 60 Hz corrective loop. I have inspected the abstract plus substantial introduction/method text, but not every experiment table in full detail, so the mechanism judgment is firmer than the exact empirical margin audit.
notes.overview: OmniVTA targets contact-rich manipulation tasks where vision alone underspecifies the state because force, friction, slip, and subtle contact transitions matter. The paper contributes both a large visuo-tactile-action dataset, OmniViTac, and a four-part control stack: a tactile representation model, a two-stream visuo-tactile world model for short-horizon prediction, a contact-aware fusion policy that compares predicted and observed tactile features, and a reflexive latent tactile controller running at 60 Hz for fast correction. The point is not merely to add touch to a policy, but to use predictive contact dynamics to structure closed-loop control.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is a clean example of multimodal structure paying rent. The predictive piece affects control, which is the criterion we should keep using when papers throw around “world model” language.
notes.finalDecision: Worth preserving and likely worth a real read. Even if some of the naming is slightly ambitious, the mechanism is concrete and the control logic is defensible.

notes.title: MosaicMem: Hybrid Spatial Memory for Controllable Video World Models
notes.whySelected: It proposes a patch-level hybrid spatial memory that is more usable than raw frame memory and less brittle than a fully explicit 3D cache.
notes.verdictText: This is a good memory-interface paper, even if I would not oversell the world-model label. The central idea—patches as the memory unit—is practical and transferable. It gives enough explicit structure for retrieval and editing without forcing the system into a rigid global cache.
notes.overview: MosaicMem targets long-horizon controllable video rollouts where revisit consistency and camera adherence matter. Instead of storing whole frames or a monolithic explicit scene cache, it stores patches as memory units. These patches are lifted into 3D with an external estimator, retrieved for a queried view, aligned with warped attention/latent mechanisms, and injected back into a controllable video diffusion model as conditioning. The result is a hybrid explicit/implicit memory interface.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is a good example of structure paying rent by changing retrieval and editability, not just adding terminology.
notes.finalDecision: Worth skimming carefully. Useful memory/interface ideas, with less conceptual force than VGGT-World.

notes.title: GSMem: 3D Gaussian Splatting as Persistent Spatial Memory for Zero-Shot Embodied Exploration and Reasoning
notes.whySelected: It frames memory quality around post-hoc re-observability, which is a better criterion than just storing snapshots or object labels.
notes.verdictText: This is not a breakthrough in world modeling, but it contains one genuinely worthwhile idea: persistent spatial memory should support re-rendering from better viewpoints after the fact. That is a real memory interface improvement. I inspected the abstract and substantial introduction/method text, but not the full empirical section.
notes.overview: GSMem uses 3D Gaussian Splatting as a persistent embodied memory so an agent can render new views of already explored regions instead of being trapped by whatever snapshots it first saw. To make that practical, it combines an object-level scene graph with an online language field over the Gaussian memory for retrieval, then selects candidate viewpoints around retrieved regions and renders them for downstream VLM reasoning. It also mixes semantic task relevance with a 3DGS coverage objective during exploration, so memory construction is supposed to be both useful and geometrically complete.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it sharpens a good criterion: memory is useful when it lets the system recover missing information, not just remember a lossy first pass.
notes.finalDecision: Worth preserving as adjacent inspiration. The memory-interface idea is stronger than the broader world-model framing.

notes.title: Edit-As-Act: Goal-Regressive Planning for Open-Vocabulary 3D Indoor Scene Editing
notes.whySelected: It frames 3D editing as symbolic goal satisfaction with explicit preconditions and effects, which is a real mechanism rather than pseudo-planning wallpaper.
notes.verdictText: This is not a direct world-model paper, but it is exactly the kind of explicit-structure paper worth tracking. The key move is simple and strong: treat editing as valid state transitions toward a desired target world state, not as free-form regeneration.
notes.overview: Edit-As-Act converts language-guided 3D editing into backward planning over symbolic predicates and action schemas. It introduces a PDDL-like action language for scene editing with preconditions, add/delete effects, and geometric constraints such as collision, support, and stability. An LLM proposes actions, a validator rejects bad or non-monotone moves, and source-aware regression pushes remaining preconditions backward until they are grounded in the source scene. The resulting plan is then executed by a deterministic runtime.
notes.whyItMatters: It is a clean example of explicit structure that has operational consequences. That is exactly the kind of paper worth preserving.
notes.finalDecision: Read if you care about structured generation, editing, or symbolic interfaces. Mechanism-first and actually respectable.

notes.title: WorldStereo: Bridging Camera-Guided Video Generation and Scene Reconstruction via 3D Geometric Memories
notes.whySelected: It introduces a believable two-memory recipe for geometry-consistent multi-view generation, even if the world-model framing is overstated.
notes.verdictText: This is a mechanism paper, not a foundational world-model paper. Its real contribution is the split between coarse global geometric memory and local stereo-style memory for fine consistency. That split is worth stealing. The “powerful world model” branding is doing more work than the underlying concept.
notes.overview: WorldStereo starts with a pretrained camera-guided video diffusion model and bolsters it with two explicit memory systems. A global geometric memory accumulates a point-cloud cache from generated views to anchor coarse scene structure and camera consistency. A spatial stereo memory retrieves overlapping reference views, builds 3D correspondences, and restricts attention to matched target-reference pairs so fine details stay more consistent across trajectories. The result is a pragmatic system aimed at generating videos that are more reconstructible in 3D.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it offers a credible modularity lesson: if different kinds of consistency matter, give them different memory mechanisms instead of pretending one giant latent state will gracefully do everything.
notes.finalDecision:
Skim first, then mine the mechanism. Useful for memory design; weaker as a conceptual anchor.

---

notes.title: Imagine a City: CityGenAgent for Procedural 3D City Generation
notes.whySelected: It uses executable hierarchical programs for 3D city generation, so its decomposition is real rather than prompt-shaped theater.
notes.verdictText: This is not a core world-model paper, but it is a respectable structured-generation paper. The main reason to keep it is that its block-level and building-level programs are executable, editable, and tied to different responsibilities. The main reason not to oversell it is that parts of the reward/evaluation story lean too heavily on GPT judging and hand-designed priors.
notes.overview: CityGenAgent frames city-scale 3D generation as hierarchical program synthesis from natural language. One module generates a block-level program describing the city layout and coarse object footprints. A second module generates building-level programs that fill in architectural detail. The system is trained first to produce valid structured programs and then refined with RL using layout- and appearance-oriented rewards. Because the representation is executable, edits can target the actual intermediate structure rather than just re-prompting the model and hoping.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it is a good example of decomposition that survives execution. If structure cannot be edited, constrained, or run, it is often just a narrative overlay.
notes.finalDecision:
Useful but not urgent. Good decomposition example; not the center of gravity.

---

notes.title: Beyond Pixel Histories: World Models with Persistent 3D State
notes.whySelected: It proposes a real representational shift for interactive world models by storing a persistent latent 3D world-state instead of pretending frame history is memory.
notes.verdictText: This is the strongest paper in the batch because it changes the memory substrate rather than polishing the output surface. The core idea—persistent latent 3D state plus explicit camera querying—is conceptually clean, highly transferable, and much more serious than “longer-context video world model” theater. The main caveat is that the current evidence leans on simulator-side 3D and camera supervision, so real-world robustness is not yet the headline.
notes.overview: PERSIST treats the world model as a system that should remember a world, not just recent frames. It maintains a persistent latent 3D voxelized scene state, predicts how that state evolves under actions, predicts the camera state, projects the relevant latent world features into view space, and renders the next frame through a learned image generator. That decomposition gives fixed-cost memory over long rollouts, cleaner revisitation behavior, and a more defensible route to off-screen persistence than ordinary rolling-window video prediction.
notes.whyItMatters: Because it sharpens the actual question: what should a world model remember? If the answer is still “recent frames,” we are often just doing prettier imitation. This paper points toward a stronger answer.
notes.finalDecision:
Read carefully. This is a serious paper, not just another world-model title with nicer samples.

---

related.title: Explicit Structure in World Models and Planning
related.overview: A useful split is emerging between papers that merely generate futures and papers that impose structure that actually changes planning.

related.title: State That Carries the Claim
related.overview: A useful pattern is crystallizing across recent agent, memory, world-model, interpretability, and evaluation papers: the best work does not merely claim that some hidden state matters. It makes that state carry a specific job, then tests whether it survives the moment where surface fluency would otherwise let the system fake it.

related.title: Structured Memory Beyond Latent Mush
related.overview: A useful shift is happening across recent embodied, VLA, and world-model papers: “memory” is slowly stopping its job as a vague synonym for longer context.

related.title: VLA Memory and Continual Learning
related.overview: Recent VLA memory papers are converging on a more useful and more uncomfortable truth: “memory” is not one thing, and most papers still underspecify it.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-05

## Theme

Today's strongest pattern is **world models are being pulled into the evaluation and control loop, not just the video-generation stack**. **PiL-World** is the most relevant paper because it makes generated rollouts answer a closed-loop VLA evaluation question: if the policy sees generated observations and acts again, do imagined success rates track real robot success rates? **World-Language-Action** is the best architecture paper because it splits next state into textual intention plus compact physical dynamics, then uses that split to tie language progress, future-state supervision, and action generation together. **MPCoT** and **CLAW** are useful adjacent context, but I am not preserving full notes for them today.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider, but it returned `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv search was also attempted from the CLI path and returned HTTP 403. The arXiv export API returned `Rate exceeded`, so discovery used arXiv category listings, ordinary web search, and direct arXiv pages/PDFs. This makes discovery less broad than a working Brave-plus-AlphaXiv pass, but the preserved papers are not abstract-only.

I inspected arXiv PDFs for **PiL-World: A Chunk-Wise World Model for VLA Policy-in-the-Loop Evaluation**, **World-Language-Action Model for Unified World Modeling, Language Reasoning, and Action Synthesis**, **MPCoT: Reward-Guided Multi-Path Latent Reasoning for Test-Time Scalable Vision-Language-Action**, and **CLAW: Learning Continuous Latent Action World Models via Adversarial Latent Regularization**. I also screened today's arXiv robotics, computer vision, AI, and ML listings for world-model, VLA, memory, planning, action, and 3D-generation candidates. PiL-World and WLA are preserved. MPCoT is treated as useful citation material for latent test-time compute. CLAW is promising but less directly useful today than the closed-loop evaluation and language-world-action papers.

**PiL-World** is the cleanest hit. It targets the gap between open-loop action-conditioned prediction and real VLA evaluation, where the policy repeatedly observes, acts, and re-plans. The paper alternates a frozen VLA policy with a chunk-wise world model, feeding terminal generated observations back into the policy. It reports the average real-imagined success-rate gap dropping from 63.2% for Ctrl-World to 12.0%, and a 0.94 Pearson correlation across task-checkpoint settings.

**World-Language-Action** is the broader architecture paper. It argues that the next state for embodied control should include both semantic textual intention and compact physical dynamics. A World Expert supervises the physical-dynamics latent during training, while an Action Expert maps that latent plus proprioception into action chunks. The World Expert can be disabled for fast inference or used for test-time scaling. The most useful evidence is not the leaderboard sweep by itself, but the RMBench result: removing language subtask prediction drops average success from 56.5% to 17.3%, suggesting the textual progress trace is doing real work on memory-dependent tasks.

**MPCoT** is a reasonable mechanism paper, but I am keeping it as citation material rather than a full note. Its multi-path latent reasoning layer improves CALVIN long-horizon success and preserves the action interface without generating reasoning tokens. The idea is useful, but the paper is narrower and sits closer to an internal compute module than to a new world-model/state contract.

**CLAW** is good adjacent latent-action work. It jointly learns continuous latent actions and a diffusion world model from action-free videos, using adversarial regularization to discourage future-frame leakage. It is worth remembering for latent action learning from observation, but today's stronger cabbageland signal is about closed-loop evaluation and explicit semantic/physical state interfaces.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **PiL-World: A Chunk-Wise World Model for VLA Policy-in-the-Loop Evaluation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it makes imagined robot rollouts answer the right question: whether generated observations can stay credible enough for the policy to act on them again and preserve real policy ranking.

### 2. **World-Language-Action Model for Unified World Modeling, Language Reasoning, and Action Synthesis**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as an architecture and long-horizon memory paper.

Why it matters: it gives future state a semantic subtask trace and a compact physical-dynamics latent, then uses both to shape action generation.

### 3. **MPCoT: Reward-Guided Multi-Path Latent Reasoning for Test-Time Scalable Vision-Language-Action**

**Verdict:** mostly citation material today.

Why it matters: it is a clean example of token-free latent test-time compute for VLA policies, with useful depth/width ablations, but it is less central than the world-model papers.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** PiL-World.

The steal-worthy idea is the evaluation contract. A generated rollout should not merely be visually plausible under a fixed action path. It should remain useful as the policy's next observation. That distinction matters because VLA errors compound through the observation-action loop. PiL-World directly tests whether imagined success rates match real robot success rates across policy checkpoints, and it adds a hallucination-free ratio so that matching a success label does not hide an incoherent process.

WLA is the architecture to keep close behind it. The useful part is the split next-state interface: textual intention for semantic progress, compact physical dynamics for action-relevant transition information, and optional future-frame prediction for supervision or candidate scoring. That is a better story than asking a giant latent to somehow be memory, dynamics, and policy all at once.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**PiL-World** raises the evaluation bar for robot world models. If a paper claims policy evaluation from generated rollouts, open-loop prediction on pre-collected actions is no longer enough. The generated observations should be fed back into the policy, and the paper should report whether imagined success rates track real success rates.

**WLA** raises a framing question for WAM/VLA papers: where does semantic progress live, and does future-state supervision actually affect action? Its ablations suggest that language subtask memory and world-model supervision can be more than decoration, at least on long-horizon manipulation benchmarks.

**MPCoT** is useful baseline pressure for test-time compute claims. It shows that explicit textual chain-of-thought is not the only way to add deliberation; latent depth and width can improve long-horizon execution while keeping the action interface unchanged.

**CLAW** is useful background for latent action learning. If future papers claim action-free video pretraining for robot control, they should address leakage, collapse, and how latent actions are grounded back into executable controls.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **PiL-World** because it makes world models serve closed-loop policy evaluation instead of open-loop video prediction. The best architecture paper is **World-Language-Action**, because it gives next state two operational faces: language-level progress and compact physical dynamics. The day also surfaced useful supporting work on latent test-time compute and action-free latent-action world models, but the main lesson is sharper: world models become valuable when they define what the policy can observe, remember, test, or score next.

## Detailed notes

- [PiL-World note](../paper_notes/pil_world_chunk_wise_world_model_vla_policy_in_loop_evaluation.md)
- [World-Language-Action note](../paper_notes/world_language_action_model_unified_world_modeling_language_reasoning_action_synthesis.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-04-28

## Theme

Today’s strongest pattern is explicit intermediate structure that actually constrains behavior. The good papers do not merely say “hierarchical” or “compositional.” They introduce a concrete state, phase split, or proxy representation that changes what the model is allowed to ignore.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run, but discovery was blocked because the Brave Search API key is missing. I then used direct arXiv API scouting and inspected the abstract plus substantial method text from arXiv HTML pages for **CodeGraphVLP: Code-as-Planner Meets Semantic-Graph State for Non-Markovian Vision-Language-Action Models**, **Move-Then-Operate: Behavioral Phasing for Human-Like Robotic Manipulation**, **Prox-E: Fine-Grained 3D Shape Editing via Primitive-Based Abstractions**, and **MoT-HRA: Learning Human-Intention Priors from Large-Scale Human Demonstrations for Robotic Manipulation**. The first three survived the bar; MoT-HRA looks ambitious and potentially useful, but I am not preserving a note today because the current evidence still looks more like a large-pipeline representation package than a clean mechanism paper.

The strongest direct hit is **CodeGraphVLP**. It addresses a real long-horizon VLA failure mode, namely that short-horizon controllers and history stuffing both break when the evidence you need is sparse, occluded, or drowned in clutter. The useful move is to externalize task progress into a persistent semantic graph, then run an executable code planner over that state instead of repeatedly asking a VLM to reason from snapshots.

**Move-Then-Operate** is simpler but sharper than most VLA mixture-of-experts papers. Its claim is that coarse transport and contact-critical manipulation have meaningfully different action statistics, so training them as one policy produces interference and underlearns the delicate part. That could easily have been empty branding, but the phase split is at least concrete, and the paper ties it to chunk-level routing and phase-supervised flow-matching experts rather than generic MoE mush.

**Prox-E** is the most useful adjacent paper. It is not about robotics, but it is a clean example of using an explicit proxy representation so a vision-language model can edit structure rather than just vibe over pixels. The primitive abstraction is doing real work: it gives the model a small symbolic-ish handle for metric edits, part insertion, deletion, and local preservation that 2D-image-driven 3D editors usually fake badly.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **CodeGraphVLP: Code-as-Planner Meets Semantic-Graph State for Non-Markovian Vision-Language-Action Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it replaces history mush and repeated VLM replanning with an explicit persistent scene state plus executable planner logic, which is much closer to a real controllable interface for long-horizon manipulation.

### 2. **Move-Then-Operate: Behavioral Phasing for Human-Like Robotic Manipulation**

**Verdict:** useful and plausibly steal-worthy.

Why it matters: it makes a narrow but defensible claim that action generation should separate relocation from contact-critical adjustment, and then actually builds that split into the policy instead of leaving it as motivational poetry.

### 3. **Prox-E: Fine-Grained 3D Shape Editing via Primitive-Based Abstractions**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it shows how a crude explicit proxy can make a strong generative model much more controllable by routing edits through interpretable primitives rather than trusting pixel-space editors to understand geometry.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** CodeGraphVLP.

The paper’s best idea is not “use code” in the vague current-fashion sense. It is to maintain a compact semantic graph of task-relevant entities and relations, update it online, and make the planner operate over that explicit state. That directly attacks two recurring failure modes: first, a history buffer is expensive and still easy to lose the one crucial past fact inside; second, language-only subtask interfaces leave grounding too brittle when scenes are cluttered.

What is worth stealing is the interface discipline. The planner does not reason over raw images every time. It reasons over a compressed task state that has names, relations, and update rules. Then it outputs both the next subtask and the relevant objects, which are used to suppress clutter before the downstream VLA acts. Even if the exact implementation is fragile, the decomposition is genuinely good.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

CodeGraphVLP strengthens the case that memory for VLAs should often be explicit state, not just more context tokens. A persistent graph plus cheap programmatic progress checks is a better baseline than either blind history stuffing or endlessly re-querying a VLM.

Move-Then-Operate adds a narrower baseline challenge: if a manipulation benchmark is dominated by easy transport frames, average action loss can hide the fact that the interesting operate phase is underfit. That is a useful criticism of monolithic policy training even if the two-phase split is not the final answer.

Prox-E matters mostly for framing. It is a good reminder that “training-free” can still mean structurally opinionated in a good way, and that explicit coarse abstractions are often enough to make big generators substantially less slippery.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The good papers today all put something explicit between raw perception and final action or generation. CodeGraphVLP adds a persistent semantic graph and executable planner. Move-Then-Operate adds a hard behavioral phase split between transport and precision interaction. Prox-E adds a primitive proxy that converts a fuzzy text-guided edit problem into a constrained structural editing problem. None of these fully solve their domains, and all still depend on learned components that can fail. But they are moving in the right direction: if you want controllability, compositionality, or long-horizon reliability, give the model a representation where cheating is harder.

## Detailed notes

- [CodeGraphVLP note](../paper_notes/codegraphvlp_non_markovian_vla_semantic_graph_planner.md)
- [Move-Then-Operate note](../paper_notes/move_then_operate_behavioral_phasing_human_like_robotic_manipulation.md)
- [Prox-E note](../paper_notes/prox_e_primitive_based_3d_shape_editing.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-03-26

## Theme
The interesting world-model papers this week are not merely predicting prettier futures. They are changing the planning substrate: compressing state hard enough to make decision-time planning feasible, or making the simulator stable enough to serve as a data engine. The weak point is obvious too: several papers are still better at selling “interactive world models” than at proving the structure is the right one.

## Short overview
Today’s strongest paper is **Planning in 8 Tokens: A Compact Discrete Tokenizer for Latent World Model**. It is the cleanest mechanistic hit because it attacks a real bottleneck: token count. Instead of treating photorealistic reconstruction as sacred, it uses an aggressively compressed discrete tokenizer built on frozen vision features, then trains a world model in that compact latent space for planning. The result matters because it reframes tokenizer design around decision-time control rather than image fidelity.

The second worthwhile paper is **Interactive World Simulator for Robot Policy Training and Evaluation**. This is less elegant conceptually, but more ambitious operationally: an action-conditioned latent video simulator fast enough for interactive rollout, long enough to train policies inside it, and grounded enough that simulator performance correlates with real-world performance. If the claim holds under wider stress, this is useful infrastructure. The caution is that pixel-level consistency and policy utility do not automatically mean the simulator learned the right internal state.

I also inspected **Beyond Dense Futures: World Models as Structured Planners for Robotic Manipulation**. The framing is attractive — replace dense rollouts with sparse, kinematically meaningful structured frames — but I only had abstract-level access, not enough method detail to trust the mechanism yet. For now it looks promising but unverified.

## Ranked papers

1. **Planning in 8 Tokens: A Compact Discrete Tokenizer for Latent World Model**  
   - Verdict: **Highly relevant**  
   - Role: **Directly relevant**  
   - Why it matters: It makes world-model planning computationally plausible by compressing each observation to a tiny discrete state that still preserves action-relevant structure.

2. **Interactive World Simulator for Robot Policy Training and Evaluation**  
   - Verdict: **Useful**  
   - Role: **Directly relevant**  
   - Why it matters: It treats the world model as a practical interactive simulator for data generation and policy evaluation, not just a demo video generator.

3. **Beyond Dense Futures: World Models as Structured Planners for Robotic Manipulation**  
   - Verdict: **Skimmable for now**  
   - Role: **Adjacent inspiration**  
   - Why it matters: The sparse structured-frame idea could be important, but I do not yet trust the paper enough to preserve a full note.

## Most relevant to cabbageland
**Planning in 8 Tokens** is the best fit. The key point is not just speed. It is that the paper treats compression as an architectural filter on what the model is allowed to remember. If planning only needs semantics and spatial relations, then a tokenizer optimized for reconstruction is probably optimizing the wrong thing.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact
- **Planning substrate:** CompACT is a useful citation against the lazy assumption that better world models require fatter latents. Sometimes the right move is harsher compression with better inductive bias.
- **Evaluation framing:** Interactive World Simulator is useful if we need to argue that world models should be judged by downstream data utility and checkpoint-ranking fidelity, not only rollout visuals.
- **Structured-planning caution:** StructVLA may become a good citation for sparse physically meaningful planning targets, but right now my confidence is too low because I only inspected the abstract and metadata.
- **Confidence note:** I inspected the abstract plus substantial method text for **Planning in 8 Tokens** and **Interactive World Simulator**. For **Beyond Dense Futures / StructVLA**, I only inspected the abstract, so I am explicitly not claiming a full read.

## One-paragraph takeaway
The useful question today is: what is the world model actually storing, and at what computational cost? **Planning in 8 Tokens** says the state should be brutally compact and optimized for planning rather than reconstruction. **Interactive World Simulator** says the state should at least be stable and interactive enough to support long rollouts, synthetic demonstrations, and reproducible policy evaluation. **StructVLA** suggests another route — sparse kinematic milestones instead of dense futures — but it still needs a real read before it graduates from interesting title to trustworthy mechanism. The shared lesson is simple: if a paper says “world model” without specifying the planning object, the state bottleneck, and the failure mode under long horizons, it is probably selling atmosphere.

## Detailed notes
- [Planning in 8 Tokens note](../paper_notes/planning_in_8_tokens_compact_discrete_tokenizer_world_model.md)
- [Interactive World Simulator note](../paper_notes/interactive_world_simulator_robot_policy_training_evaluation.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-26

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **aggregate scores hide the failure surface**. A saturated benchmark can still reveal scaffold dependence, unreliable confidence, cost differences, and human-agent uplift. A factuality metric that collapses all retrieved evidence into one corpus misses the case where some sources support a claim and others contradict it. A model-diffing tool that reports reconstruction fidelity can miss the single feature that actually gates tool use.

I kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan covered evaluation, interpretability, agent memory, medical VQA and CT reasoning, retrieval-memory validity, coding-agent verification, SAE infrastructure, multi-model routing, 3D/generative media, scientific ML, and robotics/VLA titles. Robotics/VLA candidates seen in the listings included **Fast LeWorldModel**, **LiMoDE**, **WatchAct**, **Improving Vision-Language-Action Model Fine-Tuning with Structured Stage and Keyframe Supervision**, **Hallucination in World Models is Predictable and Preventable**, and **World Action Models Enable Continual Imitation Learning with Recurrent Generative Replays**; I did not preserve them because today's strongest inspected mechanisms were non-robotics evaluation and interpretability work.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv pages were reachable for the three preserved arXiv IDs, but I used them only as supplemental reachability checks. Discovery therefore relied on arXiv new listings, arXiv abstract pages, direct arXiv PDFs, and targeted full-text inspection. Discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

At 08:00 Pacific on June 26, arXiv listed a large June 26 batch across AI, ML, CL, CV, medical imaging, scientific ML, interpretability, agent systems, and robotics. Full PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text with targeted reads through methods, experiments, results, and limitations for **Life After Benchmark Saturation**, **ConflictScore**, **Localizing RL-Induced Tool Use to a Single Crosscoder Feature**, **Detecting and Controlling Sycophancy with Cascading Linear Features**, **Memory Depth, Not Memory Access**, **Temporal Validity in Retrieval Memory**, **At the Edge of Understanding**, **Discovering Millions of Interpretable Features with Sparse Autoencoders**, **Just how sure are you?**, **CORTEX**, **Instruction Bleed**, **The Verification Horizon**, **When Does Combining Language Models Help?**, and **The Capability Frontier**. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

**Life After Benchmark Saturation** is the most relevant paper today. It argues that benchmark usefulness does not end when accuracy saturates; the remaining signal lives in validity threats, efficiency, reliability, scaffold effects, out-of-distribution behavior, and real human-agent uplift.

**ConflictScore** is the strongest evidence-evaluation paper. It fixes a real blind spot in factuality metrics: a claim can be supported by some retrieved documents and contradicted by others, and a metric that collapses the corpus hides that conflict.

**Localizing RL-Induced Tool Use to a Single Crosscoder Feature** is the sharpest internal-mechanism paper. It finds that an RL-induced tool-use behavior in a Qwen2.5-3B pair can be strongly steered through a tiny A-exclusive crosscoder feature set, with one feature producing a large tool-correctness jump.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Life After Benchmark Saturation: A Case Study of CORE-Bench**

**Verdict:** must read, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it is a clean antidote to accuracy-only agent evaluation. When top agents tie near the ceiling, the benchmark can still expose whether the agent is validly solving the task, how much scaffold matters, how reliable and efficient the system is, and whether it actually helps humans.

### 2. **ConflictScore: Identifying and Measuring How Language Models Handle Conflicting Evidence**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for RAG, memory, and factuality evaluation.

Why it matters: it makes disagreement inside retrieved evidence measurable at the claim-document level, then shows that conflict feedback can improve TruthfulQA answers while prompt-only balancing gives limited leverage.

### 3. **Localizing RL-Induced Tool Use to a Single Crosscoder Feature**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for mechanistic interpretability of agentic behavior.

Why it matters: it suggests that at least some post-training-installed agent skills can condense into sparse, steerable internal features rather than living only as diffuse behavioral changes.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Life After Benchmark Saturation.

The steal is the measurement frame. Once headline accuracy saturates, do not throw the benchmark away by reflex. First ask whether stronger agents reveal validity bugs, shortcuts, scaffold sensitivity, confidence failures, compute inefficiency, out-of-distribution gaps, or human workflow uplift. Those are often the parts that matter for deployment.

ConflictScore gives the evidence version of the same lesson. Do not ask only whether an answer has support somewhere in the retrieved context. Ask whether the answer acknowledged the contradictory evidence it was also shown.

The crosscoder tool-use paper gives the internal version: do not trust reconstruction metrics alone. A representation can reconstruct well while the behaviorally decisive signal lives in a tiny feature subset.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Life After Benchmark Saturation** is strong because it does not merely complain about benchmark saturation. It repairs CORE-Bench Hard into CORE-Bench v1.1, builds a 19-task CORE-Bench OOD suite, and then asks what else can still be measured. The main practical results are useful: top agents cluster near 97% to 100% accuracy, Codex CLI with GPT-5.4 medium beats CORE-Agent with the same model by roughly 44 points on v1.1, agents report confidence far below their empirical pass rate, and a small randomized human-agent study estimates manual sessions took 2.11 times as long as human-agent sessions. The caveat is real: the uplift study has only 20 papers, 5 participants, no independent ground-truth reproduction outcome, and non-representative reproducers.

**ConflictScore** is useful because it changes the unit of factuality from "does the corpus support the claim?" to "which documents support, contradict, or ignore each atomic claim?" This distinguishes ordinary support from unresolved conflict. On a ConflictingQA slice, stronger conflict-aware prompts only modestly change model behavior, suggesting prompt prose is not enough. On TruthfulQA, conflict-aware regeneration improves multiple-choice accuracy across the reported models; on conflict-detected subsets, originally wrong answers are corrected much more often than originally correct answers are harmed. The main caveats are cost, claim-decomposition sensitivity, evidence-labeling errors, and the current lack of source-reliability weighting.

**Localizing RL-Induced Tool Use** is sharp but narrow. The paper trains 48 crosscoder variants over a ToolRL-fine-tuned Qwen2.5-3B pair and finds that post-reconstruction improves the RL model's tool correctness by 31.1 points on average, while a frozen base model gains 6.8 points of tool correctness through capability spillover. The most striking result is steering: one A-exclusive feature at layer 13 raises tool correctness by 65 points in the reported cell, and the effect generalizes across most probed layers. The caveat is scope: one model pair, one tool-call behavior, 100 held-out prompts per sweep variant, 40 prompts per steering cell, and no claim that all RL-induced agent skills will localize this cleanly.

**Detecting and Controlling Sycophancy with Cascading Linear Features** was the strongest safety-control runner-up. It uses graded behavior generation plus SAE feature selection to find sycophancy features that scale monotonically and can be used for detection and steering. I kept it below the note line because the crosscoder tool-use paper was a cleaner agentic-behavior mechanism today, but CLiF is worth revisiting for behavior-control tooling.

**The Verification Horizon** is an important field report from the Qwen team. Its main message is right: coding-agent reward design needs co-evolving verifiers, not one fixed reward. I kept it as framing rather than a preserved note because it is broad, partly internal-benchmark-driven, and less crisp as a single transferable mechanism than CORE-Bench.

**Just how sure are you?** is the strongest medical calibration runner-up. Its 2 by 2 image/text perturbation training signal and composite calibration loss are useful, and the reported calibration reductions are large. I kept it below the line because it is a domain-specific training method, while ConflictScore is more immediately reusable for agent evidence handling.

**CORTEX** is a useful medical benchmark resource: it restores 3D chest CT reasoning as four clinical stages and adds stage-level rubrics. It is more dataset construction than tested model mechanism, so it stays as adjacent healthcare infrastructure.

**Memory Depth, Not Memory Access** and **Temporal Validity in Retrieval Memory** both line up with recent Paper Daily memory themes. I kept them below the line to avoid repeating yesterday's source-versus-conclusion story. Memory Depth is an interesting synthetic split between retrieval access and parametric goal persistence, but it is narrow and its stale-memory boundary is explicitly unresolved. Temporal Validity has a strong deterministic supersession idea for structured mutable facts, but the current claim depends on structured single-value templates and extraction quality.

**When Does Combining Language Models Help?** and **The Capability Frontier** pull in opposite directions on routing. The former says the all-models-wrong tail bounds model orchestration; the latter says single-model benchmarks understate achievable frontier performance. The useful synthesis is that routing value depends on heterogeneity, co-failure, cost, and whether a real router can approach the oracle. Neither beat today's top three, but both sharpen evaluation framing.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all reject the easy aggregate. **Life After Benchmark Saturation** says saturated accuracy is not saturated evaluation. **ConflictScore** says a supported answer can still be misleading if it ignores contradictory retrieved evidence. **Localizing RL-Induced Tool Use** says reconstruction quality is not enough; the behavior may be controlled by a sparse feature hidden inside the representation. Same rule across levels: measure the thing that can fail, not the headline number that stays smooth while the failure moves underneath.

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-05

## Theme

Today’s strongest paper is not the biggest release. It is the one with the clearest structural bet: combine an explicit particle physics prior with an equivariant learned correction so low-data manipulation dynamics stay physically plausible over longer horizons. The rest of the shortlist is more mixed. MolmoAct2 is a serious open VLA release with meaningful engineering choices, but it is also a bundle paper, so the transferable mechanism is less crisp than the headline scale. Latent Bridge is useful systems work on skipping redundant VLM calls, though it is best understood as a practical efficiency patch, not as a new action model.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run, but discovery was blocked because the Brave Search API key is missing. I then scouted recent arXiv listings directly, especially cs.RO, cs.AI, and cs.CV, and inspected abstracts plus substantial method text from arXiv HTML pages for **Learning Equivariant Neural-Augmented Object Dynamics From Few Interactions**, **MolmoAct2: Action Reasoning Models for Real-world Deployment**, **Latent Bridge: Feature Delta Prediction for Efficient Dual-System Vision-Language-Action Model Inference**, and **Semantic Risk-Aware Heuristic Planning for Robotic Navigation in Dynamic Environments**.

**Learning Equivariant Neural-Augmented Object Dynamics From Few Interactions** is the clear direct hit. The useful move is to split the dynamics model into an explicit spring-mass simulator that enforces short-horizon physical feasibility and an action-conditioned equivariant graph network that nudges that simulator over longer horizons. I inspected the abstract, introduction, problem formulation, related-work positioning, and substantial method text from the arXiv HTML page, including the action canonicalization argument and the hybrid analytical-plus-neural setup. The main attraction is that the structure is doing real work rather than merely naming a hybrid.

**MolmoAct2** is important, but more as a major open-systems release than as a single elegant conceptual advance. I inspected the abstract, introduction, the Molmo2-ER training recipe, and the architecture description available in the arXiv HTML page. The strongest specific mechanism is probably the per-layer KV-cache conditioning used to graft a continuous flow-matching action expert onto a discrete-token VLM, plus the adaptive-depth reasoning variant that only re-predicts changed depth regions. Still, a lot of the paper’s weight comes from scale, curation, and bundling multiple improvements at once.

**Latent Bridge** is useful adjacent inspiration. I inspected the abstract, introduction, problem formulation, and architecture section from the arXiv HTML page. The core idea is simple: treat consecutive VLM states in a dual-system VLA as redundant, predict latent deltas between backbone calls, and use DAgger to train against the bridge’s own rollout distribution. That is a sensible deployment-minded move, but it is an efficiency wrapper around existing backbones and action heads, not a deeper representational change.

**Semantic Risk-Aware Heuristic Planning** did not survive filtering. The paper calls its cost shaping “LLM-inspired,” but the accessible evidence is basically a hand-designed A* heuristic evaluated in a tiny gridworld. That is exactly the sort of renamed mush the repo should not reward.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Learning Equivariant Neural-Augmented Object Dynamics From Few Interactions**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it uses explicit physical structure and symmetry constraints to make learned manipulation dynamics more data-efficient and more stable, especially for deformable objects.

### 2. **MolmoAct2: Action Reasoning Models for Real-world Deployment**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it is a substantial open VLA package with real deployment ambition, but the paper is more valuable as a reference point for architecture, data, and systems choices than as one clean new mechanism.

### 3. **Latent Bridge: Feature Delta Prediction for Efficient Dual-System Vision-Language-Action Model Inference**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it frames VLA latency as redundant latent-state recomputation and replaces some backbone calls with a lightweight learned bridge.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Learning Equivariant Neural-Augmented Object Dynamics From Few Interactions.

The strong part is the division of labor. Instead of asking a graph network to learn all object dynamics from scratch, the paper uses a spring-mass simulator to preserve basic physical sanity, then uses an action-conditioned equivariant graph network to provide the corrective signal that the analytical model cannot capture. That is exactly the kind of explicit-state, explicit-bias arrangement worth paying attention to. The model is not pretending the neural part alone discovered physics, and it is not pretending the analytical model alone can explain real deformable behavior.

I also like that the symmetry story seems operational rather than decorative. The paper does not just say “equivariance” because it sounds principled. It explicitly argues that low-data action effects should transform consistently with object pose, then canonicalizes actions around that fact. If that holds up empirically, it is a good example of using symmetry as a sample-efficiency tool rather than as branding.

The main caveat is scope. I inspected substantial method text, but not every table and appendix detail, and the task domain is still tabletop object manipulation rather than a richer persistent world setting. So this is a strong mechanism paper for local object dynamics, not a full answer to long-horizon world modeling.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

PIEGraph sharpens a good baseline question for manipulation world models: if a method claims data efficiency or long-horizon physical plausibility, where exactly is the physical constraint living? If the answer is “only in the training data” or “only in the architecture marketing,” that is weak. Here the answer is concrete: an explicit simulator handles feasibility while the learned model handles residual structure.

MolmoAct2 matters more for framing than for a single clean baseline replacement. It strengthens the case that open VLAs can now compete seriously when they combine stronger embodied reasoning data, better action interfaces, and deployment-conscious design. But because the paper bundles backbone specialization, new datasets, a tokenizer, a new action connection, and a reasoning variant, it is harder to isolate which ingredient future work should copy first.

Latent Bridge affects evaluation taste. For dual-system VLAs, papers should probably stop quoting only per-step model quality while ignoring whether they are recomputing nearly identical VLM states every control cycle. Still, it is an optimization paper, not a new cognitive architecture.

## One-paragraph takeaway

Today’s best paper earns attention by putting explicit structure where it counts: PIEGraph combines a spring-mass dynamics prior with an equivariant action-conditioned graph model so learned object dynamics stay more physically plausible and data-efficient under limited real interaction data. MolmoAct2 is a real open VLA milestone, but it is better read as a large integrated release than as one sharply steal-worthy mechanism. Latent Bridge is a pragmatic efficiency fix for dual-system VLAs and worth remembering for deployment. The broader lesson is simple: when a robotics paper claims better reasoning or better dynamics, ask whether the improvement comes from an explicit commitment in the state, symmetry, or simulator, or whether it is mostly packaging. Today, the explicit commitment won.

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-19

## Theme

Today’s useful signal is **explicit side channels for information that should not be forced through one monolithic backbone**. The best paper is **Key-Gram: Extensible World Knowledge for Embodied Manipulation** because it externalizes instruction-side world knowledge into a hash-addressed memory and leaves the visuomotor backbone to do scene reasoning and action prediction. **DARE-EEG** is the best non-robotics paper because it notices a real representation failure mode, namely that masked views of the same EEG sample can drift apart in latent space, then adds an explicit alignment mechanism instead of hoping reconstruction loss fixes it. **Actionable World Representation** is the most thematically adjacent 3D/world-model paper, but it overclaims relative to what it actually demonstrates.

## Short overview

Brave Search was unavailable in this run because the environment is missing a Brave API key, so discovery relied on direct inspection of recent arXiv category pages and PDF full text for selected candidates. I inspected PDF full text for **Key-Gram**, **DARE-EEG**, **Actionable World Representation**, **Incantation**, and **Robo-Cortex**. Confidence is strongest on the method structure, problem framing, and headline results for **Key-Gram** and **DARE-EEG**, and weaker on appendix-only details and exact optimization minutiae where the PDF text extraction was messy.

**Key-Gram** is the strongest paper today and the most relevant to cabbageland. Its core move is simple and good: do not let reusable linguistic task knowledge fight for space inside the same dense stream as visual tokens. Instead, parse the instruction into a few reusable key-grams, hash them into a static external memory, and inject those retrieved embeddings into selected backbone layers through gated fusion. That is much more interesting than yet another VLA paper that claims “better multimodal fusion” while keeping the same entangled architecture.

**DARE-EEG** is a strong adjacent representation-learning paper. The useful insight is not EEG-specific hype, it is the insistence that masked views of the same underlying signal should land in a consistent latent subspace. The method adds anchor alignment to full-signal targets plus mask alignment across multiple masked views, which is a clean fix for a real invariance problem in self-supervised learning under partial observation.

**Actionable World Representation** is worth a skim but not a preserved note today. The paper tries to unify articulated, skinned, and soft-object state modeling through a keypoint-conditioned point-cloud generator. That is a legitimate object-state representation problem. The problem is the framing: it sells itself as a building block for physical world models, but the actual evidence is much closer to conditional deformation modeling than to action-conditioned predictive world modeling.

I also inspected **Incantation** and **Robo-Cortex**. Incantation has one real idea, namely using natural language as a per-entity action interface for multi-entity video world models, but the result is mostly about control protocol and long-horizon streaming engineering in games. Robo-Cortex is energetic and sometimes interesting, yet a lot of its “self-evolving cognition” framing is fluff wrapped around heuristic extraction and memory scaffolding.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Key-Gram: Extensible World Knowledge for Embodied Manipulation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it makes language-side world knowledge explicit and extensible instead of hiding it inside a single VLA or world-action backbone.

### 2. **DARE-EEG: A Foundation Model for Mining Dual-Aligned Representation of EEG**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it turns incomplete-observation invariance into an explicit training target instead of a vague hope.

### 3. **Actionable World Representation**

**Verdict:** skimmable adjacent material.

Why it matters: the object-state representation problem is real, but the paper’s world-model rhetoric runs ahead of the evidence.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Key-Gram: Extensible World Knowledge for Embodied Manipulation.

The useful part is not the particular benchmark win. It is the architectural contract. Key-Gram treats instruction-side world knowledge as something that should be stored, addressed, and expanded separately from scene-dynamics computation. It decomposes instructions into compact reusable phrases, retrieves static embeddings through deterministic hashing, and injects them into selected backbone layers with context-aware gating. That gives the paper a real answer to a common failure mode in embodied models: the same backbone is asked to remember object/task priors, parse language, track visual state, and emit actions, then people act surprised when continual extension is brittle.

This matters for cabbageland because it is a concrete mechanism for separating reusable knowledge from online perceptual reasoning without pretending everything must become symbolic. The main caveat is that the key-gram extraction itself is a load-bearing preprocessing step, and some of the paper’s training-objective details are less explicit in the accessible text than the memory mechanism is.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

The main framing update today is that **external memory is most convincing when it carries a clearly typed burden**. Key-Gram is not just another retrieval garnish. It assigns one specific job to memory, reusable instruction-side knowledge, and leaves the backbone to handle visual reasoning and control. That is a cleaner decomposition than most current VLA papers.

DARE-EEG sharpens a different lesson. If learning happens from aggressively masked observations, then invariance across different masks of the same latent state should probably be enforced directly. Reconstruction alone often teaches the model to survive masking, not to represent the underlying state consistently. That general point transfers beyond EEG.

Actionable World Representation is useful mostly as a framing check. It is trying to represent stateful object geometry across articulated, skinned, and soft objects under one transformer-style decoder, which is fine. But calling that a physical world-model building block is still too generous unless the model also earns stronger claims about action-conditioned prediction, composition, or planning.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **Key-Gram** because it gives embodied control a real separation between reusable language-side knowledge and online visual reasoning, instead of shoving both into one latent soup and calling it multimodal intelligence. **DARE-EEG** is a good adjacent note because it makes mask-invariance explicit in self-supervised representation learning under partial observation. **Actionable World Representation** is interesting but mostly as a reminder to be strict about the difference between state-conditioned deformation models and actual world models. The broader pattern is healthy: if a paper claims structure, ask whether the structure has a narrow job and whether that job actually matters.

# Daily Digest — 2026-04-15

## Theme

Today’s useful pattern is explicit structure again, but in three different guises. Lyra 2.0 keeps long-horizon 3D generation from collapsing by separating geometry-based memory routing from pixel synthesis. VGA argues that robot manipulation should be grounded in native 3D geometric representations rather than 2D language or video priors, which is a sharper claim than the current VLA mush. HazardArena is the most practically important paper of the set because it points at a failure mode many VLA papers still dodge: competent action execution can still be semantically unsafe.

## Short overview

Brave search was unavailable in this run because the Brave API key is missing, so discovery fell back to direct arXiv search/result inspection and primary-source reading on arXiv abstract and HTML pages. I inspected the abstract plus substantive method/introduction text from the arXiv HTML pages for the ranked papers. I did not audit appendices or every quantitative table, so the judgments below are strongest on mechanism and framing, slightly softer on exact empirical margins.

The strongest paper today is **Lyra 2.0: Explorable Generative 3D Worlds**. The key idea is not just “generate long videos and reconstruct them into 3D.” The real move is to keep an explicit per-frame 3D proxy only for routing memory and establishing correspondences, while leaving actual appearance synthesis to the video model. That separation matters because it tries to avoid the common failure mode where a corrupted reconstructed scene then poisons future generations. It is a good example of explicit geometry doing real work instead of serving as decorative supervision.

**Robotic Manipulation is Vision-to-Geometry Mapping (VGA)** is the most provocative robot paper in the batch. Its core claim is that manipulation should be grounded in a native 3D world-model backbone rather than a vision-language or video backbone, because physical action is fundamentally about geometry. That claim is a little too sweeping, and the paper still uses language for instructions, so it is not some pure anti-language manifesto. But the structural point is good: if the downstream problem is geometric control, it is healthier to keep geometry native instead of repeatedly squeezing 3D evidence through 2D semantic bottlenecks.

**HazardArena: Evaluating Semantic Safety in Vision-Language-Action Models** is the most useful evaluation paper. The paper’s contribution is not another generic safety score. It builds safe/unsafe twin scenarios that hold motor demands fixed while flipping the semantic permissibility of the action, which is exactly how you test whether a model understands why an action should not be executed rather than merely failing to execute it. The attached Safety Option Layer is less interesting than the benchmark itself, but the benchmark is worth preserving.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Lyra 2.0: Explorable Generative 3D Worlds**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it treats geometry as a memory-routing substrate instead of forcing a single noisy reconstructed world representation to drive both synthesis and consistency.

### 2. **Robotic Manipulation is Vision-to-Geometry Mapping (VGA)**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it makes a clean argument that robot manipulation backbones should stay in native 3D geometry rather than relying on semantically strong but physically misaligned 2D representations.

### 3. **HazardArena: Evaluating Semantic Safety in Vision-Language-Action Models**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it isolates semantic safety from motor failure with safe/unsafe twin tasks, which is a much better evaluation design than unconditional hazard rates.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant:** Lyra 2.0.

The reason is not just that it is a 3D generation paper. It matters because it shows a disciplined way to combine explicit structure with generative priors. The geometry proxy is used for retrieval and correspondence, not for hard rendering-based control of every future frame. That is a nice middle path between “let the latent mush handle it” and “fully trust an accumulated 3D memory that may already be corrupted.” For any future work on world models, spatial memory, or controllable generative environments, that separation feels steal-worthy.

VGA is the better direct robotics provocation. It is useful mainly as framing pressure against the lazy assumption that VLA backbones are automatically the right foundation for manipulation just because they are fashionable.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

Lyra 2.0 is framing pressure on long-horizon scene-generation work that uses a single accumulated 3D memory as both constraint and synthesis driver. The paper’s geometry-for-routing-only stance is genuinely distinctive and worth remembering.

VGA is framing pressure on language-heavy robot stacks. Its strongest contribution is not proving that language is useless, because it plainly is not. Its strongest contribution is highlighting how often current systems project 3D evidence into 2D-centric latent spaces and then act surprised when spatial generalization is brittle.

HazardArena is baseline pressure on nearly every VLA paper that reports safety through end outcomes alone. If a model avoids danger only because it is clumsy, that is not semantic safety. Safe/unsafe twin tasks are a better default for this problem.

## One-paragraph takeaway

Today’s common lesson is that explicit structure should be used where it actually reduces ambiguity. Lyra 2.0 uses geometry as a routing interface for long-horizon generation. VGA keeps manipulation grounded in native 3D representations instead of flattening everything into 2D semantic latents. HazardArena holds motor demands fixed so semantic safety can be measured directly rather than inferred from failure. Different domains, same basic standard: if memory, geometry, or safety semantics matter, they should appear somewhere concrete in the system instead of being left to latent vibes.

## Detailed notes

- [VGA note](../paper_notes/robotic_manipulation_is_vision_to_geometry_mapping.md)
- [HazardArena note](../paper_notes/hazardarena_evaluating_semantic_safety_in_vlas.md)
