# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-24

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **the proxy only counts if it preserves the interface that later does work**. ImageNet FID is not a sufficient proxy for text-to-image DiT progress. A volumetric Gaussian render is not the same thing as usable surface geometry. A file path is not the same thing as a diagnostic handoff to a code-repair agent.

I deliberately kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan covered generative-model evaluation, 3D scene generation, code-repair agents, medical robustness, agent training data, video evidence grounding, agent memory systems, continual learning, scientific/medical AI, and robotics/VLA candidates. The best robotics/VLA candidates were **InSight**, **World Value Models**, and **RoBoSR**, but none beat the strongest non-robotics papers on transferable mechanism today.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv pages were reachable for the serious arXiv IDs I checked, but I used them only as supplemental metadata reachability checks. Discovery therefore relied mainly on the arXiv API and direct arXiv PDFs; discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

At 08:00 Pacific on June 24, the arXiv API returned June 23 uploads as the newest batch in the checked AI, ML, CV, CL, IR, robotics, HCI, statistics, medical, signal-processing, and neuro/scientific lanes. Full PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text with targeted reads through method, experiments, ablations, results, and limitations for **DiffusionBench**, **FLAT**, **SHERLOC**, **BenchX**, **OpenThoughts-Agent**, **GeoT2V-Bench**, **SER**, **DeepBD**, **Can Scale Save Us From Plasticity Loss in Large Language Models?**, **World Models in Pieces**, **Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System?**, **InSight**, **World Value Models**, **RoBoSR**, and several adjacent candidates. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

**DiffusionBench** is the most relevant paper today. It makes a clean evaluation argument: if a DiT method claims broad generative progress, it should not get to hide behind class-conditional ImageNet FID after that proxy stops predicting text-to-image behavior.

**FLAT** is the strongest 3D/generative-media paper today. It decodes video-diffusion latents into explicit triangle splats, and its ablations show that geometry-friendly representation requires real parameterization work rather than a surface-shaped label.

**SHERLOC** is the strongest agent-engineering paper today. It treats code localization as a structured diagnostic object that has to improve a downstream repair agent, not just as a file-retrieval score.

Several runner-ups were useful but stayed below the note line. **BenchX** is a strong medical robustness benchmark: 85,355 CT scans, 12 tumor-detection models, and subgroup/protocol analysis that exposes failures hidden by average F1. I kept it as a runner-up because its main contribution is evaluation coverage rather than a reusable modeling primitive, but it is good deployment-pressure material. **OpenThoughts-Agent** is a serious open data-recipe report with more than 100 ablations and a 100K-example agentic SFT set; it is useful, but more training-data operations than mechanism. **GeoT2V-Bench** is a sharp reconstruction-based audit for camera-prompted text-to-video models, but DiffusionBench and FLAT covered the day's evaluation and 3D representation lanes more directly. **SER** has a good idea, semantic evidence rewards for video reasoning, but the gains are modest and the VLM-referee reward is a place to watch for reward hacking. **DeepBD** is an interesting grounded medical-agent workflow, but its strongest evidence is from an in-house cohort and needs external/prospective validation. **Can Scale Save Us From Plasticity Loss in Large Language Models?** is a useful continual-learning warning, but the model scale remains far below frontier LLMs and the probe design is narrow.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **DiffusionBench: On Holistic Evaluation of Diffusion Transformers**

**Verdict:** must read, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it turns "ImageNet FID improved" from a broad progress claim into a narrower proxy claim that must be tested against text-to-image behavior. The useful move is not another metric; it is a controlled cross-task harness that shows the proxy can flip conclusions.

### 2. **FLAT: Feedforward Latent Triangle Splatting for Geometrically Accurate Scene Generation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for 3D generation and usable scene representations.

Why it matters: it asks the generated scene to become an explicit surface object, not just a pretty volumetric render. The ray-centered triangle parameterization and product window function are the actual mechanism; the win is that geometry becomes part of the output contract.

### 3. **SHERLOC: Structured Diagnostic Localization for Code Repair Agents**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for tool-using code agents and agent handoff design.

Why it matters: it treats localization as a diagnostic interface. A downstream repair agent needs root cause, dependencies, solution direction, and testing impact, not just "probably this file."

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** DiffusionBench.

The steal is the cross-task proxy audit. If a paper claims a model is better at a broad thing, force it to show that the easy benchmark still transfers to the thing being claimed. If the easy benchmark does not transfer, keep it as one diagnostic axis and stop letting it carry the whole story.

FLAT adds the complementary representation lesson: the output format is part of the model's truth claim. If the claim is "usable scene geometry," a Gaussian radiance blob is not enough. You need the generated state to support the downstream operation.

SHERLOC adds the agent-interface version of the same point: handoff state should be shaped for the next actor. A location alone is a lossy proxy for diagnosis; a structured finding can change the repair trajectory and reduce wasted search.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**DiffusionBench** raises the bar for DiT evaluation. NanoGen trains comparable ImageNet and T2I variants by swapping the dataset loader and conditioner, using Qwen3-0.6B text conditioning and JourneyDB plus BLIP-3o caption splits for T2I. Across 21 latent diffusion models, ImageNet FID does not strongly correlate with GenEval, DPG-Bench, or GenAIBench, with Pearson correlations between -0.377 and -0.580 in the main analysis. The caveats are real: the result is limited to the authors' compute scale, T2I metrics remain hackable, and DiffusionBench itself will need refreshing.

**FLAT** is valuable because it makes representation tradeoffs visible. Under matched training, triangle splats get much better normal geometry than 2DGS or 3DGS, with average normal cosine 0.853 versus 0.587 and 0.116. For opaque mesh conversion, triangle outputs are far stronger than 2DGS/3DGS conversions on the reported PSNR numbers. The caveat is that triangles are brittle around thin structures, reflections, transparency, and watertightness; this is not a clean mesh generator yet.

**SHERLOC** is strong because it evaluates whether localization transfers. Its best localizer reaches 84.33 percent accuracy@1 on SWE-Bench Lite and 81.27 percent recall@1 on SWE-Bench Verified; the roughly 30B version still beats the listed 32B baselines on Verified. Injected findings improve average repair resolve rate by 5.95 points while reducing localization tokens by 36.7 percent and total tokens by 23.1 percent. The major caveat is SWE-Bench familiarity: the authors estimate about 58 percent recall from masked issue text alone, so held-out repository distributions remain necessary.

**BenchX** is the strongest healthcare runner-up. It reports large hidden subgroup and protocol failures in tumor detection, including weak performance on rare demographic/protocol combinations. Its LLM-assisted metadata extraction is useful but also a potential audit point; benchmark construction quality matters enormously in this setting.

**OpenThoughts-Agent** is useful because its ablations show that task-source choice and task-description diversity matter more than a vague "more agent data" story. The paper's 100K Qwen3-32B SFT result is strong, but the preserved note bar today went to papers with cleaner reusable mechanisms.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all punish a bad substitute. **DiffusionBench** says ImageNet FID is not the same thing as text-to-image progress. **FLAT** says a Gaussian render is not the same thing as explicit scene geometry. **SHERLOC** says a file path is not the same thing as a repair-ready diagnosis. Different domains, same standard: do not flatten the thing that the next system actually needs.

- [FLAT note](../paper_notes/flat_feedforward_latent_triangle_splatting.md)

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-28

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **the coordinate system is part of the claim**. A Top-k SAE is not interpretable merely because it has k active units; the unused activation tail and effective support still matter. A physical world model is not grounded merely because it predicts video; the state space should carry geometry and motion directly. An uncertainty score is not deployment-relevant merely because it is proper or calibrated; it needs to align with the decision utility it is supposed to serve.

I kept robotics and VLA work out of the top three. The scan deliberately covered interpretability, uncertainty evaluation, 3D/scientific world modeling, medical VLMs, neuro/cognitive modeling, generative media, continual learning, and robotics/VLA. Robotics/VLA had many fresh titles in the June 26 arXiv batch, including world-action and VLA safety work, but none beat the best non-robotics mechanisms today after the topic-balance guardrail.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv pages were reachable for the three preserved arXiv IDs, and I used them as a reachability supplement. Discovery therefore relied on arXiv recent category listings, arXiv abstract pages, downloaded arXiv PDFs, and one direct project page check for PhysiFormer. Discovery quality may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

At 08:00 Pacific on Sunday, June 28, arXiv's visible recent AI/ML/CV/CL/RO/eess/q-bio lists were still anchored on the Friday, June 26 batch. I treated today's run as a second-pass scout over candidates not already preserved in the June 26 and June 27 digests. I inspected full PDFs, with targeted reads through methods, experiments, results, ablations, and limitations, for **Beyond the Hard Budget**, **PhysiFormer**, **Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification**, and **TAVR-VLM**. I also scanned title listings across the relevant lanes, including medical imaging, neuro/cognitive systems, 3D/video generation, robotics/VLA, uncertainty evaluation, interpretability, and scientific ML. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

**Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification** is the most relevant paper today. It gives a decision-theoretic way to ask whether an uncertainty metric actually ranks models by downstream usefulness, then shows why many standard scores are misaligned or secretly encode strange priors.

**PhysiFormer** is the strongest world-model mechanism. It predicts full 3D mesh trajectories directly in world coordinates instead of doing view-bound video prediction or autoregressive coordinate rollout.

**Beyond the Hard Budget** is the strongest interpretability training detail. It shows Top-k SAEs still benefit from soft regularization when the pressure is applied to pre-selection activations and masked to batch-active units.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification**

**Verdict:** must read, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it turns uncertainty evaluation into an explicit claim about downstream utility. The useful move is not another calibration number; it is exposing the decision prior a metric silently optimizes.

### 2. **PhysiFormer: Learning to Simulate Mechanics in World Space**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for geometry-level world models.

Why it matters: it models physical dynamics in a state space that actually carries the structure: mesh vertices in world coordinates. Full-trajectory diffusion avoids the compounding failures of autoregressive rollouts in the paper's setup.

### 3. **Beyond the Hard Budget: Sparsity Regularizers for More Interpretable Top-k Sparse Autoencoders**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for SAE training hygiene.

Why it matters: it shows that hard sparsity is not enough. The unselected activation tail, dead-unit dynamics, and effective support shape whether sparse features are clean enough to inspect.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Decision-Aligned UQ.

The steal is the metric audit. If a score is used to decide whether an agent should act, ask for help, route to another model, retrieve more evidence, or abstain, the score should declare which decision family it serves. "Good calibration" is not the same thing as "useful for this decision."

PhysiFormer gives the representation version of the same lesson. If the goal is physical reasoning, use a state space where geometry and motion are first-class. Beyond the Hard Budget gives the feature-dictionary version: sparse does not automatically mean clean, and the regularizer has to target the part of the code where the failure lives.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Decision-Aligned UQ** is strong because it gives a formal test for whether an uncertainty metric preserves expected downstream utility under a prior over decision parameters. The paper then uses that test to show that common metrics are often not aligned with common decision families or are aligned only under pathological priors. Its proposed prior-weighted utility metrics are proper scoring rules by construction and are empirically better aligned with controlled utilities and applied economic case studies. The caveat is that prior elicitation becomes part of evaluation, and no single PWU metric can cover all deployment objectives.

**PhysiFormer** is strong because it changes the modeling substrate. It predicts full future vertex trajectories in world coordinates, conditioned on initial positions, velocities, and material type, using a diffusion transformer with spatial, object-level, and temporal attention. On the 10k rigid dataset, it beats autoregressive baselines on long-horizon MSE and rigidity loss, and the paper shows qualitative generalization to unseen geometries, more objects, and mixed materials. The caveat is serious: it is still simulator-trained, 49-frame, bounded-environment dynamics with best performance around the tested mesh scale, and the authors report spurious contacts, interpenetration, and rare orientation discontinuities.

**Beyond the Hard Budget** is strong because it names a subtle Top-k SAE failure: the model can satisfy the k budget while leaving noisy off-support activations and brittle dependence on the training k. The off-support l1 regularizer improves monosemanticity and class purity most; the l1/l2 ratio regularizer concentrates information and improves robustness to inference-time k changes. The active-unit mask ablation is the key evidence: without the mask, regularization kills many more units. The caveat is scope: vision embeddings, proxy interpretability metrics, and no causal steering tests.

**TAVR-VLM** was the strongest healthcare runner-up. Its useful mechanism is a "risk -> region -> word" grounding path: predict procedural risk, use it to select risk-relevant anatomical evidence, and constrain clinically salient token grounding inside that support. The paper reports lower hallucination and better mIoU on a 1,482-patient multimodal TAVR cohort. I did not preserve it as a full note because the dataset is private/new, external validation is future work, and the evidence is more domain-system packaging than broadly reusable evaluation or representation mechanism.

**Robotics/VLA** was deliberately capped today. The cs.RO listing was dense with continual imitation, VLA routing, embodied test-time scaling, physical feasibility, tactile WAM, and manipulation benchmarks. Several are probably worth later inspection, but after two robotics-heavy months and two strong non-robotics days, none cleared a higher bar than the three preserved mechanisms.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all make the hidden coordinate system visible. Decision-Aligned UQ says an uncertainty metric is secretly a decision prior, so write that prior down or stop pretending the metric is deployment-neutral. PhysiFormer says physical prediction should happen in world-space geometry, not in pixels when mesh state is available. Beyond the Hard Budget says Top-k sparsity is only a hard cardinality rule; feature cleanliness still depends on how the unused activation tail is shaped. Same rule across levels: do not trust structure just because the paper named it; check whether the coordinates make the claimed behavior possible.

## Detailed notes

- [PhysiFormer note](../paper_notes/physiformer_world_space_mechanics_diffusion.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-03-27

## Theme
Today’s useful papers are all really about one question: where does the structure live? In the strongest case, it lives in the training signal and latent state, not in slow theatrical inference. In the weaker-but-still-useful cases, it lives in geometric constraints or in repurposed generative features. The common lesson is harsh: a lot of current “world model” and “3D-aware” work is still selling outputs, while the interesting papers are changing the representation or constraint object itself.

## Short overview
Today’s strongest paper is **Fast-WAM: Do World Action Models Need Test-time Future Imagination?** It asks a real question instead of decorating a familiar pipeline: if world-action models help, is that because they explicitly imagine futures at inference time, or because video co-training shapes better internal state during training? Their answer is the useful one. Keep the world-model objective, drop the expensive test-time future generation, and most of the benefit remains. That matters because it cuts through a lot of unnecessary generative theater in embodied control.

The second worthwhile paper is **VEGA-3D: Generation Models Know Space**. This is more adjacent than direct, but it is still worth preserving because it treats video generators as sources of geometric priors rather than as output machines. The mechanism is simple enough to matter: extract intermediate spatiotemporal features from a frozen video diffusion model, fuse them with semantic vision features, and use that to improve spatial reasoning and scene understanding. The paper is strongest as a representation argument, not as proof that video generators are full world models.

The third paper worth logging is **Interact3D: Compositional 3D Generation of Interactive Objects**. It is not conceptually as deep as the first two, but it does something many “compositional 3D” papers avoid: it imposes explicit geometric alignment and collision penalties instead of hoping composition emerges from raw generation. The agentic-refinement layer is less interesting than the registration-plus-SDF core.

## Ranked papers

1. **Fast-WAM: Do World Action Models Need Test-time Future Imagination?**  
   - Verdict: **Highly relevant**  
   - Role: **Directly relevant**  
   - Why it matters: It argues that the benefit of WAMs mostly comes from training-time video co-modeling, not from slow imagine-then-execute inference.

2. **VEGA-3D: Generation Models Know Space: Unleashing Implicit 3D Priors for Scene Understanding**  
   - Verdict: **Useful**  
   - Role: **Adjacent inspiration**  
   - Why it matters: It repurposes video-generation features as geometric priors for downstream spatial reasoning, which is a cleaner use of generative models than simply making prettier outputs.

3. **Interact3D: Compositional 3D Generation of Interactive Objects**  
   - Verdict: **Useful**  
   - Role: **Adjacent inspiration**  
   - Why it matters: It treats compositional 3D generation as constrained registration and collision-aware optimization, not just latent scene vibes.

## Most relevant to cabbageland
**Fast-WAM** is the best fit. The important claim is not “we are faster.” The important claim is that explicit future imagination at inference time may be mostly optional once video modeling has already shaped the latent representation during training. If that survives broader scrutiny, it is a strong argument for separating representation learning from decision-time rollout cost.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact
- **World-model framing:** Fast-WAM is a useful citation against the lazy assumption that embodied world models need visible imagined futures at deployment time. It sharpens the distinction between training objective and inference contract.
- **Representation reuse:** VEGA-3D is useful if we need to argue that generative models may contain transferable spatial priors even when explicit 3D supervision is scarce.
- **Constraint-first 3D generation:** Interact3D is a reminder that explicit registration and collision penalties still beat vague compositional branding when geometry actually matters.
- **Confidence note:** I inspected substantial method text for **Fast-WAM**, **VEGA-3D**, and **Interact3D** via arXiv HTML/text, not just abstracts. I did **not** inspect every appendix/result table in full, so the mechanism judgments are stronger than my confidence in every reported metric.

## One-paragraph takeaway
The real split today is between papers that use generation as computation and papers that use generation as costume. **Fast-WAM** is the clearest win because it tests whether imagined futures are doing real work and finds that much of the value may already be baked into the representation learned during training. **VEGA-3D** is useful because it mines geometric priors from a frozen video generator instead of pretending language-only reasoning will discover spatial structure by moral effort. **Interact3D** is useful in a more old-fashioned way: it replaces compositional hand-waving with explicit alignment and collision constraints. The shared lesson is simple: if a paper claims structure, check whether it changes the latent state, the constraint object, or the inference contract. If not, it is probably mostly branding.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-14

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **small interfaces beat decorative generality when they are tested honestly**. There is no fresh Sunday arXiv batch in the scoped categories, so today's scan revisited the current June 10-11 arXiv robotics/CV/AI/CL batch and avoided papers already preserved in the June 12-13 digests. **muVLA** is the strongest paper because it isolates recurrence itself inside a pretrained VLA and shows exactly where minimal latent memory helps and where it fails. **Sparse2Act** is the strongest representation note because it uses task-space robot actions as supervision for sparse 3D features, rather than hoping reconstruction or downstream behavior cloning will discover control relevance. **DIRECT** is the best adjacent systems note: test-time compute should be routed by task demand, not paid uniformly as a tax.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable at the homepage level, but the lightweight fetched `/search` URL returned 404 again, so it was not useful for discovery. The arXiv API `submittedDate:[202606120000 TO 202606142359]` query over relevant categories returned zero entries even though the arXiv recent category pages listed the Friday June 12 batch, so today's discovery used arXiv recent category pages plus direct arXiv pages and PDFs. I inspected full arXiv PDFs for **muVLA: On Recurrent Memory for Partially Observable Manipulation in VLA Models**, **Improving Robotic Generalist Policies via Flow Reversal Steering**, **Sparse2Act: Learning Action-Aligned Sparse 3D Representations for Cross-Domain Robot Manipulation**, **Mana: Dexterous Manipulation of Articulated Tools**, **DIRECT: When and Where Should You Allocate Test-Time Compute in Embodied Planners?**, **SERF: Spatiotemporal Environment and Robot Feature Map for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation**, and **MCR-Bionic Hand: Anatomical Structural Priors for Dexterous Manipulation**. muVLA and Sparse2Act are preserved today.

**muVLA** is the strongest direct hit. It adds a small bank of recurrent memory tokens to OpenVLA-OFT and deliberately avoids retrieval modules, compression heads, hierarchical memory, and auxiliary objectives. The payoff is a cleaner measurement: minimal recurrence lifts partially observable MIKASA-Robo training tasks sharply, transfers modestly to held-out tasks with matching memory semantics, and mostly fails when the memory semantics change. That limit is the value. The paper gives future VLA memory work a baseline and a warning: if a fancier memory system cannot beat tiny recurrent tokens under the same cadence and latency budget, it is probably ornament.

**Sparse2Act** is the best representation paper today. It pretrains sparse point-cloud encoders by masking 3D tokens and predicting one-step task-space end-effector actions, then transfers only the encoder initialization into downstream policies. The ablations are the useful part: action-only and reconstruction-only help, but masked action alignment helps far more, and the gain persists with simplified downstream decoders. The design lesson is portable: use robot action to organize geometry around control, then let the downstream policy choose its own action parameterization.

**DIRECT** is adjacent but practically important. It treats the high-level embodied planner as a routed variable across reasoning depth, model size, and memory history. The paper's best claim is not "bigger reasoning helps"; it is the opposite: compute axes help on different task types and can hurt or waste latency elsewhere. A lightweight multimodal router recovers much of the expensive planner's success at lower cost in simulation and Franka DROID experiments. This is more systems and deployment than core representation, so I did not preserve a separate note today, but the framing is worth stealing.

**Flow Reversal Steering** is good policy-improvement material. It reverses a flow-matching VLA from coarse reference actions into latent noise, then denoises back into in-distribution actions that follow the rough semantic direction. It is especially useful for turning human or VLM guidance into noise-space BC or RL warm starts. I am not preserving it today because it is a steering wrapper over a behavioral prior rather than a stronger state, memory, or representation interface.

**SERF** is a strong explicit-memory mobile-manipulation paper, but with simulation caveats. It builds a spatiotemporal feature map of environment and robot neural points, updates environment points by object-level SE(3) tracking and robot points by forward kinematics, then conditions a VLA on map tokens. The idea is aligned with cabbageland: persistent spatial memory should be an input, not hidden in image history. The limitation is also clear: prior map features, privileged simulator instance labels, rigid-object updates, and no real-world mobile-manipulation validation yet.

**Mana** and **MCR-Bionic Hand** are useful physical-structure papers. Mana turns articulated tool manipulation into an animation-like data pipeline: human marks functional affordances, the system samples grasp keyframes, plans geometric phases, and uses RL only for short contact-rich transitions before training a point-cloud diffusion policy for zero-shot sim-to-real. MCR-Bionic is more hardware/anatomy than learning: it argues that wrist-finger tenodesis, extensor hoods, and intrinsic pathways are physical computation, not mere biomimetic decoration. Both are adjacent inspiration for "structure does work," but neither displaces today's two preserved representation/memory papers.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **muVLA: On Recurrent Memory for Partially Observable Manipulation in VLA Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it isolates recurrent memory as the only major treatment inside a pretrained VLA, showing both the real gains and the semantic-transfer limits of minimal latent recurrence.

### 2. **Sparse2Act: Learning Action-Aligned Sparse 3D Representations for Cross-Domain Robot Manipulation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it uses task-space robot actions as geometric supervision for sparse 3D encoder pretraining, creating a reusable representation shaped around controllable workspace motion.

### 3. **DIRECT: When and Where Should You Allocate Test-Time Compute in Embodied Planners?**

**Verdict:** adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it makes test-time compute a routed interface with task-contingent value, instead of treating chain-of-thought, bigger models, or longer memory as uniformly good.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** muVLA.

The steal-worthy idea is the controlled memory baseline. VLA memory papers should not get to hide behind a bundle of recurrence, retrieval, compression, scratchpads, and auxiliary losses. First ask: what happens if the same backbone gets only a few recurrent tokens, temporal training order, an action-copy guard, and a sane update cadence? muVLA says that buys a lot on trained partial-observability structures, a little on matched variants, and not much on genuinely new memory semantics.

Sparse2Act adds the representation companion. If the system has a metric 3D observation, action should supervise the representation before the policy head starts learning task behavior. Geometry is not merely something to reconstruct; it is a workspace for possible motion.

DIRECT adds the deployment companion. Memory, thinking, and model size are not moral virtues. They are budgeted resources. Route them when the task asks for them, and do not pay for them when the scene is simple.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**muVLA** raises the baseline for VLA memory claims. Any new memory architecture should compare against minimal recurrent tokens under matched inference cadence and should report semantic-shift splits, not only average held-out task success.

**Sparse2Act** raises the baseline for sparse 3D representation learning. Reconstruction and dynamics pretraining are not enough when the claimed use is manipulation; action-aligned geometry should be in the comparison set.

**DIRECT** sharpens test-time compute framing. It is not enough to say chain-of-thought, larger planners, or longer memory improve average success. A robot planner needs a success-cost frontier and a routing policy.

**SERF** is useful framing for persistent spatial memory, but the privileged-map caveats matter. It supports the argument that VLA policies need explicit spatial state, while also reminding us that map construction assumptions can dominate the comparison.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **muVLA** because it gives VLA memory a controlled lower bound: tiny recurrent tokens can be powerful, but they do not magically generalize to new memory semantics. **Sparse2Act** is the representation note to keep because it uses robot action to shape sparse 3D geometry around control before downstream policy training. **DIRECT** is the adjacent systems lesson: expensive reasoning, bigger planners, and longer memory should be routed by task demand. The common thread is that useful long-horizon systems need small explicit interfaces with honest budgets, not bigger hidden mush.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-11

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **the world-action interface is becoming the actual research object**. **Making Foresight Actionable** is the strongest paper because it does not accept "the world model made a plausible video" as evidence that the action head can use the representation. It probes where action attention and causal sensitivity land, then regularizes WAM hidden states toward spatially coherent DINOv2 features so the action decoder reads task-relevant interaction regions. **World Pilot** is the complementary integration recipe: route a WAM's scene-evolution latent into VLA hidden states and its anticipated trajectory into the action generator as a soft prior. **DAM-VLA** is the sensor-time version of the same idea: stop forcing vision, language, force, proprioception, and action onto one synchronous clock, and let each modality keep its own buffer and update rhythm.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable at the site level. Discovery and inspection for this run used arXiv API search over the June 8-10, 2026 batch plus direct arXiv PDFs. I inspected full arXiv PDFs for **Making Foresight Actionable: Repurposing Representation Alignment in World Action Models**, **World Pilot: Steering Vision-Language-Action Models with World-Action Priors**, **DAM-VLA: Decoupled Asynchronous Multimodal Vision Language Action model**, **PLUME: Probabilistic Latent Unified World Modeling and Parameter Estimation for Multi-Finger Manipulation**, **DIRECT: When and Where Should You Allocate Test-Time Compute in Embodied Planners?**, **Slots, Transitions, Loops: Learning Composable World Models for ARC**, **World Model Self-Distillation: Training World Models to Solve General Tasks**, **VICX: Generalizable Robot Manipulation via Video Generation and In-Context Operator Network**, **VLGA: Vision-Language-Geometry-Action Models for Autonomous Driving**, **ATM: Action-Consistency Transfer Matrix for Diagnosing and Improving Latent World Models**, **Plan-and-Verify Video Reward Reasoning with Spatio-Temporal Scene Graph Grounding**, **ISAP-3D: Identity-Slot Aligned Part-Aware 3D Generation**, and **CP4D: Compositional Physics-aware 4D Scene Generation**. AGRA, World Pilot, and DAM-VLA are preserved today.

**Making Foresight Actionable** is the strongest direct hit. The paper diagnoses a concrete failure mode in world-action models: a WAM can generate a plausible future while the action decoder attends to background, static hands, or other task-irrelevant regions. AGRA adds an auxiliary alignment loss between selected video-diffusion hidden states and DINOv2 patch features, which makes the feature field more spatially coherent and action-readable. The paper's best contribution is not the headline success number; it is the attention plus causal-intervention audit that turns "world model features" into something testable.

**World Pilot** is the best companion integration paper. It keeps the WAM frozen and injects two priors into a VLA: Latent Steering routes the scene-evolution latent through residual cross-attention into VLM hidden states, while Action Steering compresses the WAM's anticipated trajectory into a single prefix token for the flow-matching action generator. The ablations are useful: latent injection beats decoded future images, a single trajectory token beats per-step or raw trajectory conditioning, and even a scene-prediction-only Cosmos model helps before action post-training.

**DAM-VLA** is the strongest asynchronous multimodal VLA paper. Its argument is clean: a synchronous VLA oversamples slow vision and language, undersamples fast contact signals, and gates action generation on a complete observation bundle. DAM-VLA keeps per-modality latent buffers, refreshes them at their sensor rates, and lets the action head read them continuously through gated cross-attention. The real-robot evidence is small but sharp: seven contact-rich tasks, 15 trials each, and a large gap between the full model and synchronous or concatenation baselines.

**PLUME** is strong adjacent inspiration and may deserve a later dedicated note. It learns a latent belief over physical parameters and rewards, updates that belief online with a flow-matching world model, and plans with likelihood-penalized rollouts. The hardware screwdriver result is especially relevant for explicit physical state. I am not preserving it today because the top three form a tighter VLA/WAM interface story, not because PLUME is weak.

**DIRECT** is strong systems framing for embodied planner deployment. The key point is that test-time compute has different capability profiles depending on whether it is reasoning depth, model size, or memory history. The router is useful, but it is more about compute allocation for high-level planners than about state/action representation.

**Loop-OWM** is useful compositional-reasoning inspiration. It frames ARC as object-centric transition learning over structured visual-symbolic states. I am not promoting it above today's robotics papers because the internal recurrent steps are not yet semantically stable, and the result is more a controlled reasoning lens than an embodied mechanism.

**World Model Self-Distillation**, **VICX**, **VLGA**, **ATM**, **SG-PVR**, **ISAP-3D**, and **CP4D** are all citation material for narrower purposes: data-free video-world-model task transfer, video-plan-to-trajectory grounding, dense driving geometry supervision, latent-world-model diagnostics, structured video reward reasoning, identity-slot 3D parts, and physics-aware 4D composition. None displaced the three preserved notes today.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Making Foresight Actionable: Repurposing Representation Alignment in World Action Models**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it shows that predictive visual futures are not enough; the world-action interface must expose interaction-relevant, action-readable structure.

### 2. **World Pilot: Steering Vision-Language-Action Models with World-Action Priors**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it gives a concrete modular recipe for steering a VLA with WAM priors at the perception and action-generation layers without co-training the WAM.

### 3. **DAM-VLA: Decoupled Asynchronous Multimodal Vision Language Action model**

**Verdict:** highly relevant for multimodal VLA architecture.

Why it matters: it makes sensor timing and memory horizon explicit instead of flattening heterogeneous modalities into one synchronous token stream.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Making Foresight Actionable.

The steal-worthy idea is to audit the interface, not just the rollout. If a world model's hidden states are supposed to guide action, ask whether perturbing task-critical interaction tokens changes the action more than perturbing background tokens. Ask whether action-head attention lands on the contact site. If the answer is no, the system has a world-model branding problem, not a working action interface.

World Pilot then shows how to route priors when the interface is usable: scene-evolution latents belong near perception tokens, while coarse motion priors belong near the action generator. DAM-VLA adds the timing lesson: a modality is not just another input field. It has a natural update rate, retention horizon, and failure mode.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Making Foresight Actionable** raises the baseline for WAM papers. A plausible generated future is no longer enough. Papers should show whether the action decoder uses the future representation in task-relevant regions, and whether background perturbations causally disturb actions.

**World Pilot** raises the baseline for WAM-to-VLA fusion. Future images are a weak interface if the latent already contains the useful dynamics and the decoded image adds artifacts. The ablation that a single trajectory-level token beats per-step trajectory conditioning is also useful: priors should steer, not shackle, the action generator.

**DAM-VLA** raises the baseline for multimodal VLAs with force, tactile, or proprioceptive streams. Synchronous concatenation is now a suspect baseline for contact-rich tasks. A stronger comparison needs native-rate buffers, sparse visual re-encoding, and modality-specific gates.

**PLUME** is worth citing when the claim is about physical parameter uncertainty. If a task's correct strategy depends on friction, object shape, or resistance, a parameter-agnostic policy is a weak baseline.

**DIRECT** is useful when arguing that "more thinking" or "more memory" should be routed by task demand rather than paid on every step.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **Making Foresight Actionable** because it makes the world-action interface inspectable: a useful future representation should focus the action head on interaction regions and be causally robust to irrelevant background changes. **World Pilot** is the matching integration recipe, routing WAM latents and trajectory priors into different parts of a VLA. **DAM-VLA** generalizes the same taste to multimodal timing, with per-modality buffers and gated updates instead of synchronous token mush. The common lesson is blunt: a "world model" only matters when its hidden state reaches the control computation in the right form, at the right layer, and at the right time.

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-14

## Theme

Today’s signal is **explicit memory and explicit scene structure earning their keep, while another supposed world model mostly looks like fancy view synthesis**. The strongest paper is **Retrieve-then-Steer** because it turns repeated deployment into a concrete non-parametric adaptation loop instead of pretending every robotic episode is independent. **Flame3D** is the best adjacent paper because it makes a real argument for editable 3D memory plus composable tools over brute-force 3D-language finetuning. **RoboMemArena** is useful as benchmark infrastructure, but its main baseline contribution is less convincing than the benchmark itself. **Embody4D** has some engineering value, but I do not think it really upgrades the conceptual standard for embodied world models.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run and was unavailable because the current environment is missing a Brave API key. I therefore used direct arXiv discovery and inspected accessible arXiv abstracts plus substantial HTML full text for **Retrieve-then-Steer: Online Success Memory for Test-Time Adaptation of Generative VLAs**, **Flame3D: Zero-shot Compositional Reasoning of 3D Scenes with Agentic Language Models**, **RoboMemArena: A Comprehensive and Challenging Robotic Memory Benchmark**, and **Embody4D: A Generalist 4D World Model for Embodied AI**.

**Retrieve-then-Steer** is the most relevant paper today. Its central move is simple and good: if a frozen generative VLA operates repeatedly in the same environment, successful executions should become reusable evidence instead of discarded episodes. The paper stores progress-calibrated successful observation-action segments, retrieves state-relevant chunks at inference, filters inconsistent candidates, aggregates them into an elite prior, and injects that prior into the intermediate state of the flow-matching sampler with confidence-adaptive strength. That is not a deep new memory architecture, but it is a clean mechanism with a believable deployment story.

**Flame3D** is more adjacent to cabbageland, but honestly more interesting than a lot of trained 3D-language mush. It builds an explicit visual-textual 3D scene memory, exposes it through spatial tools, and lets a tool-calling multimodal model synthesize new spatial programs at inference time. The strongest part is not the benchmark score. It is the insistence that editable explicit memory plus composable operations may be a better path for open-ended 3D reasoning than endlessly aligning point-cloud tokens into another latent soup.

**RoboMemArena** looks worthwhile as benchmark scaffolding. The benchmark design itself is the main contribution: long trajectories, a high fraction of genuinely memory-dependent subtasks, multimodal memory annotations, and paired real-world tasks. I am less convinced by the accompanying **PrediMem** baseline as a lasting architectural contribution, but the benchmark seems useful for forcing future memory papers to confront something harder than toy recall.

**Embody4D** is the weakest of the serious candidates. It is competent engineering around monocular-to-novel-view video synthesis for embodied scenes, with compositional data synthesis, confidence-aware noise injection, and interaction-aware attention. But the paper still mostly cashes out as view-consistent video generation. Calling that a “generalist 4D world model” feels too generous unless downstream planning really depends on explicit predictive state rather than prettier generated views.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Retrieve-then-Steer: Online Success Memory for Test-Time Adaptation of Generative VLAs**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it treats persistent deployment as a memory problem and gives a concrete non-parametric mechanism for reusing successful local experience without retraining the policy.

### 2. **Flame3D: Zero-shot Compositional Reasoning of 3D Scenes with Agentic Language Models**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it argues, with a fairly explicit mechanism, that editable 3D memory and composable tool abstractions may beat another round of expensive 3D-language finetuning for open-ended scene reasoning.

### 3. **RoboMemArena: A Comprehensive and Challenging Robotic Memory Benchmark**

**Verdict:** mostly citation material, but good citation material.

Why it matters: the benchmark could become a better place to test whether robotic memory claims are real, especially for long-horizon partial observability.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Retrieve-then-Steer.

The core reason is that it gives memory a narrow, operational job instead of a ceremonial one. The paper does not claim to solve long-horizon reasoning in general. It claims that in repeated local deployment, successful past action segments are environment-verified evidence that can steer future action generation. That is a modest claim, but it is the right kind of modest. The retrieval target is concrete, the filtering story is legible, and the guidance enters the sampler in a way that preserves observation-conditioned refinement instead of replacing it with nearest-neighbor imitation.

I also like the paper’s deployment framing. Too many robotics evaluations pretend each test episode is independent even when the real use case is repetitive work in the same or slowly changing environment. This paper explicitly says that assumption is wrong and builds around the correction. The main caveat is that the memory object here is still just successful observation-action segments, not a richer structured state, so the reuse mechanism may saturate once tasks require deeper causal abstraction rather than local behavioral priors.

My confidence is fairly high on the mechanism description because I inspected the abstract, introduction, method sections on memory construction, retrieval filtering, and confidence-adaptive guidance in the arXiv HTML. My confidence is lower on the exact strength of the empirical gains because I did not fully audit every experimental table and appendix detail.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

The main framing update is that some “test-time adaptation” for VLAs should be understood less as parameter editing and more as **memory-guided sampling control under persistent deployment**. Retrieve-then-Steer is useful because it makes that framing explicit and concrete.

Flame3D sharpens a different but related point. If a paper claims compositional 3D reasoning, it should probably expose an explicit scene memory and actual operations over that memory, not just hide 3D inside point-cloud tokens and hope the language model discovers structure by osmosis. Whether Flame3D fully wins that argument remains open, but at least it is fighting on the right terrain.

RoboMemArena mostly affects baseline expectations. A memory paper that only looks good on short, weakly history-dependent tasks should now look less impressive. Embody4D is the negative framing update: better multi-view video synthesis is not automatically the same thing as a better world model, and cabbageland should keep pushing on that distinction.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **Retrieve-then-Steer** because it treats repeated robotic deployment as a real memory reuse problem and implements a clean way to bias a frozen generative VLA toward previously successful local behavior without retraining. **Flame3D** is the most interesting adjacent paper because it bets on explicit editable 3D memory plus composable tools instead of more 3D-native latent branding. **RoboMemArena** is mainly valuable as benchmark pressure, not as an architectural leap. **Embody4D** looks like competent view-synthesis engineering but not yet a convincing upgrade in explicit predictive state. The common lesson is that structure matters when it constrains action or reasoning in a legible way, not when it is just another glossy rendering pipeline.

- [Flame3D note](../paper_notes/flame3d_zero_shot_compositional_reasoning_3d_scenes_agentic_language_models.md)

# Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-17

## Theme

Today’s signal is **trying to cash out embodiment hype into usable structure**. The strongest paper is **Articraft** because it treats articulated-asset generation as constrained code synthesis with validation, not as vague multimodal prompting. **Hand-in-the-Loop** is the best adjacent paper because it attacks a real failure mode in dexterous intervention, takeover discontinuity, instead of merely reporting another dexterous VLA score. **Evo-Depth** is useful but narrower: a pragmatic depth-bias retrofit for VLAs rather than a deeper rethink of representation.

## Short overview

Brave Search was unavailable in this run because the current environment is missing a Brave API key, so discovery was narrower than usual and relied on direct recent arXiv inspection. I fetched accessible arXiv pages and inspected substantial arXiv HTML for **An Agentic System for Scalable Articulated 3D Asset Generation**, **Hand-in-the-Loop: Improving Dexterous VLA via Seamless Interventional Correction**, **Evo-Depth: A Lightweight Depth-Enhanced Vision-Language-Action Model**, and **A Unified Embodied Intelligence Model for Understanding, Reasoning, Imagination and Action**. Confidence is strongest on the high-level mechanism and contribution framing, and weaker on appendix-level ablations because I did not fully audit the later experimental sections.

**Articraft** is the most relevant paper today. Its core move is to reduce articulated-object generation to writing a single executable program against a deliberately narrow SDK, then let an LLM iterate inside a harness that validates geometry, articulation, and tests. That is much better than the usual "agentic 3D" mush because the representation does real work: the asset is code, joints are explicit, and failures are exposed through a structured execution environment rather than aesthetic human preference.

**Hand-in-the-Loop** is good adjacent robotics work. The useful contribution is not just "human in the loop" branding. It specifically addresses gesture jumps when a human takes over a dexterous policy mid-rollout by mapping *relative* fingertip motion at takeover time instead of snapping to the operator’s absolute hand pose, while arm corrections are injected as residual twists. That is a real systems mechanism for harvesting on-policy correction data without destroying the current grasp.

**Evo-Depth** is a respectable efficiency paper, but I would keep the enthusiasm calibrated. The idea is to inject lightweight implicit depth features from multi-view RGB into a 0.9B VLA through a modulation module rather than through a heavier explicit 3D stack. That is practically useful, especially if the reported memory and latency numbers hold up, but conceptually it is still a retrofit of spatial bias into an otherwise standard VLA pipeline.

**Pelican-Unified**, despite the grand claims, mostly reads like unification rhetoric plus a large shared stack. I did not preserve a note for it because the accessible text leaned much harder on manifesto framing than on a crisp new computational contract.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **An Agentic System for Scalable Articulated 3D Asset Generation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it turns articulated asset generation into executable, validated program synthesis with explicit joints, part structure, and tests.

### 2. **Hand-in-the-Loop: Improving Dexterous VLA via Seamless Interventional Correction**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it addresses a concrete intervention failure mode in high-DoF dexterous control and makes on-policy correction data collection less destructive.

### 3. **Evo-Depth: A Lightweight Depth-Enhanced Vision-Language-Action Model**

**Verdict:** useful, but mainly as an engineering recipe.

Why it matters: it offers a comparatively cheap way to bias VLA representations toward spatial grounding without adding explicit 3D sensors.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Articraft.

The useful part is not that it uses an LLM to make 3D stuff. Plenty of papers already do that in decorative ways. The useful part is that it makes the artifact itself legible and revisable by forcing generation through a constrained program with named parts, articulation objects, motion limits, and test hooks. That means the agent is not merely sampling geometry. It is authoring an explicit object model inside an environment that can say what failed.

That matters for cabbageland because it points to a broader design rule: if you want generative systems to produce reusable structure, give them a representation that supports decomposition, validation, and repair. The main caveat is that this is still synthetic data generation rather than learned embodied interaction, so the relevance is more about representation and agent harness design than about direct robot policy learning.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

The main framing update is that **"agentic" work becomes much more credible when the agent edits an executable structured object representation inside a narrow feedback loop**. Articraft is a useful rebuttal to both one-shot text-to-3D hype and to heavyweight pipelines that need Blender or image-based critique just to stay on the rails.

Hand-in-the-Loop sharpens a different point. If dexterous VLAs are going to learn from intervention, the intervention interface itself is part of the method. Abrupt authority transfer can destroy the very contacts you are trying to preserve, so relative retargeting and residual shared control deserve to be treated as core mechanism, not user-interface detail.

Evo-Depth mostly affects baselines and design priors. It suggests that some of the recent rush toward heavy geometry foundations for VLA spatial grounding may be overkill when a lighter implicit-depth path can buy a decent chunk of the gain.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today is **Articraft** because it gives the "agentic 3D generation" story an actual computational spine: explicit parts, explicit joints, explicit tests, and a harness that turns failure into structured repair rather than vibes. **Hand-in-the-Loop** is the strongest adjacent robotics paper because it solves a real takeover problem in dexterous intervention and turns that fix into better on-policy correction data. **Evo-Depth** is useful but narrower, a plausible lightweight depth bias for VLAs rather than a major representational shift. The broader lesson is that embodiment papers get more interesting when they stop chanting unification and start specifying the representation, control interface, or validation loop that really constrains the system.

# Daily Digest — 2026-04-17

## Theme

Today’s strongest pattern is anti-decorative structure. The papers worth keeping are not just saying “3D,” “reasoning,” or “RL” louder. R3D is useful because it shows that some supposed architectural limits in 3D policy learning were really training hygiene failures. StreamCacheVGGT is useful because it notices that bounded-memory streaming geometry should compress medium-value structure instead of only deleting tokens. The shortest-path paper matters because it isolates a recurring language-model embarrassment: models can transfer locally learned rules to new instances, but longer horizons still destabilize the composition.

## Short overview

Brave search was unavailable in this run because the Brave API key is missing, so discovery fell back to direct arXiv API queries plus primary-source inspection on arXiv abstract and PDF text. I inspected the abstract and first several PDF pages for all shortlisted papers, including introduction/method framing and early results discussion for R3D, StreamCacheVGGT, RAD-2, and Generalization in LLM Problem Solving: The Case of the Shortest Path. I did not fully audit appendices, every benchmark table, or implementation details hidden in supplements, so the judgments below are strongest on mechanism and framing, slightly softer on exact empirical margins.

The strongest paper today is **R3D: Revisiting 3D Policy Learning**. The useful claim is not “3D is good.” It is that the field may have misread a bunch of negative evidence because it was training stronger 3D backbones with bad normalization and weak augmentation. If the main reason PointNet kept winning was accidental optimization sabotage, then a lot of prior 3D-policy conclusions need recalibration.

**StreamCacheVGGT: Streaming Visual Geometry Transformers with Robust Scoring and Hybrid Cache Compression** is the cleanest adjacent systems idea. Its core move is simple and good: for streaming 3D geometry under fixed memory, don’t treat token management as keep-or-delete only. Score importance across layers to reduce noisy one-layer decisions, then merge medium-value tokens instead of throwing away distributed geometric context. That is exactly the kind of “explicit structure doing actual work” move worth preserving.

**Generalization in LLM Problem Solving: The Case of the Shortest Path** is the best reasoning paper in the batch. It uses a controlled shortest-path environment to separate spatial transfer from length scaling, then shows that reinforcement learning and inference-time tricks do not rescue the harder failure: recursive instability over longer horizons. The setup is synthetic, but the diagnosis is useful.

A nearby paper worth mentioning but not worth a full note today is **RAD-2: Scaling Reinforcement Learning in a Generator-Discriminator Framework**. The generator-discriminator split for driving is sensible, but the accessible text still reads more like a well-engineered planner stack than a deeper representational shift.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **R3D: Revisiting 3D Policy Learning**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it argues that some of 3D policy learning’s apparent scaling failures were self-inflicted by bad training choices rather than by 3D representations themselves.

### 2. **StreamCacheVGGT: Streaming Visual Geometry Transformers with Robust Scoring and Hybrid Cache Compression**

**Verdict:** useful.

### 3. **Generalization in LLM Problem Solving: The Case of the Shortest Path**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it gives a cleaner failure diagnosis for compositional generalization than most natural-language reasoning benchmarks manage.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant:** R3D.

The reason is not merely that it is another robotics paper. It challenges a deeper research-hygiene failure mode: people often attribute disappointing results to representation limits when the actual problem is an unstable training recipe. StreamCacheVGGT is the most steal-worthy systems paper because it treats memory pressure as a structured compression problem rather than a deletion game. R3D is framing pressure on a lot of recent 3D policy comparisons. If stronger backbones were being handicapped by BatchNorm and missing 3D augmentation, then “simple PointNet beats scalable 3D encoders” may have been a misleading lesson.

## One-paragraph takeaway

Today’s lesson is that explicit structure is most valuable when it corrects a specific failure mode rather than decorating a model with new nouns. R3D uses geometry plus better training hygiene to reopen the case for scalable 3D policies. StreamCacheVGGT uses cross-layer scoring and token merging to make bounded-memory geometry less lossy. # Daily Paper Digest — 2026-05-07

## Theme

Today’s best paper is a planning paper with an actual decomposition argument instead of generic hierarchy theater. **HDFlow: Hierarchical Diffusion-Flow Planning for Long-horizon Tasks** uses diffusion where diversity matters, high-level subgoal proposal, and rectified flow where speed matters, low-level dense trajectory generation. That division is not profound on its own, but the paper backs it with a reasonably explicit architecture, a contrastively shaped world-model latent space, and an energy-guided high-level planner. The rest of the shortlist is more mixed. **ConsisVLA-4D** has real structure in its multi-view semantic and geometric filtering stack, but the framing is a bit over-eager and the method still smells like a carefully engineered bundle around strong pretrained components. **From Pixels to Tokens** is the most useful framing paper of the day: not a big architecture leap, but a clean comparison study on latent-action supervision choices for VLAs.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first in this run, but discovery was blocked because the Brave Search API key is missing in the current environment. I then scouted recent arXiv submissions directly from recent cs.RO, cs.AI, and cs.CV listings, and inspected primary-source arXiv abstract pages plus accessible HTML method text where available.

I inspected the abstract and substantial method text for **HDFlow: Hierarchical Diffusion-Flow Planning for Long-horizon Tasks**, **ConsisVLA-4D: Advancing Spatiotemporal Consistency in Efficient 3D-Perception and 4D-Reasoning for Robotic Manipulation**, and **From Pixels to Tokens: A Systematic Study of Latent Action Supervision for Vision-Language-Action Models**. I also skimmed recent abstracts for **Driver-WM** and a few adjacent robotics entries, but they did not beat the main three for today’s digest.

**HDFlow** is the clearest direct hit. The main useful idea is not just “use a hierarchy,” it is that different levels of the hierarchy want different generative behavior. The paper uses a high-level diffusion planner for exploratory subgoal generation, then a low-level rectified-flow planner for fast dense trajectory synthesis, and adds an energy-based model to score strategic subgoal sequences. That is a more honest decomposition than papers that keep diffusion everywhere and call the result efficient.

**ConsisVLA-4D** is more of a structured VLA systems paper. The strongest part is its attempt to compress multi-view perception into instruction-filtered object-semantic tokens plus aggregated geometric tokens before action prediction, then use those for limited future-scene reasoning. The paper clearly wants to move beyond plain 2D VLA input-output mapping, and there is real engineering structure in CV-Aligner, CO-Fuser, and CS-Thinker. But it still relies heavily on a stack of pretrained perception modules, and the “4D reasoning” label looks somewhat more ambitious than the inspected mechanism.

**From Pixels to Tokens** is less exciting architecturally but more useful than its headline might suggest. It isolates four latent-action supervision strategies under one VLA baseline and reports a clean formulation-task split: image-derived latent actions help long-horizon reasoning and scene-level generalization, while action-derived latent tokens help harder motor control. That is exactly the kind of comparative result this literature usually avoids.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **HDFlow: Hierarchical Diffusion-Flow Planning for Long-horizon Tasks**

**Verdict:** highly relevant.

Why it matters: it actually assigns different model classes to different planning roles, uses a structured world-model latent space rather than raw observation planning, and introduces explicit high-level energy guidance instead of pretending plausible subgoals are automatically good subgoals.

### 2. **ConsisVLA-4D: Advancing Spatiotemporal Consistency in Efficient 3D-Perception and 4D-Reasoning for Robotic Manipulation**

**Verdict:** useful.

Why it matters: it is a serious attempt to make multi-view VLA perception more selective and more geometrically coherent without just stapling on full point-cloud pipelines or brute-force temporal context.

### 3. **From Pixels to Tokens: A Systematic Study of Latent Action Supervision for Vision-Language-Action Models**

**Verdict:** useful adjacent inspiration.

Why it matters: it is a rare comparative paper that tells you when different latent-action supervision schemes help, instead of just presenting one favored design as universally right.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** HDFlow.

The main reason is that the paper makes a clean claim cabbageland should care about: the right generative primitive depends on the level of abstraction. High-level planning wants diversity and strategic branching, so diffusion is a plausible fit. Low-level trajectory synthesis wants speed and a smoother deterministic path to an already chosen target, so rectified flow is a better fit. That is much more defensible than using one fashionable model class everywhere.

I also like that the world-model latent space is not treated as a neutral container. The paper explicitly adds a contrastive objective so intermediate successful states are organized relative to goals, and it adds an inverse-dynamics term to keep the latent useful for control. Then the high-level planner is guided by an energy model that is supposed to distinguish viable strategic sequences from plausible-looking dead ends. Whether that fully works in all regimes is another question, but at least the mechanism is legible.

The caveat is that I inspected the abstract, introduction, formal preliminaries, and a substantial portion of the method text from the arXiv HTML, including the world-model training objective, contrastive shaping, inverse-dynamics auxiliary loss, and the planner split. I did not audit every experiment table or appendix detail. So confidence is good on the architectural logic and weaker on the full empirical story.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

HDFlow sharpens a useful evaluation question for long-horizon generative planners: should the same generator family really handle exploratory subgoal search and time-sensitive dense control? If a paper says yes by default, it now has a stronger burden of proof. HDFlow’s hybrid answer is not the final word, but it is at least a coherent alternative.

ConsisVLA-4D matters more as systems framing than as a single clean steal. It pushes on the right weakness in current VLAs, shallow 2D perception plus weak future-scene reasoning, but it does so with a fairly assembled stack of SigLIP, DINOv2, VGGT, instruction filtering, view fusion, geometry fusion, and downstream reasoning tokens. Useful, yes. Conceptually clean, not entirely.

From Pixels to Tokens affects training taste more than benchmark rankings. It suggests that latent-action supervision should be chosen according to the failure mode you care about, rather than adopted as a generic badge of sophistication. That is a helpful correction for a literature that keeps turning intermediate tokens into branding.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best paper today earns attention by making a real decomposition choice instead of a decorative one. **HDFlow** argues that long-horizon planning should separate strategic subgoal exploration from fast dense execution and use different generative tools for each. **ConsisVLA-4D** is a worthwhile structured VLA paper, but it is more engineering bundle than crisp conceptual move. **From Pixels to Tokens** is the kind of comparative supervision paper that helps clear fog from the field, even if it is not an architectural landmark. The broader lesson is simple: when a paper claims hierarchy, consistency, or latent structure, check whether those words correspond to actual role separation and measurable mechanism, not just more modules.

# Daily Paper Digest - 2026-06-19

## Theme

Today's useful pattern is **state has to survive the moment it is not convenient**. The best papers do not ask whether a model can emit plausible surface behavior. They ask whether the hidden state, task state, or evaluation state remains explicit enough to be checked when the easy observation disappears.

I kept robotics/VLA work as a lane rather than the center. The scan deliberately covered video world-model evaluation, tool-using agents, generative-model evaluation, diffusion-LM transparency, surgical/medical deployment, neurosymbolic counterfactuals, long-video temporal reasoning, spatial tool-use agents, skill mining, and physical-AI serving. No robotics/VLA paper landed in the top three today.

## Short overview

Brave Search was attempted first through the OpenClaw web search provider and failed with provider `brave` / `missing_brave_api_key`. AlphaXiv was reachable for individual paper pages, but the fetched content was mostly title/navigation stubs rather than useful related-paper text. I used the arXiv API, arXiv new listings, individual AlphaXiv title checks, and direct arXiv PDFs for full-text inspection. Discovery may be narrower than a healthy Brave-plus-AlphaXiv run.

Full-text PDFs were available for the serious candidates. I inspected the full text, especially method, results, and limitations, for **Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core**, **LedgerAgent: Structured State for Policy-Adherent Tool-Calling Agents**, **The FID Lottery**, **How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?**, **TimeProVe**, **GEN-Guard**, **DeepSWIP**, **MemoryWAM**, **S-Agent**, **SoftSkill**, **Automating SKILL.md Generation**, and **Execution-State Capsules**. No preserved note today is abstract-only.

**Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core** is the most relevant paper today. It turns "world model" into an intervention test: move the camera away, return, and ask whether the object state kept evolving while unobserved. Across 9,600 videos from 23 models, the answer is mostly no; visible quality and re-observation access do not imply re-observed state correctness.

**LedgerAgent** is the cleanest agent-systems mechanism. It stores successful read-tool returns in a typed ledger, renders that observed state back into the prompt, and checks environment-changing calls against executable policy predicates before they touch the external system. It is not glamorous, but it is exactly the kind of explicit state boundary tool agents usually fake.

**The FID Lottery** is the strongest evaluation paper today. It treats FID as a random variable over both training seeds and sampling seeds, then shows that retraining the same recipe moves FID much more than redrawing samples from one fixed model. The useful lesson is not just "report error bars"; it is that many single-seed generative-model gains sit below the evaluation noise floor.

Several other papers were worth reading but stayed below the preservation line. **How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?** is a strong foundation-model behavior audit: the token bottleneck between denoising steps appears much more interpretable than the worst-case latent-reasoning story, but algorithmic transparency remains hard because the model can revise the whole canvas non-chronologically. **GEN-Guard** is a useful surgical-AI deployment paper because it names "performance leakage" in federated model selection and tests a client-blocked detection/correction stack; I kept it below the top three because the mechanism is more specialized. **TimeProVe** is a good long-video evidence search system, reducing VLM calls and cost through propose-then-verify temporal grounding, but it is less conceptually sharp than LedgerAgent today. **MemoryWAM** was the best robotics/VLA candidate, with hybrid recent-frame, anchor-frame, and gist-token memory for long-horizon manipulation, but it did not beat the non-robotics top three on transfer value.

## Ranked papers

### 1. **Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core**

**Verdict:** highly relevant, and the most relevant paper today.

Why it matters: it gives a direct benchmark shape for world-state persistence. A system that only resumes the last visible state when the camera returns is not modeling a world; it is replaying an observed shot.

### 2. **LedgerAgent: Structured State for Policy-Adherent Tool-Calling Agents**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as an agent architecture pattern.

Why it matters: it moves task state out of prompt soup and into a typed, inspectable ledger that gates external writes. This is the right design instinct for any agent that changes real state.

### 3. **The FID Lottery: Quantifying Hidden Randomness in Generative-Model Evaluation**

**Verdict:** highly relevant as an evaluation audit.

Why it matters: it shows that generative-model leaderboards can be reordered by training-seed randomness. If a claimed improvement is smaller than the measured seed floor, the paper has not earned the claim.

## Most relevant to cabbageland

**Most relevant today:** Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core.

The direct steal is the observability intervention. If a system claims to maintain state, hide the evidence temporarily, let the state evolve, then return and check the endpoint. This applies far beyond video: memory systems, agent ledgers, planning stacks, retrieval state, clinical monitors, and evaluation caches all need tests where the state is not continuously visible.

LedgerAgent contributes the complementary implementation pattern. Task-relevant facts should have stable addresses, update rules, and action-boundary checks. The agent can still use language reasoning, but the validity of external writes should not depend on the model re-reading an unstructured transcript and hoping it remembered the right JSON.

The FID Lottery contributes the statistical discipline. Do not compare single numbers when the training run itself is a draw. If the variance lives on the axis the paper did not sample, the leaderboard is measuring luck plus method.

## Novelty / framing / baseline impact

**Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core** raises the bar for world-model claims. WRBench separates camera execution, visible consistency, re-observation support, and re-observed state consistency instead of collapsing them into one attractive video score. The caveat is that this is a benchmark/diagnostic paper, not a new architecture, and the automatic evaluation still rests on human-calibrated judgments rather than a formal state oracle.

**LedgerAgent** is not novel because it invents "state"; it is novel because it enforces the boring boundary in the right place. Successful read-tool returns become schema-anchored state, and proposed write calls are checked against executable predicates before execution. The limitation is clear: the method only covers observed, structured, predicate-encoded state.

**The FID Lottery** is a useful correction to generative-model evaluation practice. It shows that sampling-seed error bars on one fixed network understate the uncertainty; training-seed variance is the larger lottery. The limitation is scope: the measured 1-2 percent coefficient-of-variation floor is for SiT flow-matching models on class-conditional ImageNet with Inception FID, not a universal constant.

**How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?** is the important runner-up. It suggests DiffusionGemma's intermediate denoising bottleneck can be compressed through a small set of interpretable likely tokens without much capability loss, reducing the apparent opaque serial-depth problem. The red flag is that similar monitorability on current evaluations does not settle single-canvas latent reasoning or future RL-trained diffusion reasoners.

**MemoryWAM** clears the robotics lane but not the top-three bar. Hybrid short-term, event-boundary, and gist-token memory is a real mechanism, and the latency/memory trade-off is useful. Still, today already had stronger non-robotics state papers, so another WAM note would have pulled the digest back toward its known robotics attractor.

## One-paragraph takeaway

The best papers today all punish fake state. **Current World Models Lack a Persistent State Core** asks whether a video model keeps an event endpoint alive when the camera is not watching. **LedgerAgent** asks whether a tool agent has a real observed-state object before it changes the world. **The FID Lottery** asks whether a generative-model claim survives the hidden state of training randomness. Different domains, same standard: if the state matters, isolate it, perturb observability, and make it carry the claim.

- [LedgerAgent note](../paper_notes/ledgeragent_structured_state_tool_calling_agents.md)
